```text
        +-- Treasury / ALM        VaR 20m, EVE sensitivity, NII sensitivity
              +-- Liquidity portfolio  DV01 1.5m/bp, credit spread CS01 0.3m/bp
```

The children's VaR limits (35m + 20m = 55m) exceed the parent's (50m). This is intentional: VaR diversifies, so the parent's actual VaR is below the sum of the children's. Each level is checked against its own limit using its own aggregated measure, rather than by summing children.

**Types of limits.**

| Limit type | Measures | Typical level |
|---|---|---|
| VaR / ES | Portfolio loss at a confidence level | Bank, division, desk |
| Stress loss | Loss under defined scenarios | Bank, division |
| Sensitivity | DV01, CS01, Vega, FX delta, by bucket | Desk, book |
| Stop-loss / drawdown | Cumulative loss over a period | Desk, trader |
| Notional / volume | Gross size of positions | Book, product |
| Concentration | Single issuer, sector, country | Bank, portfolio |
| Net open position | FX exposure | Desk, bank |
| Counterparty / issuer | Credit exposure | Counterparty group |

**Anatomy of a limit record.** In a limit system, each limit is a data object, typically with:

- the node in the hierarchy (bank, division, desk, book) and a scope filter (products, currencies, tenors);
- the metric and its calculation source;
- thresholds: warning level (for example 80% or 90%) and hard limit (100%);
- validity dates, currency, approver and approval date;
- whether the limit is checked pre-trade, intraday or end of day.

**Key takeaways**

- Limits cascade from the board's risk appetite to division, desk, book and trader levels.
- Diversifying measures (VaR, ES) are checked at each level on the aggregated portfolio; children's limits can sum above the parent.
- Different limit types control different risks: VaR, stress, sensitivities, stop-loss, notional, concentration.
- A limit is a governed data object with scope, metric, thresholds, validity and approval.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Why can't a bank rely only on a bank-wide VaR limit?
> 2. **Intermediate:** In the hierarchy above, the rates desk's DV01 is within its 2m limit, but both books are at 100% of their DV01 limits in the same direction. Is the desk limit then binding? What if the two books have opposite signs?
> 3. **Interview:** "Design the data model for a limit hierarchy that supports reorganizations without losing history." *Hint:* consider versioned hierarchy nodes with effective dates, limits attached to nodes rather than to people, scope expressed as filters on trade attributes, and audit records linking each breach to the limit version in force at the time.

#### Real-Time vs End-of-Day Limit Checks

**Why it matters.** A limit that is only checked the next morning cannot stop a trader from exceeding it today. But some measures, such as full revaluation VaR, take hours to compute. Banks therefore combine real-time checks for measures that can be computed quickly and end-of-day checks for measures that need the full risk engine. Choosing which limit is checked when, and how intraday approximations relate to official numbers, is a core design decision.

**Comparison.**

| Aspect | Real-time (pre-trade / intraday) | End-of-day (EOD) |
|---|---|---|
| Timing | Before or immediately after each trade | After the official close and batch run |
| Typical metrics | Notional, NOP, DV01, delta, counterparty PFE via add-ons, settlement limits | VaR, ES, stress tests, full-revaluation sensitivities |
| Accuracy | Approximate (sensitivities, add-ons) | Official, full revaluation |
| Data | Live trades and live or snapshot market data | Official closing market data, complete trade population |
| Purpose | Prevent breaches before they happen | Official measurement, regulatory and management reporting |
| Latency target | Milliseconds to seconds | Hours |

**Pre-trade vs post-trade.** A pre-trade check blocks or warns before the trade is executed (hard block for automated trading, warning for voice trades). A post-trade check runs immediately after booking and raises alerts but cannot prevent the trade.

**Architecture.**

```text
  Trading systems (FX, rates, MM)            Overnight batch
          | trade events                            |
          v                                         v
  +--------------------+                  +--------------------+
  | Event bus / stream |                  | Risk engine (VaR,  |
  +---------+----------+                  | ES, stress, sens.) |
            v                             +---------+----------+
  +--------------------+  incremental             |
  | Real-time limit    |  update of               v
  | engine (in-memory  |  positions      +--------------------+
  | positions, sens.)  |                 | EOD limit check    |
  +---------+----------+                 +---------+----------+
            |                                      |
            +---------------+----------------------+
                            v
                 +------------------------+
                 | Limit store, breaches, |
                 | workflow, dashboards   |
                 +------------------------+
                            ^
       start of day: real-time engine reloads official EOD positions
```

**Keeping the two consistent.** The real-time engine starts each day from the official EOD position and risk, then applies intraday trades incrementally (for example adding each trade's DV01 or delta). Intraday VaR can be approximated by combining the morning's scenario P&L vectors with sensitivity-based P&L vectors of new trades. Differences between intraday estimates and the next EOD figures should be monitored; a systematic gap indicates missing trades or model mismatches.

**Example.** At 10:15 a dealer requests a USD 50m purchase against EUR. The real-time engine converts it at the live EURUSD rate, adds it to the USD net position, recomputes per-currency and overall NOP in under a millisecond, finds USD utilization rising from 70% to 88% (above the 80% warning), and returns "approved with warning". The VaR impact is only measured precisely in the overnight run.

**Key takeaways**

- Real-time checks prevent breaches using fast, approximate metrics; EOD checks give official figures using full models.
- Pre-trade checks can block trades; post-trade checks only alert.
- Real-time engines start from official EOD positions and update incrementally.
- Monitoring the gap between intraday and EOD numbers detects data and model problems.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Classify each limit as more suited to real-time or EOD checking: per-currency NOP, 99% VaR, stressed loss, settlement limit, DV01.
> 2. **Intermediate:** A desk's intraday DV01 shows 1.8m/bp (limit 2m) at 17:00, but the official EOD figure is 2.15m/bp. List three possible causes.
> 3. **Interview:** "Design a real-time limit service that handles 2,000 trade events per second with sub-10 ms latency." *Hint:* in-memory positions partitioned by limit scope, idempotent event processing with sequence numbers, pre-computed per-trade sensitivities, snapshotting and replay for recovery, and a separate path for slow metrics.

#### Breach Detection and Escalation

**Why it matters.** A limit has no value if breaches go unnoticed or are noticed but ignored. Regulators expect that every breach is detected, recorded, escalated to the right level of authority within defined timeframes, explained and resolved, with a complete audit trail. Market risk scandals such as large unauthorized trading losses have often involved limits that were breached repeatedly without effective escalation.

**Statuses and breach types.**

- **Warning (soft breach):** utilization above a warning threshold (for example 80-90%). Informational, prompts attention.
- **Hard breach:** utilization above 100%.
- **Active breach:** caused by a new trade; usually treated more seriously because it was a decision.
- **Passive breach:** caused by market moves, model changes or limit reductions without new trading.
- **Temporary excess:** a breach pre-approved by an authorized person for a limited time, for example to execute a large client trade.

**Lifecycle.**

```text
  +----------+   detect    +----------+   notify    +--------------+
  | Within   |-----------> | Breach   |-----------> | Acknowledged |
  | limit    |             | detected |             | by owner     |
  +----------+             +----------+             +------+-------+
       ^                                                   |
       |                                                   v
       |        resolved            +-------------------------------+
       +----------------------------| Action: reduce position,      |
       |                            | approve temporary excess,     |
       |                            | or raise limit (with approval)|
       |                            +---------------+---------------+
       |                                            |
       |                     not resolved in time   v
       |                                    +---------------+
       +------------------------------------| Escalated to  |
                     resolved               | next level    |
                                            +---------------+
```

**Escalation matrix (illustrative).**

| Severity | Condition | Escalate to | Deadline |
|---|---|---|---|
| Warning | 90-100% | Desk head (notification) | Same day |
| Level 1 | 100-110%, active or passive | Desk head and market risk manager | Within 1 hour |
| Level 2 | 110-125%, or Level 1 open > 2 days | Head of business and CRO office | Same day |
| Level 3 | > 125%, or Level 2 open > 5 days, or bank-wide limit | CRO, ALCO / board risk committee | Immediately |

**False breaches.** A large share of alerts in practice come from data problems: stale market data, a trade booked twice, a missing hedge leg, a wrong limit scope. Systems should run data quality checks before raising breaches, label suspected data issues, and still record them so the issue is investigated rather than silently ignored.

**Avoiding alert flapping.** When utilization oscillates around 100%, a naive system creates and closes breaches repeatedly. Common remedies are a hysteresis band (a breach closes only below, say, 98%) and measuring breaches at defined checkpoints.

**Key takeaways**

- Breaches are classified by severity and cause (active vs passive), with temporary excesses requiring explicit approval.
- Escalation follows a documented matrix by severity and duration, up to the CRO and board.
- Every breach needs an acknowledged owner, an action and a complete audit trail.
- Data quality checks and hysteresis reduce false and flapping alerts.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** What is the difference between an active and a passive breach, and why are they often treated differently?
> 2. **Intermediate:** Using the matrix above, a desk's VaR has been at 105% for three days because of rising volatility. Who should now be informed, and what actions are available?
> 3. **Interview:** "Design the breach record and workflow so that an auditor can reconstruct any breach from two years ago." *Hint:* store the limit version, measured value and its source run, timestamps for each state change, who acknowledged and approved what, comments and attachments, and make records immutable (append-only events).

#### Limit Reservation and Release

**Why it matters.** Limits are shared resources. Several traders, systems and channels may draw on the same counterparty or desk limit at the same time. Without coordination, two traders can each see EUR 10m of headroom, each book EUR 8m, and together breach the limit by EUR 6m. Large deals also need limit capacity guaranteed in advance: a bank arranging a syndicated loan or underwriting a bond issue must know that the limit will still be available when the deal closes days later. Reservations solve both problems.

**What a reservation is.** A reservation earmarks part of a limit's headroom for a specific purpose for a limited time. Reserved amounts count toward utilization for everyone else, so they cannot be used twice.

**Lifecycle.**

```text
  Request --> Check headroom --> RESERVED (with expiry) --+--> Trade booked:
                (atomic)                                  |    convert reservation
                                                          |    into utilization
                                                          |
                                                          +--> Deal cancelled:
                                                          |    RELEASED
                                                          |
                                                          +--> Expiry reached:
                                                               EXPIRED (auto-release)
```

**Example: the race condition.**

```text
  Limit 50m, utilization 40m, headroom 10m

  Without reservation:
  09:00:00.100  Trader A reads headroom = 10m
  09:00:00.120  Trader B reads headroom = 10m
  09:00:00.200  A books 8m  -> utilization 48m
  09:00:00.210  B books 8m  -> utilization 56m  (BREACH, 112%)

  With atomic check-and-reserve:
  09:00:00.100  A reserves 8m: headroom 10m >= 8m, granted -> headroom 2m
  09:00:00.120  B reserves 8m: headroom 2m < 8m, rejected (or partial / escalate)
  09:00:00.200  A books trade: reservation 8m converted to utilization 48m
```

**Design considerations.**

- **Atomicity:** the check and the reservation must happen as one operation, using a database transaction with row locking, optimistic concurrency (a version number on the limit) or a single-writer service per limit.
- **Hierarchy:** a reservation on a book must also reserve at every parent level (desk, division, counterparty group), all-or-nothing.
- **Expiry:** every reservation has an expiry time, so forgotten reservations do not block capacity forever. Long-dated pipeline reservations (for example loan commitments) may need approval and periodic review.
- **Idempotency:** retried requests carry a unique reservation key so that a network retry does not reserve twice.
- **Conversion matching:** the booked trade must reference the reservation ID; differences between the reserved and actual amount are adjusted on conversion.
- **Reporting:** utilization reports should show actual and reserved amounts separately.

**Analogy.** A reservation is like holding a hotel room with a booking: the room is not occupied yet, but nobody else can take it until you check in, cancel or the hold expires.

**Key takeaways**

- Reservations prevent concurrent users from consuming the same headroom twice and guarantee capacity for pipeline deals.
- A reservation is created atomically, counts toward utilization, and is converted, released or expired.
- Reservations must propagate through the limit hierarchy and be idempotent and time-bound.
- Reports should distinguish actual utilization from reserved amounts.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** A limit of EUR 100m has utilization of EUR 70m and reservations of EUR 20m. How much headroom is available for a new request?
> 2. **Intermediate:** A reservation of EUR 15m is made at book level, but the request fails at the counterparty-group level because of insufficient headroom. What must happen to the book-level reservation, and why?
> 3. **Interview:** "Design a limit reservation API used by five trading systems." *Hint:* define reserve, convert, release and query operations, idempotency keys, expiry semantics, atomic multi-level reservation, behaviour when the limit service is unavailable (fail closed vs fail open per limit type), and events published for monitoring.

---

<a id="9-regulatory-framework"></a>
## 9. Regulatory Framework

Almost every number a bank treasury produces, from the capital ratio to the liquidity buffer to a single derivative trade, ends up in front of a regulator. This chapter explains where those rules come from (the Basel standards and their regional implementations), how liquidity is regulated, how banks report to supervisors and what data quality supervisors demand, and the conduct rules (AML, sanctions, market abuse, trade reporting and record-keeping) that apply to treasury activity. For engineers, regulation explains why systems need versioned rule sets, attribute-level lineage, strict reporting deadlines and immutable audit trails, and why getting them wrong leads to fines, capital add-ons and, in the worst cases, the loss of a licence.

<a id="91-basel-accords"></a>
### 9.1 Basel Accords

This subchapter follows the international capital standards from their origins in 1988 to the 2017 finalisation package, explains the three-pillar structure that organizes them, and shows how the EU, the US and the UK turn non-binding Basel standards into enforceable law.

#### Evolution from Basel I to Basel III

**Why it matters.** Banks compete across borders. If one country lets its banks hold less capital, those banks can lend more cheaply and win business, and regulators elsewhere come under pressure to relax their own rules: a "race to the bottom". The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) was created to set common minimum standards so that banks compete on service and efficiency rather than on how thin their safety margin is. Each version of the Basel Accord was a response to weaknesses exposed by a crisis, so knowing the history explains why today's rules look the way they do.

**The Basel Committee.** The BCBS was founded in 1974 by the central bank governors of the G10 countries after the failure of Bankhaus Herstatt in Germany. Herstatt was closed mid-day while its counterparties had already paid Deutsche Marks and were still waiting for US dollars, which also gave its name to settlement risk (Chapter 2.1). The Committee is hosted by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) in Basel and today includes authorities from 28 jurisdictions. Its standards have **no legal force**: they apply only once each jurisdiction writes them into its own law (see Regional Implementations below). The Committee checks how faithfully members do this through its Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP).

**Timeline.**

```text
 1974  BCBS founded after Herstatt failure
   |
 1988  Basel I       Credit risk only; 8% capital / RWA; 5 broad risk weight buckets
   |
 1996  Market Risk Amendment   Trading book capital; banks may use internal VaR models
   |
 2004  Basel II      Three pillars; risk-sensitive credit weights (ratings, IRB models);
   |                 operational risk capital; supervisory review; disclosure
   |
 2009  Basel 2.5     Post-crisis patch to the trading book: stressed VaR,
   |                 incremental risk charge, tougher securitisation rules
   |
 2010  Basel III     More and better capital (CET1), buffers, leverage ratio,
   |                 first global liquidity standards (LCR, NSFR)
   |
 2017  Basel III     "Finalising post-crisis reforms": output floor, revised standardized
       final         approaches, limits on internal models, new CVA and op risk frameworks
                     (see next topic)
```

**What each accord changed.**

| Accord | Problem it addressed | Key features | Weakness later exposed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Basel I (1988) | Falling capital levels at internationally active banks in the 1980s debt crisis | Capital at least 8% of RWA, Tier 1 at least 4%; risk weights 0%, 10%, 20%, 50%, 100% by broad counterparty type (OECD government, bank, mortgage, corporate) | Not risk-sensitive: an AAA corporate and a near-bankrupt corporate both weighted 100%, so banks kept the risky loans and securitized the safe ones (regulatory arbitrage) |
| Market Risk Amendment (1996) | Rapid growth of trading books | Capital for market risk; first use of internal models (VaR) for regulatory capital | VaR at 99%/10 days on calm data underestimated tail risk |
| Basel II (2004) | Basel I arbitrage | Pillar 1 (credit, market, operational risk), Pillar 2 (supervisory review), Pillar 3 (disclosure); standardized approach based on external ratings; internal ratings-based (IRB) approach | Capital quality too low; procyclical; trading book and securitisation risk underestimated; no liquidity or leverage limits |
| Basel 2.5 (2009) | Trading book losses in 2007-2008 | Stressed VaR, incremental risk charge, comprehensive risk measure for correlation trading | Patchwork, not a redesign (later replaced by FRTB) |
| Basel III (2010) | Global financial crisis | CET1 minimum 4.5%, Tier 1 6%, total 8%; capital conservation and countercyclical buffers; G-SIB surcharges; 3% leverage ratio; LCR and NSFR | Large variation in RWA between banks using internal models for similar portfolios |

**Quality and quantity of capital.** Under Basel I, only half of the 8% had to be Tier 1, and Tier 1 could include hybrid instruments, so a bank could meet the rules with common equity of about 2% of RWA. Many banks that failed in 2008 reported Tier 1 ratios above 8% while their loss-absorbing common equity was a fraction of that. Basel III made common equity Tier 1 (CET1) the core requirement and added buffers on top (Chapter 7.2):

```text
  Minimum common equity in % of RWA
  Basel I / II     ~2.0%   (implicit: half of the 4% Tier 1 minimum)
  Basel III         4.5%   CET1 minimum
                  + 2.5%   capital conservation buffer
                  = 7.0%   before countercyclical, systemic and Pillar 2 add-ons
```

**Example: one portfolio under three regimes (EUR millions).**

```text
  Exposure                     Amount   Basel I RW   Basel II SA RW   Basel III final SA RW
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Loan to AAA-rated corporate    100       100%           20%               20%
  Loan to unrated corporate      100       100%          100%              100%
  Residential mortgage, LTV 70%  100        50%           35%               30%
  AA-rated sovereign bond        100         0%            0%                0%
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Credit RWA                               250            155               150

  Capital required
    Basel I     total 8% x 250 = 20.0     of which common equity as low as ~2% x 250 = 5.0
    Basel II    total 8% x 155 = 12.4     of which common equity as low as ~2% x 155 = 3.1
                (plus a new operational risk charge)
    Basel III   CET1 (4.5% + 2.5%) x 150 = 10.5;  total capital incl. buffer 10.5% x 150 = 15.75
```

Basel II made the weights more risk-sensitive, which cut RWA for safe exposures. Basel III kept that sensitivity but more than tripled the common equity required for the same RWA.

**Analogy.** The Basel Accords are like successive versions of a building code. The first version said "every building needs walls of a certain thickness". Later versions differentiate by earthquake zone (risk sensitivity), then, after a disaster, demand better materials (CET1), fire exits (liquidity rules) and a backup check that does not depend on the architect's own calculations (the leverage ratio and the output floor).

**Key takeaways**

- The BCBS sets global minimum standards; they become binding only through national or regional law.
- Basel I (1988) introduced the 8% of RWA minimum but was not risk-sensitive, which encouraged regulatory arbitrage.
- Basel II (2004) introduced the three pillars, rating-based and model-based (IRB) risk weights and operational risk capital.
- Basel III (2010) raised the quality and quantity of capital, added buffers, the leverage ratio and the first global liquidity standards.
- Each revision answered a specific crisis, so the rules are best understood together with the failures that prompted them.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Name the crisis or event that triggered each of: the creation of the BCBS, Basel 2.5, and Basel III.
> 2. **Intermediate:** In the example portfolio, replace the AAA corporate loan with a loan to a corporate rated BBB (Basel II and Basel III standardized risk weight 100%). Recompute credit RWA under all three regimes and explain why the Basel I figure does not change.
> 3. **Interview:** "Why did Basel II not prevent the 2008 crisis, even though many failing banks reported capital ratios above the minimum?" *Hint:* consider the quality of capital counted as Tier 1, trading book and securitisation risk weights relying on ratings and calm-period VaR, procyclicality of risk-sensitive weights, the absence of leverage and liquidity requirements, and off-balance-sheet vehicles.

#### Basel III Endgame / Basel IV

**Why it matters.** After 2010, supervisors found that banks using internal models produced very different risk weights for similar portfolios: in BCBS benchmarking exercises, the same hypothetical portfolio could produce RWA that differed by a factor of two or more across banks. If capital depends more on the model than on the risk, capital ratios cannot be compared and lose credibility. The December 2017 package, officially "Basel III: Finalising post-crisis reforms", aims to restore trust in RWA. It is the largest change to how RWA is calculated since Basel II, and it changes the systems of every bank.

**Names.** The package has several names, which can be confusing:

| Name | Who uses it |
|---|---|
| Basel III: Finalising post-crisis reforms / Basel III final | BCBS (official) |
| Basel IV | Industry and consultants, especially in Europe, to stress the size of the impact |
| Basel III endgame | United States |
| Basel 3.1 | United Kingdom |
| CRR3 / CRD6 | EU legal texts that implement it |

**What it contains.**

| Component | Change | Main effect |
|---|---|---|
| Output floor | Total RWA at least 72.5% of RWA under standardized approaches (Chapter 7.2) | Caps the benefit of internal models; bites for low-risk portfolios such as prime mortgages |
| Revised standardized credit risk approach | More granular weights: mortgages by loan-to-value, corporates by rating with a separate treatment for unrated investment-grade corporates, specialised lending, a due diligence requirement on external ratings | Standardized RWA becomes more risk-sensitive and more data-hungry (LTV, property values, revenue) |
| Constraints on IRB | Advanced IRB no longer allowed for large corporates (revenue above EUR 500m) or for banks and other financial institutions; no IRB for equity; floors on PD, LGD and CCF inputs | Less variation between banks' models |
| CVA risk framework | Internal model approach removed; basic (BA-CVA) and standardized (SA-CVA) approaches | Derivatives desks need sensitivity-based CVA capital |
| Operational risk | All earlier approaches, including internal models (AMA), replaced by a single standardized measurement approach (SMA) | Op risk capital depends on business size and, optionally, loss history |
| Leverage ratio | G-SIB leverage buffer of 50% of the G-SIB risk-based surcharge; revised exposure measure | Large banks face a higher non-risk-based floor |
| Market risk (FRTB) | Finalised separately in 2016 and revised in 2019; implemented together with this package | New standardized and internal model approaches with Expected Shortfall (Chapter 8.1) and desk-level model approval |

**Operational risk under the SMA.** The new approach shows the general design philosophy: a simple, standardized formula, with limited room for bank-specific inputs.

```text
  Business Indicator (BI)  ~ size of business: interest, leases and dividends component
                             + services component (fees, other income/expenses)
                             + financial component (trading and banking book P&L)

  BI Component (BIC)       = 12% of BI up to EUR 1bn
                           + 15% of BI between EUR 1bn and 30bn
                           + 18% of BI above EUR 30bn

  Loss Component (LC)      = 15 x average annual operational losses over 10 years

  Internal Loss Multiplier = ln( e - 1 + (LC / BIC)^0.8 )      (jurisdictions may set ILM = 1)

  Op risk capital          = BIC x ILM            Op risk RWA = 12.5 x capital
```

**Example.** A bank has a Business Indicator of EUR 3bn and average annual operational losses of EUR 40m.

```text
  BIC = 12% x 1,000 + 15% x 2,000          = 120 + 300 = EUR 420m
  LC  = 15 x 40                            = EUR 600m
  LC / BIC = 1.4286;   (1.4286)^0.8        = 1.3302
  ILM = ln(1.7183 + 1.3302) = ln(3.0485)   = 1.1146

  Capital with ILM:       420 x 1.1146 = EUR 468.1m   ->  RWA = EUR 5,851m
  Capital with ILM = 1:   EUR 420.0m                  ->  RWA = EUR 5,250m   (EU choice)
```

A bank whose historical losses are high relative to its size pays more capital, but the effect is dampened by the logarithm and the 0.8 exponent. The EU, the UK and the US proposal set the ILM to 1, so in those jurisdictions only business size matters.

**Implementation status.** The BCBS set 1 January 2023 as the start date (after a one-year delay due to COVID-19), with the output floor phased in to 72.5% by 2028. Jurisdictions have moved at different speeds, and dates have shifted several times, so always check the current legal texts.

| Jurisdiction | Legal vehicle | Start of application | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| EU | CRR3 (Regulation (EU) 2024/1623) and CRD6 (Directive (EU) 2024/1619) | 1 January 2025 | Output floor phased in from 50% (2025) to 72.5% (2030), some transitional arrangements until 2032; FRTB capital requirements postponed, at the time of writing, to 1 January 2027 |
| UK | PRA rules ("Basel 3.1") | Postponed to 1 January 2027 | Transitional period ending in 2030 |
| US | 2023 proposal by the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC | Not finalised at the time of writing | The 2023 proposal applied to banks above USD 100bn and removed internal credit models entirely; the agencies have signalled a revised proposal with a lower capital impact |
| Others | Canada, Australia, Japan, Switzerland and others | Mostly 2023 to 2025 | Several adopted the package close to the BCBS timeline |

**Analogy.** If internal models are self-assessed tax returns, the output floor is a minimum tax: you may use deductions, but you cannot pay less than 72.5% of what the simple official calculation would give.

**Key takeaways**

- The 2017 package targets the variability of RWA from internal models; it is called Basel IV, Basel III endgame or Basel 3.1 depending on the region.
- The output floor, IRB constraints and input floors limit model benefits; standardized approaches become more granular.
- Operational risk moves to a single standardized approach based on the Business Indicator; CVA internal models are removed.
- Implementation dates differ by jurisdiction and have moved repeatedly, so systems must support parallel rule sets and phase-in parameters.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** List four components of the 2017 Basel III finalisation package and state in one sentence what problem each addresses.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Compute the SMA operational risk capital and RWA for a bank with a Business Indicator of EUR 1.5bn and average annual losses of EUR 10m, first with the ILM formula and then with ILM = 1. Which is lower, and why?
> 3. **Interview:** "Your bank uses IRB models for most portfolios. What changes in the RWA system to support the output floor?" *Hint:* every exposure needs a standardized RWA calculated in parallel (dual stack), including data the IRB process never needed (LTV, external ratings, revenue); the floor applies at total RWA level and to a phase-in percentage that changes over time; consider reconciliation between the two stacks, performance, and explaining floor impact by portfolio.

#### Pillar 1, 2 and 3

**Why it matters.** A single formula cannot capture every risk a bank faces. Some risks are hard to standardize (interest rate risk in the banking book, concentration risk, business model risk), and some weaknesses only show up in governance and controls rather than in numbers. Basel II therefore organized regulation into three complementary pillars: a formula-based minimum, supervisory judgment on top of it, and market discipline through public disclosure. The structure still frames all capital and liquidity regulation.

```text
                       +------------------------------------------+
                       |        Safety and soundness of banks      |
                       +-------------+--------------+-------------+
                       |  PILLAR 1   |   PILLAR 2   |  PILLAR 3   |
                       |  Minimum    |  Supervisory |  Market     |
                       |  require-   |  review      |  discipline |
                       |  ments      |              |             |
                       |             |  Bank:       |  Public     |
                       |  Credit     |  ICAAP,      |  disclosure |
                       |  Market     |  ILAAP       |  of capital,|
                       |  Operational|  Supervisor: |  RWA,       |
                       |  CVA        |  SREP -> P2R,|  liquidity, |
                       |  Leverage   |  P2G, other  |  risk       |
                       |  LCR / NSFR |  measures    |  profile    |
                       +-------------+--------------+-------------+
```

**Pillar 1: minimum requirements.** Formula-based requirements that every bank in scope must meet at all times: the minimum capital ratios on RWA for credit, counterparty, market, CVA and operational risk; the leverage ratio; large exposure limits; and the LCR and NSFR (Chapter 9.2). Pillar 1 is objective and comparable, but it is calibrated for an average bank.

**Pillar 2: supervisory review.** Pillar 2 covers what Pillar 1 misses.

- **The bank's own assessment.** The bank must run an Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP, Chapter 7.2) and an Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Process (ILAAP, Chapter 9.2), in which it identifies all material risks, measures them with its own methods and shows that it holds enough capital and liquidity.
- **The supervisor's review.** In the EU this is the Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP). The supervisor scores four elements, usually from 1 (low risk) to 4 (high risk): business model viability, internal governance and risk management, risks to capital, and risks to liquidity and funding. The outcome is a set of measures:
  - **Pillar 2 Requirement (P2R):** binding additional capital for risks not covered or underestimated by Pillar 1, for example IRRBB (Chapter 6.2), credit concentration or pension risk.
  - **Pillar 2 Guidance (P2G):** a non-binding expectation of additional capital to cover stress test outcomes.
  - **Qualitative and liquidity measures:** for example, remediation of control weaknesses, restrictions on business, or bank-specific liquidity requirements.

EU terminology for the resulting stack, in total capital terms:

```text
  Pillar 1 minimum (8%) + P2R                 = TSCR  (Total SREP Capital Requirement)
  TSCR + combined buffer requirement          = OCR   (Overall Capital Requirement)
  OCR + P2G                                   = overall supervisory expectation
```

**Pillar 3: market discipline.** Banks must publish standardized disclosures so that investors, depositors and analysts can compare risk profiles and penalize weak banks through higher funding costs. The BCBS defines templates with fixed formats, implemented in the EU through Part Eight of the CRR and EBA technical standards. Examples:

| Template | Content | Typical frequency for a large bank |
|---|---|---|
| KM1 | Key metrics: own funds, RWA, capital ratios, leverage ratio, LCR, NSFR | Quarterly |
| OV1 | Overview of RWA by risk type and approach | Quarterly |
| CC1 / CC2 | Composition of regulatory capital and reconciliation to the published balance sheet | Semi-annual / annual |
| LIQ1 / LIQ2 | LCR and NSFR components | Quarterly / semi-annual |
| LR1 to LR3 | Leverage ratio exposure measure | Quarterly to annual |
| IRRBB1 | Changes in EVE and NII under the standard shock scenarios (Chapter 6.2) | Annual |

Under CRR3, the EBA also collects the disclosures of EU banks on a central data hub, so that they can be compared in one place.

**Example: from SREP to the requirement a bank manages against.** A bank receives a P2R of 2.25% and a P2G of 1.25%; its combined buffer requirement is 4.0%.

```text
  Pillar 1 total capital                         8.00%
  P2R                                          + 2.25%
  TSCR                                         = 10.25%
  Combined buffer requirement                  + 4.00%
  OCR                                          = 14.25%   breach of buffers => MDA restrictions
  P2G                                          + 1.25%
  Supervisory expectation                      = 15.50%
  Management buffer (bank's risk appetite)     + 1.50%
  Internal target                              = 17.00%   total capital / RWA
```

The same RWA, own funds and ratios appear in COREP (supervisor), in Pillar 3 (public) and in the ICAAP (internal). If they differ without explanation, supervisors and analysts will ask why, so all three must come from the same reconciled data (see Chapter 9.3).

**Analogy.** Pillar 1 is the driving test everyone must pass, Pillar 2 is the instructor watching how you actually drive and adding conditions to your licence, and Pillar 3 is the public rating on a ride-hailing app that lets passengers choose who to ride with.

**Key takeaways**

- Pillar 1 sets formula-based minimum requirements; Pillar 2 adds bank-specific requirements from supervisory review; Pillar 3 requires public disclosure.
- In the EU, the SREP results in P2R (binding), P2G (expectation) and qualitative measures; TSCR and OCR describe the resulting stack.
- ICAAP and ILAAP are the bank's own Pillar 2 assessments of capital and liquidity.
- Pillar 3 templates are standardized and must be consistent with supervisory reporting and financial statements.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Assign each item to Pillar 1, 2 or 3: the LCR minimum; a capital add-on for IRRBB; publication of the KM1 template; the leverage ratio; a supervisory finding on weak model governance.
> 2. **Intermediate:** A bank has P2R of 3.0%, a combined buffer requirement of 3.5%, P2G of 1.0% and total RWA of EUR 40bn. Compute TSCR, OCR and the total capital needed to meet the supervisory expectation, in percent and in EUR.
> 3. **Interview:** "The CET1 ratio in our Pillar 3 report differs from the one in COREP by 5 basis points. How would you find out why?" *Hint:* compare reference dates, scope of consolidation, version of the data snapshot, inclusion of interim profits, transitional vs fully loaded figures and manual adjustments; the long-term fix is generating both from one controlled data set.

#### Regional Implementations (CRR/CRD, US Rules)

**Why it matters.** A bank never applies "Basel" directly; it applies the law of the jurisdictions in which it operates. A group with entities in Frankfurt, London and New York must meet three different rule sets that share a Basel core but differ in scope, timing, calibration and reporting. For engineers, this means rule engines with jurisdiction-specific parameters, multiple reporting outputs from the same positions, and careful tracking of which legal entity holds which trade.

**From standard to law.**

```text
   BCBS standard (not binding)
          |
          +---------------------+---------------------+
          v                     v                     v
   EU                       US                     UK
   Regulation (CRR)         Rules by Federal       PRA Rulebook and
   + Directive (CRD)        Reserve, OCC, FDIC     retained/onshored law
   + EBA technical          in 12 CFR, adopted     + PRA supervisory
     standards (RTS/ITS)      after public           statements
   + EBA guidelines           comment
          |                     |                     |
   Supervised by ECB/SSM    Fed (holding cos),     PRA (prudential)
   (significant banks)      OCC (national banks),  and FCA (conduct)
   and national authorities FDIC (state non-member)
```

**European Union.**

- **CRR (Capital Requirements Regulation)** is directly applicable in every member state without national transposition. It contains the Pillar 1 rules, liquidity ratios, leverage, large exposures, reporting and disclosure.
- **CRD (Capital Requirements Directive)** must be transposed into national law. It covers licensing, governance, remuneration, Pillar 2 and SREP, and most capital buffers, where national flexibility is needed.
- **Versions:** CRR/CRD IV (2013, Basel III), CRR2/CRD5 (2019: NSFR, binding leverage ratio, SA-CCR, TLAC), CRR3/CRD6 (2024: Basel III finalisation).
- **Single rulebook:** the European Banking Authority (EBA) writes binding technical standards (RTS and ITS, adopted by the Commission), guidelines and Q&As that detail the rules. The ECB supervises significant banks directly under the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM); national authorities supervise smaller banks.
- **Notable EU deviations from Basel:** the SME and infrastructure supporting factors that reduce RWA for those loans, exemptions from CVA capital for certain corporate and sovereign counterparties, transitional treatment of unrated corporates and low-risk mortgages under the output floor, and Level 1 HQLA status for extremely high quality covered bonds.

**United States.**

- Rules are issued jointly by the **Federal Reserve** (bank holding companies and state member banks), the **OCC** (national banks) and the **FDIC** (state non-member banks), through notice-and-comment rulemaking, and are codified in the Code of Federal Regulations (for example Regulation Q, 12 CFR Part 217, for the Fed).
- **Tailoring (2019):** requirements depend on the category of the banking organization:

| Category | Scope | Examples of requirements |
|---|---|---|
| I | US G-SIBs | Full requirements, G-SIB surcharge, enhanced supplementary leverage ratio, full daily LCR and NSFR |
| II | At least USD 700bn total assets or USD 75bn cross-jurisdictional activity | Full LCR/NSFR, advanced approaches |
| III | At least USD 250bn, or high nonbank assets, short-term wholesale funding or off-balance sheet exposure | Full or reduced LCR/NSFR depending on short-term wholesale funding |
| IV | USD 100bn to 250bn | Reduced or no LCR/NSFR, less frequent stress testing |

- **US-specific features:** the Collins Amendment floor (risk-based ratios are the lower of the standardized and advanced approach results, so standardized RWA is often binding); the **stress capital buffer (SCB)**, derived from the Federal Reserve's annual stress test, which replaces the fixed capital conservation buffer for large banks and is at least 2.5%; and the supplementary leverage ratio. Foreign banks with large US operations must hold them in an **intermediate holding company (IHC)** subject to US rules.

**United Kingdom.** After Brexit, EU rules were onshored and are progressively replaced by PRA rules. The PRA implements Basel 3.1 with its own calibration and timetable, and applies a simpler regime for small domestic banks.

**Example: the same group, three rule sets.** A European banking group has its parent in Germany, a branch in London and a US IHC.

| Topic | EU parent (CRR/CRD) | UK operations (PRA) | US IHC (Fed rules) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Capital rules | CRR3 | PRA rules (Basel 3.1 from 2027) | Regulation Q, US Category depends on IHC size |
| Capital buffer | Capital conservation buffer 2.5% | Capital conservation buffer 2.5% | Stress capital buffer, at least 2.5% |
| Liquidity ratio | EU LCR Delegated Regulation; NSFR in CRR | PRA LCR and NSFR rules | US LCR / NSFR, depending on Category |
| Main liquidity report | COREP LCR templates, ALMM | PRA returns | FR 2052a |
| Supervisor | ECB (SSM) | PRA | Federal Reserve |

A UK branch of an EU bank is not a separate legal entity, so it is supervised mainly by the home authority with PRA oversight, while a UK subsidiary would need its own capital and liquidity. The difference between branch and subsidiary is often the first question when mapping which rules apply to a trade.

**Analogy.** Basel is like a model recipe published by a culinary association. Every country's kitchen cooks it, but each changes the quantities, substitutes local ingredients and serves it at a different time, and the health inspector checks against the local version, not the original.

**Key takeaways**

- Basel standards become binding only through regional or national law; the version that applies depends on the legal entity.
- In the EU, the CRR is directly applicable, the CRD is transposed nationally, and EBA technical standards add detail.
- In the US, the Fed, OCC and FDIC issue the rules; tailoring categories, the Collins floor and the stress capital buffer are distinctive features.
- Jurisdictions deviate from Basel in scope, calibration and timing, so systems need jurisdiction-specific, versioned parameters.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain the practical difference between an EU regulation and an EU directive, and give one example of each in banking regulation.
> 2. **Intermediate:** A US bank holding company has USD 300bn of total assets and USD 20bn of cross-jurisdictional activity. Which tailoring category is it most likely in, and how would your answer change if its total assets were USD 750bn?
> 3. **Interview:** "Design the rules configuration for an RWA engine used by entities in the EU, UK and US." *Hint:* separate the calculation logic from jurisdiction parameters (risk weights, floors, phase-in percentages); version rules by effective date and jurisdiction; resolve the applicable rule set from the legal entity booking the exposure; support parallel runs for rule changes; and make every result explainable with the rule version that produced it.

<a id="92-liquidity-regulation"></a>
### 9.2 Liquidity Regulation

Before 2008 there was no global liquidity standard, and several banks with adequate capital failed because they ran out of cash. This subchapter covers the two Basel III ratios that fixed this (the LCR for 30-day stress, the NSFR for structural funding) and the supervisory tools around them: EU monitoring metrics, the bank's own liquidity assessment (ILAAP) and intraday liquidity monitoring. The underlying concepts (HQLA, run-off, survival horizon, intraday flows) are introduced in Chapter 5. This subchapter focuses on the regulatory rules and reporting.

#### Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)

**Why it matters.** Northern Rock (2007) and Lehman Brothers (2008) showed that a bank can be solvent on paper and still fail within days when depositors and wholesale lenders withdraw funding. Supervisors wanted every bank to be able to survive a severe but plausible stress on its own for long enough (30 days) for management and the authorities to react, without relying on the central bank. The LCR makes that a hard, comparable requirement.

**Definition.**

```text
                    Stock of HQLA
  LCR  =  -----------------------------------------   >=  100%
           Total net cash outflows over next 30 days

  Net cash outflows = Outflows - min( Inflows, 75% x Outflows )
```

- **Numerator:** HQLA after haircuts and caps (Chapter 5.4).
- **Denominator:** contractual and contingent cash flows over a 30-calendar-day stress, each multiplied by a regulatory **run-off rate** (outflows) or **inflow rate**.
- **Inflow cap:** inflows can offset at most 75% of outflows, so every bank must hold HQLA of at least 25% of its stressed outflows, whatever its expected inflows.
- **Scenario:** the regulatory stress combines a bank-specific shock (for example a three-notch downgrade) with a market-wide shock: partial loss of retail deposits, loss of unsecured wholesale funding, loss of secured funding except against high-quality collateral, collateral calls on downgrade, and drawdowns of committed facilities.

**Selected Basel run-off and inflow rates.**

| Item | Rate |
|---|---|
| Stable retail deposits (insured, established relationship) | 5% (3% in some jurisdictions) |
| Less stable retail deposits | 10% or higher |
| Operational deposits (clearing, custody, cash management) | 25% |
| Non-operational deposits from non-financial corporates, sovereigns | 40% (20% if fully insured) |
| Unsecured wholesale funding from financial institutions | 100% |
| Secured funding backed by Level 1 assets or with the central bank | 0% |
| Secured funding backed by Level 2A / other assets | 15% / 25-100% |
| Undrawn committed credit facilities to non-financial corporates | 10% |
| Undrawn committed liquidity facilities to non-financial corporates | 30% |
| Additional collateral needed after a three-notch downgrade | 100% of the amount |
| Inflows from performing loans to non-financial counterparties | 50% |
| Inflows from financial institutions | 100% |
| Reverse repo inflows backed by Level 1 collateral | 0% (the collateral is assumed to be rolled over) |

**Example (EUR millions).** The bank uses the HQLA stock from Chapter 5.4 (EUR 13,550m).

```text
  Outflows                                   Balance   Run-off    Outflow
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Stable retail deposits                      20,000      5%        1,000
  Less stable retail deposits                  8,000     10%          800
  Operational corporate deposits               6,000     25%        1,500
  Non-operational corporate deposits           5,000     40%        2,000
  Unsecured funding from banks and funds       5,000    100%        5,000
  Undrawn credit facilities (corporates)      10,000     10%        1,000
  Undrawn liquidity facilities (corporates)    2,000     30%          600
  Net derivative outflows                        300    100%          300
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Total outflows                                                   12,200

  Inflows (contractual, within 30 days)
  Loans to corporates maturing                 2,400     50%        1,200
  Interbank placements maturing                1,500    100%        1,500
  Reverse repos on Level 1 collateral          1,000      0%            0
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Total inflows                                                     2,700
  Cap: 75% x 12,200 = 9,150  -> not binding

  Net cash outflows = 12,200 - 2,700 = 9,500
  LCR = 13,550 / 9,500 = 142.6%
```

The largest single driver is the EUR 5,000m of funding from financial institutions, which is assumed to leave in full. Replacing it with term funding of more than 30 days would reduce net outflows by EUR 5bn and raise the LCR to 13,550 / 4,500 = 301%. Treasuries therefore manage the maturity of wholesale funding very actively around the 30-day point.

**Regulatory practice.**

- **Phase-in:** 60% in 2015, rising to 100% by 2019 under Basel (the EU applied 100% from 2018).
- **Usability:** HQLA are meant to be used in stress; a bank may fall below 100% in a stress, but must notify the supervisor immediately and present a plan to restore the ratio.
- **Currencies:** the LCR is a single-currency-equivalent ratio, but banks must also monitor it in each significant currency (in the EU, any currency representing at least 5% of total liabilities), because HQLA in EUR do not help if the stress is a run on USD funding and the FX swap market is dysfunctional.
- **Reporting:** monthly in the EU (COREP LCR templates, Chapter 9.3), daily for the largest US banks via FR 2052a; quarterly public disclosure (Pillar 3 LIQ1).
- **Regional differences:** the EU LCR is set out in a Commission Delegated Regulation; the US LCR adds a "peak day" test that captures the largest cumulative net outflow on any day within the 30 days, not just at day 30, and applies reduced versions to smaller categories.

**Analogy.** The LCR is like a rule that every household must keep enough cash and easily sold savings to pay a month of bills, assuming the main earner loses their job, the overdraft is cancelled and only half the money owed to them arrives.

**Key takeaways**

- LCR = HQLA / net stressed outflows over 30 days, at least 100%.
- Run-off rates depend on how stable the funding source is: retail deposits are assumed to be sticky, wholesale funding from financial institutions not at all.
- Inflows are capped at 75% of outflows; HQLA can be used in stress, with notification to the supervisor.
- Banks monitor the LCR daily and by significant currency, even when they report it monthly.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Compute the LCR of a bank with HQLA of EUR 5bn, stressed outflows of EUR 6bn and stressed inflows of EUR 2bn.
> 2. **Intermediate:** In the example, stressed inflows rise to EUR 10,000m because a large block of interbank placements now matures within 30 days (HQLA unchanged). Apply the inflow cap and compute the new LCR. Why does the regulation limit the benefit?
> 3. **Interview:** "Our LCR moved from 145% to 128% overnight. How would you explain the change to the treasurer by 9 am?" *Hint:* build an LCR movement analysis by component (HQLA, each outflow and inflow category), then drill down to the largest position changes; check for maturities entering the 30-day window, reclassification of deposits, changes in HQLA eligibility or encumbrance, and data issues such as missing feeds defaulting to the most punitive treatment.

#### Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR)

**Why it matters.** The LCR protects against a 30-day stress, but a bank could still fund long-term mortgages with funding that rolls over every 31 days and meet the LCR. That maturity mismatch is a structural vulnerability: when markets close for longer, refinancing fails. The NSFR requires long-term, illiquid assets to be funded by stable sources over a one-year horizon, limiting excessive maturity transformation.

**Definition.**

```text
                Available Stable Funding (ASF)
  NSFR  =  ---------------------------------------   >=  100%
                Required Stable Funding (RSF)

  ASF = sum of liabilities and capital x ASF factor (how stable is this funding over 1 year?)
  RSF = sum of assets and off-balance items x RSF factor (how much of this needs stable funding?)
```

**Selected Basel factors.**

| Available stable funding | ASF factor | Required stable funding | RSF factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| Regulatory capital; liabilities with maturity of 1 year or more | 100% | Cash, central bank reserves | 0% |
| Stable retail deposits | 95% | Unencumbered Level 1 securities | 5% |
| Less stable retail deposits | 90% | Unencumbered Level 2A assets | 15% |
| Deposits from non-financial corporates below 1 year; operational deposits | 50% | Loans to financial institutions below 6 months (unsecured) | 15% |
| Funding from financial institutions below 6 months | 0% | Level 2B assets; loans to non-financial corporates below 1 year | 50% |
| Other liabilities (for example derivative liabilities net of collateral) | 0% | Residential mortgages of 1 year or more, risk weight up to 35% | 65% |
| | | Other performing loans of 1 year or more, risk weight above 35% | 85% |
| | | Fixed assets, non-performing loans, assets encumbered for 1 year or more | 100% |
| | | Undrawn committed credit and liquidity facilities | 5% |

**Example (EUR millions).** The same bank as in the LCR example.

```text
  Available stable funding              Amount   ASF factor      ASF
  -------------------------------------------------------------------
  Regulatory capital                     6,000     100%        6,000
  Senior bonds, maturity > 1 year       10,000     100%       10,000
  Stable retail deposits                20,000      95%       19,000
  Less stable retail deposits            8,000      90%        7,200
  Corporate deposits (< 1 year)         11,000      50%        5,500
  Funding from financial inst. (< 6m)    5,000       0%            0
  Other liabilities                      6,500       0%            0
  -------------------------------------------------------------------
  Total                                 66,500                47,700

  Required stable funding               Amount   RSF factor      RSF
  -------------------------------------------------------------------
  Cash and central bank reserves         4,000       0%            0
  Level 1 government bonds               6,000       5%          300
  Level 2A covered bonds                 3,000      15%          450
  Level 2B corporate bonds               2,000      50%        1,000
  Loans to banks (< 6 months)            1,500      15%          225
  Corporate loans (< 1 year)             4,000      50%        2,000
  Residential mortgages (RW <= 35%)     30,000      65%       19,500
  Corporate loans (> 1 year)            12,000      85%       10,200
  Fixed and other assets                 2,000     100%        2,000
  -------------------------------------------------------------------
  On-balance total                      66,500                35,675
  Undrawn committed facilities          12,000       5%          600
  -------------------------------------------------------------------
  Total RSF                                                   36,275

  NSFR = 47,700 / 36,275 = 131.5%
```

Mortgages and long-term corporate loans account for over 80% of the RSF, and retail deposits for over half of the ASF. This is typical of a retail bank: the NSFR rewards deposit franchises and penalizes funding long assets with short-term wholesale money.

**Regulatory practice.**

- Basel published the final standard in 2014; it became binding in the EU in June 2021 (CRR2) and in the US in July 2021 for the larger categories.
- **Derivatives:** net derivative assets require 100% RSF, net derivative liabilities provide no ASF, and a 5% RSF add-on applies to gross derivative liabilities, so derivatives-heavy treasuries feel the NSFR.
- **Interdependent assets and liabilities** (for example pass-through funding for some promotional loans) can be given 0% factors in some jurisdictions.
- **Reporting:** quarterly in the EU (COREP NSFR templates), with semi-annual public disclosure (LIQ2).
- **Management use:** treasury computes the NSFR impact of new products and funding plans (Chapter 7.1) and includes it in funds transfer pricing (Chapter 6.4) as a liquidity cost for long-term assets.

**Analogy.** The NSFR is like a rule that you may only buy a house with a long-term mortgage, not with a credit card you hope to refinance every month.

**Key takeaways**

- NSFR = available stable funding / required stable funding over a one-year horizon, at least 100%.
- ASF factors reward capital, long-term funding and retail deposits; short-term funding from financial institutions counts for nothing.
- RSF factors grow with the illiquidity and maturity of assets; HQLA need little stable funding, long loans a lot.
- The NSFR complements the LCR: one targets a 30-day stress, the other structural maturity mismatch.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** For each item, say whether it adds to ASF or RSF and give its factor: EUR 100m of 5-year senior bonds issued; EUR 100m of stable retail deposits; EUR 100m of unencumbered Level 1 bonds held.
> 2. **Intermediate:** In the example, the bank replaces EUR 5,000m of short-term funding from financial institutions with 2-year senior bonds and uses the cash to grant additional long-term corporate loans. Compute the new NSFR. What happens to the LCR from the previous topic?
> 3. **Interview:** "The business wants to launch a 10-year fixed-rate loan product. How would treasury assess its NSFR impact, and how should that show up in pricing?" *Hint:* RSF factor of the loan by risk weight and maturity, the stable funding needed to keep the ratio above the internal target, the cost of that funding over the curve, and passing it through FTP as a term liquidity premium.

#### Additional Liquidity Monitoring Metrics (ALMM)

**Why it matters.** The LCR and NSFR compress a bank's liquidity profile into two ratios. A supervisor also wants to see the details behind them: when cash flows fall due, which counterparties and products the bank depends on, how much it pays for funding and how easily it can roll it over. In the EU, the **Additional Liquidity Monitoring Metrics** provide this information in a standard format, monthly for most banks. They have no minimum threshold but are used heavily in SREP and in early warning.

**The ALMM templates (EU).**

| Template | Content | What the supervisor looks for |
|---|---|---|
| C 66.01 Maturity ladder | Contractual outflows, inflows and counterbalancing capacity in time buckets from overnight to more than 5 years | When the cumulative gap turns negative; how much cash can be generated from assets and in which time bucket |
| C 67.00 Concentration of funding by counterparty | Top 10 counterparties or groups providing funding above 1% of total liabilities | Dependency on a few large depositors or lenders |
| C 68.00 Concentration of funding by product type | Funding by product (retail, wholesale unsecured, secured, by maturity) above 1% of liabilities | Reliance on one product, for example short-term commercial paper |
| C 69.00 Prices for various lengths of funding | Average volume and spread paid on new funding by maturity | Rising funding costs as an early warning of stress |
| C 70.00 Roll-over of funding | Daily maturing, rolled-over and new funding over the month, by maturity | Falling roll-over rates (lenders not renewing) |
| C 71.00 Concentration of counterbalancing capacity | Top 10 holdings of liquid assets or liquidity lines by issuer or counterparty | Whether the liquidity buffer depends on one issuer or one central bank line |

Smaller and non-complex institutions report less frequently (quarterly), in line with proportionality.

**Example: a simplified maturity ladder (EUR millions).**

```text
  Time bucket          Outflows   Inflows   Net flow   Cumulative   Counterbalancing   Cumulative gap
                                                        net flow     capacity (cum.)    incl. capacity
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Overnight              -1,800       900       -900        -900          13,000             12,100
  > 1 day to 7 days      -2,600       700     -1,900      -2,800          13,200             10,400
  > 7 days to 1 month    -4,100     1,200     -2,900      -5,700          13,550              7,850
  > 1 to 3 months        -5,200     2,300     -2,900      -8,600          13,800              5,200
  > 3 to 6 months        -4,500     2,800     -1,700     -10,300          14,000              3,700
  > 6 to 12 months       -6,200     3,100     -3,100     -13,400          14,000                600
  > 1 to 2 years         -7,000     4,500     -2,500     -15,900          14,000             -1,900  <--
```

Unlike the LCR, the maturity ladder uses contractual flows without behavioural run-off assumptions, and counterbalancing capacity is the cash the bank can generate from unencumbered assets and committed lines by each date. In the example, contractual outflows exhaust the liquidity buffer between one and two years. This is not a breach of any limit, but a supervisor would ask how the bank expects to refinance in that period (funding plan, deposit stability).

**Engineering view.** ALMM templates are produced from the same cash flow engine as the internal maturity ladder (Chapter 5.2), but with regulatory definitions: contractual maturity, specific buckets, counterparty grouping by legal group (requiring a reliable group hierarchy from reference data), and product classification rules. Concentration templates need consistent counterparty identifiers, typically the LEI, across all funding systems.

**Analogy.** If the LCR is a doctor's single blood pressure reading, the ALMM is the full blood test panel: no single value decides the diagnosis, but together they reveal problems early.

**Key takeaways**

- ALMM are EU supervisory templates that give the detail behind the LCR and NSFR, usually reported monthly.
- They cover the contractual maturity ladder, funding concentration by counterparty and product, funding prices, roll-over and concentration of counterbalancing capacity.
- There are no minimum thresholds, but supervisors use the metrics in SREP and for early warning.
- They require consistent counterparty, group and product reference data across funding systems.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Which ALMM template would show that a bank's three largest depositors provide 12% of its funding?
> 2. **Intermediate:** In the maturity ladder example, by how much would counterbalancing capacity have to increase, or contractual outflows in the "> 1 to 2 years" bucket decrease, for the cumulative gap to remain positive through two years?
> 3. **Interview:** "The concentration of funding template groups counterparties by legal group, but our deposit system only stores the account holder. How would you produce it?" *Hint:* map account holders to LEIs and legal entity hierarchies from a golden source of counterparty reference data; handle unmapped customers; snapshot the hierarchy as of the reporting date; and reconcile totals with the balance sheet.

#### ILAAP

**Why it matters.** Regulatory ratios use standard assumptions that cannot reflect each bank's business model. A bank with large USD funding needs, a big custody business or heavy collateral exposure to derivatives has risks the LCR captures only roughly. The **Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Process (ILAAP)** requires the bank itself to identify, measure, manage and monitor its liquidity and funding risks, and to state formally that its liquidity is adequate. It is the liquidity counterpart of the ICAAP (Chapter 7.2) and a key input to the supervisor's Pillar 2 review.

**What an ILAAP contains.** In the EU it is required by Article 86 of the CRD and detailed by EBA guidelines and, for significant banks, the ECB Guide to the ILAAP.

```text
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  |  Liquidity Adequacy Statement (LAS)  - signed by the management body      |
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  |  Governance       | Risk appetite      | Risk identification | Stress     |
  |  roles, ALCO,     | survival horizon,  | inventory of all    | testing    |
  |  three lines of   | LCR / NSFR targets,| liquidity risks:    | idiosyn-   |
  |  defence, policies| limits (Ch. 8.4)   | intraday, FX,       | cratic,    |
  |                   |                    | collateral, ...     | market,    |
  |                   |                    |                     | combined   |
  +-------------------+--------------------+---------------------+------------+
  |  Liquidity buffer and collateral (Ch. 5.4) | Funding plan (Ch. 7.1)        |
  |  Contingency funding plan (Ch. 5.4)        | FTP (Ch. 6.4)                 |
  |  Data, models, validation, internal audit                                  |
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

- **Liquidity Adequacy Statement:** a short statement by the board, backed by evidence, that the bank's liquidity is adequate, and an assessment of the main risks.
- **Internal stress testing:** bank-specific scenarios, assumptions and horizons, often longer and more severe than the LCR, and covering intraday and currency stress. Typical internal metric: the survival horizon (Chapter 5.2).
- **Integration ("use test"):** the ILAAP must actually be used in management decisions (limits, FTP, funding plan, new products), not produced only for the supervisor.
- **Annual cycle:** the bank submits its ILAAP package once a year; the supervisor assesses it in the SREP liquidity element and may impose qualitative measures or specific liquidity requirements, such as a higher minimum LCR or a minimum survival period.

**Example: internal stress results in an ILAAP (EUR millions).**

```text
  Scenario                          Horizon    Cumulative       Liquidity buffer    Survival
                                               net outflow      after haircuts       horizon
  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Idiosyncratic (downgrade, run)    90 days      -11,200            13,100           > 90 days
  Market-wide (repo market stress)  90 days       -8,700            11,400           > 90 days
  Combined, severe                  90 days      -14,300            12,600             61 days
  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Risk appetite: survival horizon >= 60 days in the combined scenario      -> met, headroom 1 day
```

The LAS would note that the combined scenario is close to the risk appetite and describe the actions planned (for example lengthening wholesale funding by EUR 2bn), while the supervisor would challenge the assumptions behind the 61 days, for example deposit run-off rates and the haircuts on the buffer.

**Analogy.** The LCR is the national driving test; the ILAAP is the transport company's own safety case for its fleet: its routes, its vehicles, its weather and its emergency plan, signed by the director who is accountable for it.

**Key takeaways**

- The ILAAP is the bank's own assessment of liquidity and funding risk, required under Pillar 2.
- It covers governance, risk appetite, identification of all liquidity risks, internal stress testing, buffers, funding plan, contingency planning and FTP.
- The management body signs a Liquidity Adequacy Statement; the ILAAP must be used in actual decisions.
- Supervisors assess it in the SREP and can impose bank-specific liquidity requirements.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Name four building blocks of an ILAAP and explain how the ILAAP differs from the LCR.
> 2. **Intermediate:** A bank's combined stress scenario shows a cumulative net outflow of EUR 9bn at day 60 and EUR 12bn at day 90, against a buffer after haircuts of EUR 10.5bn. What is the survival horizon (assume linear outflows between the points)? Does it meet a 60-day appetite, and which two actions could treasury propose?
> 3. **Interview:** "The supervisor says our ILAAP stress testing is not used in management decisions. What evidence and system changes would address that?" *Hint:* link stress results to limits and early-warning indicators, FTP liquidity charges, funding plan targets and new product approvals; run stress metrics daily rather than annually; and document decisions where stress results changed an outcome.

#### BCBS 248 Intraday Monitoring

**Why it matters.** The LCR measures liquidity at day 30, and banks also manage end-of-day balances, but payments settle in real time (Chapter 2.2). A bank that cannot fund its payments during the day delays them, which pushes the liquidity shortage onto its counterparties and can spread through the payment system. In April 2013 the Basel Committee published BCBS 248, *Monitoring tools for intraday liquidity management*, so that supervisors could see how banks use intraday liquidity and how they would cope under stress. The operational side of intraday monitoring is covered in Chapter 5.3; this topic covers the regulatory reporting framework.

**The monitoring tools.** The tools are not ratios with minimums; they are measures reported to the supervisor (monthly in the Basel design), and each applies to a specific type of bank.

| Group | Tool | Applies to |
|---|---|---|
| A (all reporting banks) | A(i) Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage: the largest negative (and positive) net cumulative position of payments during the day | All |
| | A(ii) Available intraday liquidity at the start of the business day: central bank reserves, collateral eligible for intraday credit, unused credit lines | All |
| | A(iii) Total payments sent and received | All |
| | A(iv) Time-specific obligations that must settle by a certain time (for example CLS pay-ins, margin calls) | All |
| B (correspondent banking providers) | B(i) Value of payments made on behalf of correspondent banking customers | Banks providing correspondent services |
| | B(ii) Intraday credit lines extended to customers, and their peak usage | Banks providing correspondent services |
| C (direct participants) | C(i) Intraday throughput: share of payments settled by each hour of the day | Direct participants in payment systems |

**Stress scenarios.** Banks must also assess the tools under four stresses: the bank's own financial stress (counterparties delay payments to it), a counterparty's stress (a major counterparty stops paying), a customer bank's stress (a correspondent customer stops paying while the bank keeps making its payments), and a market-wide credit or liquidity stress (the value of collateral for intraday credit falls).

**Reporting.** For each tool and each relevant currency and payment system, the bank reports monthly figures derived from daily data, for example the largest, second largest and third largest daily values in the month and the monthly average. Supervisors implement the framework differently: some collect the templates directly, others review intraday metrics as part of the ILAAP and SREP (Pillar 2).

**Example: deriving the monthly report for tool A(i) (EUR millions).** From 21 business days of data on the bank's EUR central bank account:

```text
  Daily maximum negative net cumulative position (sorted)
    -1,640  (15th, quarter-end tax payments and securities settlement)
    -1,410  (CLS pay-in day with large USD/EUR volume)
    -1,180
    -1,050 ... (17 further days between -420 and -1,000)

  Monthly report, tool A(i), EUR, TARGET2
    Largest negative position         -1,640
    Second largest                    -1,410
    Third largest                     -1,180
    Average of daily maxima             -760

  Tool A(ii): available intraday liquidity at start of day, average   2,050
    -> peak usage of 1,640 used 80% of available intraday liquidity on the worst day
```

**Example: throughput (tool C(i)).**

```text
  Time      Cumulative % of daily payment value sent
  08:00          8%
  10:00         27%
  12:00         51%
  14:00         70%
  16:00         88%
  18:00        100%
```

If throughput at 12:00 falls from around 50% to 30% over several months, the bank may be delaying payments to save liquidity, which supervisors and payment system operators watch closely.

**Engineering view.** The tools require timestamped settlement data for every payment on every account at central banks and correspondents, mapped to currencies and payment systems, plus the start-of-day collateral position. Banks build a time-series store of intraday account movements fed from RTGS statements (for example camt.053 and camt.054 messages, Chapter 12.2) and internal payment engines, and reconcile them to the end-of-day balance.

**Analogy.** BCBS 248 is like a regulator asking a delivery company not just whether all parcels were delivered by the end of the day, but at what hours, how close the vans came to running out of fuel, and what would happen if a main depot closed.

**Key takeaways**

- BCBS 248 (2013) defines monitoring tools, not minimum ratios, for intraday liquidity.
- Group A tools apply to all banks (peak usage, available liquidity, total payments, time-specific obligations); B to correspondent banks; C (throughput) to direct participants.
- Banks report monthly statistics such as the three largest daily values and averages, and assess the tools under four stress scenarios.
- Implementation requires timestamped payment and account data across all currencies and payment systems.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Which BCBS 248 tool would show that a bank sends most of its payments late in the day?
> 2. **Intermediate:** On its worst day, a bank's peak net cumulative outflow was EUR 2.1bn against available intraday liquidity of EUR 2.4bn. Under a market-wide stress, the value of collateral for intraday credit falls by 15% (the collateral provides EUR 1.6bn of the EUR 2.4bn). Does the bank still cover its peak usage?
> 3. **Interview:** "Design a pipeline that produces BCBS 248 metrics for 12 currencies and 9 payment systems." *Hint:* ingest settlement timestamps from RTGS and correspondent statements, normalize to a common event model with account, currency and system; compute net cumulative positions by time; handle late or missing statements and time zones; store daily results for monthly aggregation; and reconcile to end-of-day balances.

<a id="93-regulatory-reporting"></a>
### 9.3 Regulatory Reporting

Regulation is enforced through data: supervisors see a bank mainly through the reports it submits. This subchapter covers the main EU and US reporting frameworks, the technical formats in which reports are exchanged, and the data lineage and risk data aggregation principles (BCBS 239) that make reported numbers trustworthy. For many engineers in banks, regulatory reporting is where treasury data ends up and where every data defect becomes visible.

#### COREP and FINREP

**Why it matters.** Before 2014, each EU country had its own reporting formats, so supervisors could not compare banks across borders, and groups had to produce different reports for each subsidiary. With a single rulebook (Chapter 9.1), the EU also introduced uniform supervisory reporting: **COREP** (Common Reporting) for prudential data and **FINREP** (Financial Reporting) for accounting data. They are defined in an implementing technical standard (ITS) on supervisory reporting drafted by the EBA and adopted by the Commission (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/451, replaced from 2025 by a new ITS reflecting CRR3), and they are the backbone of how the ECB and national authorities monitor EU banks.

**What they contain.**

| Framework | Purpose | Selected templates | Frequency |
|---|---|---|---|
| COREP: own funds and requirements | Capital adequacy | C 01.00 own funds, C 02.00 own funds requirements, C 03.00 capital ratios, C 07.00 credit risk (standardized), C 08 credit risk (IRB), C 16.00 operational risk, market risk and CVA templates | Quarterly |
| COREP: large exposures | Concentration of exposures to single clients and groups | C 26 to C 29 | Quarterly |
| COREP: leverage | Leverage ratio and exposure measure | C 40 to C 48 (calculation in C 47.00) | Quarterly |
| COREP: liquidity | LCR, NSFR, ALMM | LCR C 72 to C 76; NSFR C 80, C 81, C 84; ALMM C 66 to C 71 (Chapter 9.2) | LCR and ALMM monthly, NSFR quarterly |
| FINREP | Balance sheet, P&L and breakdowns on an IFRS (or national GAAP) basis | F 01 balance sheet, F 02 P&L, F 18 performing and non-performing exposures, F 40 group structure | Quarterly, some annual |

Remittance deadlines are fixed in the ITS. For quarterly reports, they are 12 May, 11 August, 11 November and 11 February; monthly liquidity reports are due 15 calendar days after the reference date. The bank submits to its national competent authority, which forwards data to the ECB and EBA.

**Scope of consolidation.** COREP uses the **prudential** scope of consolidation (banking group, excluding insurance subsidiaries and some special purpose entities), while the published financial statements use the **accounting** scope. FINREP is reported on the prudential scope. Reconciling the two scopes is a recurring source of differences.

**How a COREP report is produced.**

```text
  Source systems              Calculation engines             Reporting layer
```
