```text
  ------------------          ---------------------           ------------------------
  Loans, deposits      ---->  RWA engine (credit, CCR)  --+
  Treasury (Murex,     ---->  Market risk / CVA engine   --+-->  Regulatory data  --> Templates
   Calypso...)                Liquidity engine (LCR,     --+     warehouse            (COREP/FINREP)
  General ledger       ---->   NSFR, ALMM)                 |     (reconciled to GL)        |
  Reference data       ---->  Own funds calculation     --+                               v
  (counterparties,                                                                Validation rules
   ratings, collateral)                                                           (EBA + national)
                                                                                         |
                                                                                         v
                                                                                 XBRL / xBRL-CSV
                                                                                 file -> supervisor
```

**Example: linking FINREP and COREP (EUR millions).**

```text
  FINREP F 01.03 Total equity (accounting, prudential scope)          7,050
  - Interim profit not yet eligible (no verified audit)                (300)
  - Proposed dividends                                                 (150)
  - AT1 instruments classified as equity in accounting                 (500)
  - Intangible assets and goodwill (net of deferred tax)               (180)
  - Deferred tax assets relying on future profitability                 (70)
  - Prudential filters and other deductions (e.g. AVA, own credit)      (50)
  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
  COREP C 01.00 Common Equity Tier 1                                  5,800
  COREP C 02.00 Total risk exposure amount (RWA)                     46,000
  COREP C 03.00 CET1 ratio                                            12.61%
```

Supervisors and auditors expect this bridge to be explainable line by line. A frequent finding is that the regulatory report uses a different data snapshot from the accounts, so the bridge contains an unexplained residual.

**Validation rules.** The EBA publishes thousands of validation rules: for example, that a total equals the sum of its components, that a ratio in C 03.00 equals capital from C 01.00 divided by RWA from C 02.00, or that a value in one template matches another. A file with blocking validation errors is rejected; non-blocking warnings must be explained.

**Analogy.** COREP and FINREP are like a standardized medical record format that every hospital in the EU must use: the doctor can compare patients from different hospitals immediately, but every hospital has to map its own notes into the official boxes.

**Key takeaways**

- COREP covers prudential data (capital, large exposures, leverage, liquidity); FINREP covers accounting data on the prudential scope.
- Both are defined in EU implementing technical standards with fixed templates, frequencies and remittance dates.
- Reports are produced from calculation engines and a regulatory data layer reconciled to the general ledger, and checked with EBA validation rules.
- The bridge from accounting equity to regulatory capital and the consistency across templates are key points of supervisory scrutiny.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Which framework (COREP or FINREP) contains: the LCR; non-performing exposures; the CET1 ratio; the income statement?
> 2. **Intermediate:** In the example, the auditors verify the interim profit of EUR 300m and the bank decides to include it in CET1 net of the proposed dividend already deducted. Recompute CET1 and the CET1 ratio.
> 3. **Interview:** "Five days before the COREP deadline, an EBA validation rule fails because the sum of exposure classes in C 07.00 does not match the total in C 02.00. How would you approach it?" *Hint:* identify which side changed since the last successful run, compare at exposure level between the two templates' data sources, check for exposures falling into no exposure class (classification gaps), rounding and FX conversion; fix at source rather than with a manual adjustment, and document any adjustment that remains.

#### FR 2052a and US Reporting

**Why it matters.** US supervisors took a different approach to liquidity reporting after 2008. Instead of collecting computed ratios in fixed templates, the Federal Reserve collects granular, product-level cash flow data from large banks, often daily, and computes the LCR and its own stress analyses itself. This report, the **FR 2052a Complex Institution Liquidity Monitoring Report**, is the core of US liquidity supervision. Any bank with a significant US presence, including foreign banks through their US intermediate holding company, has to build it.

**Structure of the FR 2052a.**

```text
  FR 2052a
  |
  +-- Inflows     Assets (I.A)  Unsecured (I.U)  Secured (I.S)  Other (I.O)
  |
  +-- Outflows    Deposits (O.D)  Wholesale (O.W)  Secured (O.S)  Other (O.O)
  |
  +-- Supplemental   Derivatives and collateral (S.DC)  LRM (S.L)  Balance sheet (S.B)
                     Informational (S.I)  Foreign exchange (S.FX)

  Each row = one combination of:
    reporting entity | product | currency | counterparty type | collateral class |
    maturity bucket  | flags (insured, operational, forward start, ...) | amount (+ market value)
```

- **Granularity:** each product code is defined precisely (for example transactional deposit accounts, operational balances, repos by collateral class), so the Fed can apply its own run-off assumptions.
- **Maturity buckets:** daily buckets for the first 60 days, then progressively wider buckets up to more than 5 years. This is what lets the Fed apply the US LCR "peak day" test.
- **Frequency:** daily for the largest firms (Category I and II, and Category III firms with high short-term wholesale funding), monthly for other firms in scope, with short submission lags set out in the report instructions.
- **Use:** the LCR and NSFR, horizontal comparisons across banks, and ad hoc stress analysis, for example during the March 2023 regional bank stress.

**Example: a few FR 2052a rows (simplified, USD millions).**

| Table | Product | Counterparty | Collateral class | Maturity bucket | Insured | Amount |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| O.D | Transactional accounts | Retail | n/a | Open | FDIC | 12,400 |
| O.D | Non-transactional relationship accounts | Non-financial corporate | n/a | Open | Uninsured | 6,800 |
| O.S | Repo | Non-bank financial | Level 1 (US Treasuries) | Day 1 | n/a | 3,200 |
| I.A | Unencumbered assets | n/a | Level 1 (US Treasuries) | Open | n/a | 9,500 |
| O.W | Unsecured wholesale funding | Bank | n/a | Day 15 | n/a | 750 |

Every row must be traceable to source positions. The Fed checks consistency of FR 2052a with the published LCR disclosure and with other reports, and runs validation edits on each submission.

**Other US reports relevant to treasury.**

| Report | Filer | Content |
|---|---|---|
| FR Y-9C | Bank holding companies | Consolidated balance sheet, income statement and regulatory capital |
| FFIEC 031 / 041 (Call Report) | Insured banks | Bank-level financial and capital data, published by the FFIEC |
| FFIEC 101 | Advanced approaches banks | Detailed risk-based capital data |
| FR Y-14A / Q / M | Banks in the Fed's stress test | Granular portfolio, loan and position data for stress testing and the stress capital buffer |
| FR Y-15 | Large holding companies | Systemic risk indicators used for G-SIB scores and tailoring categories |
| FFIEC 009 | Banks with foreign exposure | Country risk exposures |

**EU vs US approach.**

| Aspect | EU (COREP liquidity) | US (FR 2052a) |
|---|---|---|
| What is reported | Pre-computed regulatory categories in templates | Granular product-level cash flows |
| Who computes the LCR | The bank, in the template | The bank (for compliance) and the Fed (from the data) |
| Frequency | Monthly | Daily for the largest firms, monthly for others |
| Change management | Template changes with new ITS releases | Instruction updates to product definitions and flags |

**Analogy.** COREP is like handing in your tax return with the totals already calculated; FR 2052a is like handing over every receipt sorted by type, so the tax office can do the calculation itself and run any "what if" it likes.

**Key takeaways**

- FR 2052a is the Federal Reserve's granular liquidity report, filed daily by the largest firms and monthly by others.
- It is organized into inflow, outflow and supplemental tables, with rows defined by product, counterparty, collateral, maturity bucket and flags.
- The Fed uses it to monitor the LCR and NSFR and to run its own stress analyses.
- Other key US reports include FR Y-9C, the Call Report, FFIEC 101, FR Y-14 and FR Y-15.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain the main difference between how the EU and the US collect liquidity data from banks.
> 2. **Intermediate:** A USD 500m term deposit from a non-financial corporate matures in 12 days and USD 300m of it is expected to be rolled over. How would it appear in the FR 2052a, and why does the report not ask for the expected roll-over?
> 3. **Interview:** "We file FR 2052a daily and the deadline is in four hours. One source system's feed has not arrived. What do you do?" *Hint:* follow a documented fallback (for example prior-day positions adjusted for known maturities) with explicit approvals; quantify materiality; flag the estimate in internal records; resubmit if needed and notify the supervisor according to policy; and fix the root cause with monitoring of feed timeliness.

#### Reporting Taxonomies (XBRL, DPM)

**Why it matters.** A regulatory report with thousands of cells, sent by thousands of banks, cannot be processed as PDFs or spreadsheets. Supervisors need a machine-readable format with an unambiguous definition of every data point, so that values can be validated automatically and compared across banks and over time. The EU uses the **Data Point Model (DPM)** to define the meaning of each cell and **XBRL** as the exchange format. Engineers who build reporting pipelines work directly with these artefacts.

**DPM: the dictionary.** The DPM describes each reported value as a combination of a **metric** and a set of **dimensions**, independently of the template layout.

```text
  Template view (what a human sees)            DPM view (what a machine sees)
  ---------------------------------            ------------------------------------------------
  C 07.00, exposure class "Corporates",        Metric:     Exposure value (monetary, instant)
  row "Total exposures",                       Dimensions: Approach     = Standardized
  column "Exposure value"                                  Exposure cl. = Corporates
                 |                                         Base         = On- and off-balance
                 v                                         ...
             1,234,567,000                     Data point ID: unique code for this combination
```

Because two cells in different templates may refer to the same data point, the DPM makes cross-template consistency explicit. The EBA publishes each version of the DPM with its templates, data point dictionary and validation rules as a **reporting framework release** (for example 3.x, 4.x), each applicable from a given reference date.

**XBRL: the envelope.** eXtensible Business Reporting Language is an XML-based standard for business reporting:

- A **taxonomy** (schemas and linkbases) defines the concepts, dimensions, labels and validation formulas generated from the DPM.
- An **instance document** contains the reported **facts**. Each fact has a value, a concept and a **context** (reporting entity, period and dimension members).
- **Filing rules** constrain how instances are built (for example, one entity and reference date per file).
- **xBRL-CSV** represents the same facts as CSV tables plus a JSON metadata file. It is much more compact for large reports, and the EBA has moved its frameworks to it.

**Example: one fact in XBRL and xBRL-CSV (simplified, identifiers illustrative).**

```xml
<!-- context: who, when and which dimension members -->
<xbrli:context id="c1">
  <xbrli:entity>
    <xbrli:identifier scheme="http://standards.iso.org/iso/17442">529900EXAMPLE0LEI0001.CON</xbrli:identifier>
  </xbrli:entity>
  <xbrli:period><xbrli:instant>2026-06-30</xbrli:instant></xbrli:period>
  <xbrli:scenario>
    <xbrldi:explicitMember dimension="eba_dim:APR">eba_AP:x12</xbrldi:explicitMember>  <!-- approach -->
    <xbrldi:explicitMember dimension="eba_dim:EXC">eba_EC:x30</xbrldi:explicitMember>  <!-- exposure class -->
  </xbrli:scenario>
</xbrli:context>

<!-- the fact: metric, context, unit, value -->
<eba_met:mi123 contextRef="c1" unitRef="EUR" decimals="-3">1234567000</eba_met:mi123>
```

```text
  xBRL-CSV equivalent, table file c_07.00.csv:

  datapoint,factValue
  dp123456,1234567000
  dp123457,987654000
  ...
```

**Validation rule example.** A rule such as `{C 03.00, r0010} = {C 01.00, r0020} / {C 02.00, r0010}` (CET1 ratio equals CET1 divided by total RWA) is expressed as an XBRL formula and evaluated by the bank before submission and by the supervisor on receipt.

**Beyond the EU.** XBRL is also used by the US FFIEC for Call Reports, by many other banking supervisors, and by securities regulators for listed companies' financial statements (often as inline XBRL, which embeds tags in a human-readable HTML document). Initiatives such as the EU's Integrated Reporting Framework (IReF) and the Banks' Integrated Reporting Dictionary (BIRD) aim to define input data once and derive multiple reports from it.

**Analogy.** The DPM is the dictionary that defines every word, XBRL is the grammar and the envelope that lets the sentence be sent and checked by machine, and the validation rules are the spell checker that refuses a letter with obvious mistakes.

**Key takeaways**

- The DPM defines each reported value as a metric plus dimensions, independent of template layout.
- XBRL taxonomies are generated from the DPM; instance documents carry facts with contexts (entity, period, dimensions).
- xBRL-CSV encodes the same facts compactly and is the direction of travel for EBA reporting.
- Validation rules are machine-executable and checked both by banks before submission and by supervisors on receipt.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** What are the three elements of an XBRL context, and why is the period part of it?
> 2. **Intermediate:** The same data point appears in two templates and the bank reports different values. Explain why this cannot happen if the report is generated from a DPM-based data model, and how it can still happen in practice.
> 3. **Interview:** "The EBA publishes a new reporting framework release every year. How would you design the reporting platform so that releases are cheap to adopt?" *Hint:* load the DPM dictionary and validation rules as metadata rather than hard-coding templates; map internal data to data points through versioned configuration; support several framework versions in parallel by reference date; run the official validation rules in the pipeline; and automate regression comparison between releases.

#### Data Lineage Requirements

**Why it matters.** When a supervisor asks "where does this number in your LCR come from?", the bank must be able to answer precisely: which source records, which transformations and which manual adjustments produced it. Without lineage, errors cannot be traced to their origin, the impact of a system change on reports cannot be assessed, and the bank cannot prove its numbers are complete. Supervisors therefore expect documented, attribute-level lineage for regulatory and risk reports, most explicitly in the ECB's 2024 guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting.

**Concepts.**

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Data lineage | The documented path of data from its origin to its use, including every transformation |
| Business lineage | Lineage expressed in business terms: "LCR stable deposits come from the retail deposit book, classified by deposit insurance coverage" |
| Technical lineage | Lineage at system, table, column and job level |
| Attribute-level lineage | Lineage for each data element (column/field), not just each dataset; expected for critical data |
| Critical data element (CDE) | A data element whose quality materially affects a key report or decision (for example deposit insurance flag, counterparty sector, maturity date) |
| Golden source | The authoritative system of record for a data element |
| End-user computing (EUC) | Spreadsheets and tools outside controlled IT; a frequent break in lineage |

**Example: tracing one LCR value.**

```text
  [Core banking: deposit accounts]                       CDEs: balance, product code,
     account_id, balance, product_code,                        insured_flag, customer_id
     opened_date, insured_flag
            |  daily extract (job DEP_EXTRACT_01), DQ checks: completeness vs GL, null insured_flag
            v
  [Data lake: deposits_raw]
            |  join with customer master on customer_id -> customer_type (retail/SME/corporate)
            |  rule LCR_DEP_CLASS_v7: retail + insured + established relationship -> "stable"
            v
  [Regulatory data mart: lcr_deposit_positions]
            |  aggregate by LCR category, apply run-off rate table v2025.1 (5% stable)
            v
  [LCR engine result: outflow_stable_retail = 1,000]
            |  manual adjustment ADJ-2026-061 (+12, late-booked accounts, approved by Finance)
            v
  [COREP C 73.00, stable retail deposits outflow: 1,012]
```

At each step, lineage records the source, the transformation rule and its version, the controls applied, and any manual adjustment with its owner and approval. If the supervisor challenges the 1,012, the bank can show that 1,000 came from 2.4 million accounts classified by rule version 7 and that 12 came from an approved adjustment.

**How lineage is captured.**

- **Automated technical lineage:** metadata harvested from ETL tools, SQL parsers, data catalogs, or open standards such as OpenLineage emitted by data pipelines.
- **Business lineage:** documented by data owners and linked to the technical lineage in a data catalog.
- **Controls along the chain:** reconciliations (record counts, sums vs general ledger), data quality rules on CDEs, and sign-offs.
- **Weak points:** spreadsheets, manual adjustments, and transformations embedded in reporting tools that do not expose their logic.

**Analogy.** Data lineage is like a supply chain traceability system for food: if a contaminated product is found on a shelf, the producer must be able to trace it back to the farm, the truck and the factory batch within hours, and identify every other product affected.

**Key takeaways**

- Lineage documents how each reported value is derived from source data, including transformations, rule versions and manual adjustments.
- Supervisors expect attribute-level lineage at least for critical data elements of key risk and regulatory reports.
- Automated technical lineage should be linked to business lineage and to the data quality controls at each step.
- Spreadsheets and undocumented manual adjustments are the most common breaks in lineage.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain the difference between business lineage and technical lineage, with an example for the LCR.
> 2. **Intermediate:** A change is planned to the customer master's sector classification. Using the lineage example, list which reports and numbers could be affected and how you would quantify the impact before go-live.
> 3. **Interview:** "Design a lineage solution for a regulatory reporting platform with 40 source systems, a data lake and an Excel-based adjustment process." *Hint:* a graph model of datasets, columns, jobs and rules with versions; automated capture from pipelines (for example OpenLineage events or SQL parsing); replacing Excel adjustments with a controlled adjustment workflow that records owner, reason and approval; and linking CDEs to data quality results so the lineage shows both the path and the health of the data.

#### BCBS 239 Risk Data Aggregation

**Why it matters.** In 2008, many large banks could not quickly answer basic questions such as "what is our total exposure to Lehman Brothers across all entities and products?". Data was spread across incompatible systems and aggregated manually, so risk reports were slow, incomplete and sometimes wrong exactly when they were most needed. In January 2013, the Basel Committee issued **BCBS 239, Principles for effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting**, requiring banks to be able to produce accurate risk data quickly, in normal times and in a crisis. It applies to G-SIBs (from 2016) and is expected of D-SIBs, and supervisors increasingly apply it to all significant banks.

**The 14 principles.**

| Group | Principle | Short meaning |
|---|---|---|
| I. Governance and infrastructure | 1. Governance | Board and senior management own risk data aggregation; it is part of the risk framework |
| | 2. Data architecture and IT infrastructure | Integrated data taxonomies and architecture across the group, also in stress |
| II. Risk data aggregation | 3. Accuracy and integrity | Data is accurate and reconciled, aggregated largely automatically |
| | 4. Completeness | All material risk data across the group is captured |
| | 5. Timeliness | Aggregated data is available quickly, including in stress |
| | 6. Adaptability | The bank can produce ad hoc data for new questions, scenarios and crises |
| III. Risk reporting | 7. Accuracy | Reports precisely convey aggregated data and reflect risk exactly |
| | 8. Comprehensiveness | Reports cover all material risks |
| | 9. Clarity and usefulness | Reports are clear and suited to their audience |
| | 10. Frequency | Report frequency matches the needs and increases in stress |
| | 11. Distribution | Reports reach the right people, securely and in time |
| IV. Supervisory review | 12. Review | Supervisors regularly assess compliance |
| | 13. Remedial actions | Supervisors use tools to enforce remediation |
| | 14. Home/host cooperation | Supervisors cooperate across jurisdictions |

**Compliance in practice.** Implementation has been slow. The Basel Committee's progress report of November 2023 found that only two of the 31 assessed G-SIBs were fully compliant with all principles, a decade after publication. Typical supervisory findings:

- Weak ownership: no clear accountability for data at board and senior management level.
- Fragmented architecture with many manual steps, spreadsheets and reconciliations.
- Incomplete lineage and data quality controls on critical data elements.
- Inability to produce ad hoc stress reports in hours (for example exposure to a counterparty or country in distress).
- Programmes that change reporting tools but leave the underlying data problems untouched.

Supervisors now enforce these principles more directly. The ECB, for instance, can impose capital add-ons or periodic penalty payments for persistent deficiencies.

**Example: a stress-day request.** At 10:00 a large hedge fund defaults. The CRO asks for the group's total exposure by 14:00.

```text
  Capability                       Weak setup (manual)                 BCBS 239-compliant setup
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Find all legal entities of       Email to 6 entities, each with      Group-wide counterparty
  the counterparty group           its own customer IDs                hierarchy based on LEI
  Collect exposures                Spreadsheets from loans, OTC        Daily aggregated exposure
                                   derivatives, repo, prime brokerage  store, all products
  Apply netting and collateral     Inconsistent per desk               Central netting set and
                                                                       collateral data (Ch. 8.3)
  Reconcile                        Not possible in time                Automated controls vs
                                                                       source and GL
  Answer                           Next day, with caveats              Within hours, with known
                                                                       data quality status
```

**Example: data quality metrics for a CDE.** Banks typically define dimensions such as completeness, accuracy, validity, consistency and timeliness, and measure them on each critical data element.

```text
  CDE: counterparty LEI on OTC derivative trades       Threshold   Actual   Status
  completeness (trades with LEI populated)              >= 99.5%    99.82%    OK
  validity (LEI format and check digits valid)          >= 99.9%    99.97%    OK
  consistency (LEI matches counterparty master)         >= 99.5%    98.90%    BREACH -> issue owner: Ref. Data
  timeliness (available by 06:00)                       >= 98%      99.40%    OK
```

**Analogy.** BCBS 239 is like requiring an airline to be able to tell, within minutes of a storm warning, where every aircraft, crew member and passenger is, using one reliable system, rather than phoning each airport and adding up the answers on paper.

**Key takeaways**

- BCBS 239 (2013) sets 14 principles for risk data aggregation and reporting, grouped into governance and infrastructure, aggregation, reporting and supervisory review.
- Its core demands are accuracy, completeness, timeliness and adaptability, in normal times and especially in stress.
- Compliance remains incomplete across large banks; supervisors increasingly enforce it with findings, add-ons and penalties.
- In practice it requires data ownership, an integrated architecture, lineage, data quality controls on CDEs and the ability to answer ad hoc questions quickly.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Name the four groups of BCBS 239 principles and one principle from each.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Which BCBS 239 principles are most at risk if the liquidity report depends on a spreadsheet that one analyst updates manually every morning? Explain for each.
> 3. **Interview:** "You are asked to lead the BCBS 239 remediation for treasury risk data. Where do you start?" *Hint:* identify the key reports and their CDEs, assign owners, measure data quality and lineage gaps, prioritize by materiality and supervisory findings, fix data at source rather than in reporting, automate reconciliations, and prove timeliness and adaptability with stress drills.

<a id="94-conduct-and-compliance"></a>
### 9.4 Conduct and Compliance

Prudential regulation keeps banks solvent and liquid; conduct regulation keeps them honest and keeps the financial system from being used for crime. This subchapter covers the conduct rules that most directly affect treasury and its systems: anti-money laundering and know-your-customer, sanctions screening, market abuse, derivative trade reporting and record-keeping. Breaches here rarely threaten solvency directly, but they lead to some of the largest fines in banking, to criminal liability for individuals and to restrictions on doing business.

#### AML and KYC Basics

**Why it matters.** Criminals need to make the proceeds of drug trafficking, fraud, corruption or tax evasion look legitimate, and to move money for terrorism. Banks are the gateway to the financial system, so the law makes them responsible for not knowingly or negligently helping. Failures are punished severely: Danske Bank's Estonian branch processed around EUR 200bn of suspicious flows and the bank pleaded guilty in the US in 2022, and TD Bank pleaded guilty in 2024 and paid about USD 3bn in penalties, with an asset cap on its US business. **Anti-money laundering (AML)** is the overall framework; **know your customer (KYC)** is the part that establishes who the bank is dealing with.

**How money laundering works.**

```text
  Placement                     Layering                          Integration
  -----------                   ----------                        -------------
  Illicit cash enters the  -->  Funds are moved through many  --> Funds return as apparently
  financial system (cash        accounts, entities, countries     legitimate wealth (property,
  deposits, cash-intensive      and products to hide their        business investment, loans
  businesses)                   origin (wires, FX, securities,    repaid with "profits")
                                trade invoices, shell companies)
```

**Framework.**

- **International standard:** the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), founded in 1989, issues 40 Recommendations and evaluates countries; jurisdictions with strategic deficiencies are placed on its "grey" or "black" lists.
- **EU:** successive AML directives, now replaced by a 2024 AML package: a directly applicable AML Regulation (AMLR, applying from July 2027), a new directive, and a new EU Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) in Frankfurt, which will directly supervise selected high-risk institutions.
- **US:** the Bank Secrecy Act (1970) and the USA PATRIOT Act (2001), enforced by FinCEN and the banking agencies; cash transactions above USD 10,000 require a Currency Transaction Report (CTR).
- **Risk-based approach:** effort should be proportional to risk. Every customer is identified, but high-risk customers receive deeper scrutiny.

**The KYC lifecycle.**

```text
  Onboarding                 Risk rating          Ongoing monitoring              Review / exit
  -------------------        -------------        -------------------------       --------------
  Customer identification -> Customer risk   -->  Transaction monitoring    -->   Periodic review
  (CIP): name, address,      score: low /         Screening (sanctions,          (e.g. high risk 1y,
  date of birth, ID docs     medium / high        PEP, adverse media)            medium 3y, low 5y)
  Customer due diligence                          Event-driven review            Exit relationship if
  (CDD): purpose, nature,                         (new owner, alert, news)       risk unacceptable
  beneficial owners                               Suspicious activity ->
  Enhanced due diligence                          SAR / STR to the FIU
  (EDD) for high risk
```

- **Beneficial owner:** the natural person who ultimately owns or controls a customer; typically any person holding more than 25%, plus a person exercising control.
- **Politically exposed persons (PEPs):** people with prominent public functions, their family and close associates; EDD is mandatory.
- **Suspicious activity reports (SARs) / suspicious transaction reports (STRs):** filed with the national Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) when the bank suspects money laundering. The customer must not be told (the **tipping-off** prohibition).

**Why treasury cares.** Treasury deals mostly with banks, funds and corporates, not with retail customers, but:

- Every trading counterparty must be onboarded with KYC before the first trade; the system must block trading with counterparties whose KYC is missing or expired.
- **Correspondent banking** (nostro and vostro accounts, Chapter 2.1) is high risk: the bank processes payments for customers of another bank that it does not know directly, so it must assess the respondent bank's AML controls.
- Trade finance, cross-border FX and securities transactions can be used for layering.
- Counterparty identifiers (LEI) and legal hierarchies from KYC are reused for credit limits (Chapter 8.3), regulatory reporting and sanctions screening.

**Example: customer risk scoring.**

| Factor | Customer A: domestic manufacturer | Customer B: offshore trading company |
|---|---|---|
| Country of incorporation | Low risk (1) | High risk / secrecy jurisdiction (3) |
| Ownership structure | Simple, listed parent (1) | Three layers of holding companies, nominee directors (3) |
| Industry | Manufacturing (1) | Commodity trading (2) |
| Products used | Payments, FX forwards (1) | Large cross-border wires, cash deposits (3) |
| PEP connection | None (0) | Shareholder is a relative of a minister (3) |
| **Score / rating** | **4 / Low** | **14 / High: EDD, senior approval, annual review** |

**Example: a transaction monitoring rule for structuring.**

```text
  Rule STRUCT-01: possible structuring (splitting cash deposits to avoid the CTR threshold)
    IF   count(cash deposits between USD 8,000 and 9,999, same customer, rolling 10 days) >= 3
    AND  sum(those deposits) > USD 25,000
    THEN create alert, priority = medium (high if customer risk = high)

  Customer C, days 1-8: 9,500 | 9,200 | 9,800 | 9,400   -> 4 deposits, total 37,900 -> ALERT
```

An analyst investigates the alert and decides whether to close it with a documented rationale or file a SAR. Monitoring systems often produce more than 90% false positives, so tuning rules and prioritizing alerts is a major engineering and analytics topic.

**Analogy.** KYC is the check-in desk of an airport: it verifies who you are before you board. Transaction monitoring is the security camera system that watches for suspicious behaviour once you are inside.

**Key takeaways**

- Money laundering follows placement, layering and integration; banks must prevent and detect it under a risk-based approach.
- KYC identifies the customer and its beneficial owners, assesses risk and applies enhanced due diligence to high-risk customers such as PEPs.
- Ongoing transaction monitoring generates alerts; suspicions are reported to the FIU without tipping off the customer.
- Treasury systems must enforce KYC status before trading and reuse KYC reference data for limits, reporting and screening.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Map each activity to placement, layering or integration: buying a property with funds from a shell company; depositing cash in several branches; wiring funds through three countries via FX conversions.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Propose two transaction monitoring rules for a correspondent banking relationship and describe one legitimate pattern that each rule might wrongly flag.
> 3. **Interview:** "How would you make sure no trade can be booked with a counterparty whose KYC has expired?" *Hint:* a pre-trade check against a KYC status service (with clear behaviour when it is unavailable), status events published on expiry or change, blocking in all booking channels including manual ones, exception workflows with approvals, and a daily reconciliation of new trades against KYC status.

#### Sanctions Screening

**Why it matters.** Governments use economic sanctions to put pressure on countries, regimes, organizations and individuals, for example in response to wars, terrorism, weapons proliferation or human rights abuses. Banks are the main enforcement point: a sanctioned party cannot be paid, its assets must be frozen, and certain transactions are prohibited. Liability is often **strict**: a bank can be fined even if it did not know it was dealing with a sanctioned party, and fines can reach billions (BNP Paribas paid about USD 9bn in 2014 for processing payments involving sanctioned countries). Unlike AML, sanctions compliance is mostly about matching names and entities against lists, in real time, without letting anything through.

**Sources of sanctions.**

| Authority | Main lists and rules |
|---|---|
| United Nations Security Council | Consolidated UN list; implemented by member states |
| European Union | EU Consolidated Financial Sanctions List; sectoral restrictions (for example on Russian securities, deposits, financing) |
| United States (OFAC, Treasury) | Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list, sectoral lists, country embargoes; secondary sanctions on non-US persons |
| United Kingdom | UK Sanctions List; financial sanctions enforced by OFSI |
| Other national lists | Switzerland, Japan, Canada, and others |

**Key concepts.**

- **Asset freeze / blocking:** funds of listed persons must be frozen and no funds made available to them.
- **Ownership and control:** sanctions extend to entities owned or controlled by listed persons. Under OFAC's **50% rule**, an entity owned 50% or more in aggregate by one or more SDNs is blocked even if it is not named. The EU applies an ownership test (more than 50%) and a control test, with more case-by-case guidance on aggregating holdings.
- **Sectoral sanctions:** restrictions on certain activities rather than on all dealings, for example buying new debt above a certain maturity issued by listed companies.
- **Jurisdiction:** US sanctions apply to USD payments that clear through US banks, which is why non-US banks screen against OFAC lists as well.
- **Block vs reject:** under OFAC rules, property of an SDN is blocked (held in a frozen account); other prohibited transactions are rejected (returned). Both must be reported to OFAC within 10 business days.

**What is screened.**

```text
  Static (customer) screening                       Transaction (payment) screening
  ------------------------------                    ------------------------------------------
  When: onboarding, list updates (daily or          When: every payment and trade instruction,
        intra-day), customer data changes                 in real time, before release
  What: customers, beneficial owners, directors,    What: all parties and agents (ordering
        guarantors, counterparties                        customer, beneficiary, intermediary
                                                          banks, BICs), free text, addresses,
                                                          vessel names, ports, goods descriptions
                       \                                      /
                        v                                    v
                 Fuzzy matching engine (names, aliases, transliterations, dates of birth)
                        |
                        v
           Alert -> Level 1 review -> Level 2 / compliance -> release | reject | block + report
```

**Fuzzy matching.** Names are spelled inconsistently across alphabets and systems ("Mohammed", "Muhammad", "Mohamad"), so exact matching would miss true hits. Engines use edit distances (Levenshtein, Jaro-Winkler), phonetic algorithms, transliteration tables, token reordering and weighting of common words, plus secondary identifiers (date of birth, nationality, address) to separate true hits from false ones.

**Example: a name match.**

```text
  Payment beneficiary:   "Ivan Petrof"        List entry: "Ivan Petrov" (SDN), DOB 1971-03-12
  Levenshtein distance = 1 (f vs v);  length = 11
  Similarity = 1 - 1/11 = 0.91       threshold for alert = 0.85  -> ALERT

  Analyst review: beneficiary is a company account "Ivan Petrof GmbH", incorporated 2019,
  registered in Austria, no link to the listed person -> false positive, documented and released.
  Good list hygiene: add the entity to a "good guy" list so the same payment does not alert again,
  subject to periodic review.
```

**Example: ownership aggregation.**

```text
       SDN A            SDN B           Person C (not listed)
        30%              25%                  45%
          \               |                   /
           +--------------+------------------+
                          |
                    Company X (not named on any list)

  OFAC 50% rule: 30% + 25% = 55%  ->  Company X is blocked
  A payment to Company X must be blocked although its name produces no screening alert.
  -> Requires ownership data from KYC or third-party providers, not just name screening.
```

**Treasury relevance.** FX and money market payments, securities settlement, collateral transfers and correspondent banking all go through screening. Treasury must also check investment and collateral portfolios against sectoral restrictions (for example, whether a bond issuer became subject to sanctions after purchase), and screening delays must be built into intraday liquidity planning for time-critical payments.

**Analogy.** Sanctions screening is like passport control with a watch list: every traveller is checked against the list, slightly misspelled names must still be caught, and most matches turn out to be people who merely share a common name.

**Key takeaways**

- Sanctions come from the UN, EU, US (OFAC), UK and others; banks must screen against all lists relevant to their activities and currencies.
- Ownership rules extend sanctions to unlisted entities owned or controlled by listed persons; OFAC aggregates holdings under the 50% rule.
- Customers are screened at onboarding and on list updates; payments and trades are screened in real time across all parties and free text.
- Fuzzy matching is needed to catch variants, but produces many false positives that analysts must resolve and document.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain the difference between blocking and rejecting a payment under OFAC rules.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Company Y is owned 40% by SDN D, 15% by Company Z and 45% by unlisted investors. Company Z is itself owned 60% by SDN E. Is Company Y blocked under the OFAC 50% rule? Show your reasoning.
> 3. **Interview:** "Our payment screening engine adds 4 seconds per payment and generates 3,000 alerts per day, 99.5% false positives. How would you improve it?" *Hint:* tune thresholds and matching algorithms by list and field, use secondary identifiers, maintain governed good-guy lists, exploit structured ISO 20022 data, prioritize alerts by risk, measure the effect on true-hit detection with test cases before changing anything, and scale the engine horizontally for latency.

#### Market Abuse Regulation

**Why it matters.** Financial markets only work if participants trust that prices reflect genuine supply and demand and that no one is trading on secret information. Insider dealing and manipulation transfer wealth from honest investors to cheaters and, over time, drive participants away. Banks have been at the centre of major scandals: manipulation of LIBOR and other benchmarks, and collusion in FX markets (the "Cartel" chat rooms) led to fines of around USD 10bn on several banks between 2014 and 2015. The EU **Market Abuse Regulation (MAR, Regulation (EU) 596/2014)**, applicable since July 2016, is the main framework in Europe; the UK applies an onshored version, and the US relies on securities and commodities laws.

**What MAR prohibits.**

| Offence | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Insider dealing | Trading, or cancelling orders, on the basis of inside information | Buying a bank's bonds knowing it will announce an unexpected capital raise |
| Unlawful disclosure | Sharing inside information outside the normal exercise of employment | A treasury employee tells a friend about an imminent issuance |
| Market manipulation | Transactions, orders or information that give false signals or secure an abnormal price | Spoofing, wash trades, marking the close, spreading false rumours, benchmark manipulation |

**Inside information** is information that is precise, not public, relates directly or indirectly to an issuer or instrument, and would be likely to have a significant effect on prices if made public.

**Scope.** Financial instruments traded on EU regulated markets, MTFs and OTFs, and instruments whose value depends on them (including OTC derivatives), plus emission allowances and benchmarks. Spot FX is not a financial instrument under EU law, so it falls outside MAR, but FX derivatives are in scope, and FX spot conduct is covered by the industry FX Global Code (2017) and general conduct rules.

**Obligations on banks.**

- **Surveillance and STORs (Article 16):** anyone professionally arranging or executing transactions must have systems to detect suspicious orders and transactions and report them to the regulator without delay (suspicious transaction and order reports).
- **Insider lists (Article 18):** issuers and those acting for them must keep lists of everyone with access to inside information.
- **Managers' transactions (Article 19):** persons discharging managerial responsibilities must notify their own trades in the issuer's instruments.
- **Market soundings (Article 11):** before a transaction, a bank may share inside information with potential investors only under a documented procedure ("wall-crossing").
- **Safe harbours (Article 5):** buy-back programmes and stabilisation that follow defined conditions are not considered abuse.

**Why treasury is directly exposed.** Treasury is an **issuer**: it prepares bond issuances, capital transactions and buy-backs (Chapter 7.1), which are often inside information. Treasury is also a **trader**: it trades government bonds, futures and swaps for liquidity and hedging. Information barriers ("Chinese walls") between the people preparing an issuance and the people trading must be enforced, and treasury trading must be included in market surveillance.

**Example: spoofing on a bond futures order book.**

```text
  Time      Action by trader T                               Best bid / ask        Effect
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  10:00:00  Resting order: SELL 20 lots at 131.42            131.40 / 131.42
  10:00:01  Places BUY 500 lots at 131.40, 131.39, 131.38    bids look very deep   others raise bids
            (no intention to execute)
  10:00:03  Others lift the offer: T's SELL 20 fills 131.42  131.41 / 131.43
  10:00:04  Cancels all 500 BUY lots                         131.39 / 131.41       book returns
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Surveillance signals: large orders on the opposite side of a small genuine order, cancelled
  within seconds after the small order fills; pattern repeated many times per day;
  high order-to-trade ratio.
```

In the US, spoofing has been a criminal offence since the Dodd-Frank Act. In 2020, JPMorgan paid about USD 920m to settle spoofing charges in precious metals and Treasury futures.

**Engineering view.** Surveillance systems ingest every order event (new, amend, cancel, fill) with precise timestamps, market data and communications (chat, email, voice transcripts), and run pattern detection for spoofing, layering, wash trades, front-running and insider dealing around events such as issuance announcements. Each alert must be investigated, and decisions documented and retained.

**Analogy.** MAR is like the rules of a card game enforced by a casino: you may play skilfully, but not look at others' cards (insider dealing), show your cards to friends (unlawful disclosure) or stack the deck (manipulation), and the casino's cameras (surveillance) must report anything suspicious.

**Key takeaways**

- MAR prohibits insider dealing, unlawful disclosure of inside information and market manipulation, including benchmark manipulation.
- Banks must run surveillance and file STORs, keep insider lists and manage market soundings.
- Treasury is exposed both as an issuer with inside information and as an active trader.
- Effective surveillance needs complete order event data with accurate timestamps, market data and communications.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Which of these is in scope of EU MAR: a spot EUR/USD trade; an EUR/USD FX option; a government bond traded on an MTF; an interest rate swap referencing a listed bond future?
> 2. **Intermediate:** Treasury is preparing an AT1 issuance to be announced in two weeks. Describe the controls needed for the treasury traders who also manage the bank's own bond portfolio.
> 3. **Interview:** "Design a spoofing detection alert for a futures trading desk." *Hint:* reconstruct the order book from order events; look for orders on one side that are large relative to genuine orders on the other side, cancelled shortly after the other side executes; parameterize size ratios and time windows per instrument; score repeated patterns; and test against labelled historical cases to manage false positives.

#### Trade Reporting (EMIR, Dodd-Frank)

**Why it matters.** When Lehman Brothers failed in 2008, regulators could not see who was exposed to whom in the huge over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives market, and AIG had accumulated massive one-way credit default swap positions largely unnoticed. At the 2009 Pittsburgh summit, the G20 agreed that all OTC derivatives should be **reported to trade repositories**, standardized contracts **centrally cleared** and **traded on platforms**, and that non-cleared derivatives should face higher capital and margin requirements. Trade reporting gives regulators a map of the derivatives market. The EU implemented it through **EMIR** and the US through **Title VII of the Dodd-Frank Act**. For a treasury that uses swaps and FX forwards to hedge (Chapter 3.6, 6.3), every trade generates reporting obligations.

**Comparison.**

| Aspect | EU EMIR (Regulation 648/2012, as amended by EMIR Refit) | US Dodd-Frank (CFTC Parts 43 and 45; SEC for security-based swaps) |
|---|---|---|
| What | All derivatives, OTC and exchange-traded | Swaps (CFTC); security-based swaps (SEC, Regulation SBSR) |
| Who reports | Both counterparties (dual-sided); financial counterparties report on behalf of small non-financial counterparties (NFC-) | One reporting counterparty, chosen by hierarchy (swap dealer > major swap participant > financial > non-financial) |
| Where | Registered trade repositories (TRs) | Swap data repositories (SDRs) |
| When | By the end of the working day after execution, modification or termination (T+1) | Regulatory reporting T+1 or T+2 depending on counterparty type; real-time public reporting of price and volume (Part 43) as soon as technologically practicable |
| What else | Daily valuation and margin/collateral updates | Valuation and margin data for swap dealers |
| Format | ISO 20022 XML, around 200 fields since EMIR Refit (April 2024 in the EU, September 2024 in the UK) | CFTC technical specification, aligned with global data elements |

**Global identifiers.** Supervisors agreed common identifiers so that reports from different repositories can be combined:

| Identifier | Standard | Identifies |
|---|---|---|
| LEI (Legal Entity Identifier) | ISO 17442 | Counterparties, brokers, CCPs |
| UTI (Unique Transaction Identifier) | ISO 23897 | The trade; both counterparties must report the same UTI, so one side generates it and shares it |
| UPI (Unique Product Identifier) | ISO 4914 | The product type (for example a fixed-float IRS in EUR referencing EURIBOR 6M) |
| CDE (Critical Data Elements) | CPMI-IOSCO guidance | Harmonized definitions of fields such as notional, price, dates |

**Example: reporting an interest rate swap.** On 14 October 2026, a EU bank's treasury (financial counterparty) enters a EUR 100m 5-year swap with a US swap dealer, paying fixed 2.45% and receiving 6M EURIBOR, cleared at a CCP.

```text
  EMIR (bank reports its side to its TR by end of 15 October 2026)
    UTI                     generated by the swap dealer per UTI hierarchy, shared via confirmation
    Counterparty 1          bank LEI          Counterparty 2      dealer LEI
    Direction               fixed leg payer   Cleared             Y, CCP LEI, clearing timestamp
    UPI                     EUR IRS fixed-float EURIBOR 6M
    Notional                100,000,000 EUR   Effective / maturity 2026-10-16 / 2031-10-16
    Fixed rate              2.45%             Floating index      EURIBOR, 6M
    Action type             NEWT (new)        then daily: VALU (valuation), MARU (margin)

  Dodd-Frank (swap dealer is the reporting counterparty; bank only confirms its data)
    Part 45: dealer reports to an SDR, T+1
    Part 43: price and notional (capped) published anonymously in real time

  Later lifecycle events, each reported:  partial termination -> MODI / TERM,
  error in notional -> CORR, report sent in error -> EROR
```

After clearing, the original bilateral trade is terminated and replaced by two trades with the CCP, each with its own UTI, which must also be reported. This is a frequent source of reconciliation breaks.

**Data quality and reconciliation.** Trade repositories pair and match the reports of the two counterparties on key fields, and send back acceptance or rejection messages and reconciliation statuses. Supervisors monitor the number of unpaired and unmatched trades, late reports and rejected submissions, and EMIR Refit requires counterparties to notify their supervisor of significant reporting errors. Other related regimes follow the same logic: **MiFIR transaction reporting** (orders and transactions in instruments traded on venues, T+1 to the national regulator) and **SFTR** (repos and securities lending, very relevant to treasury funding and collateral activity).

**Engineering view.** A trade reporting system needs an eligibility engine (which regimes apply to which trade), field derivation from trade, static and lifecycle data, UTI generation and sharing, submission and acknowledgement handling, a daily reconciliation against the TR's view of open trades, and workflows to correct rejected and unmatched reports.

**Analogy.** Trade reporting is like requiring every car sale to be registered with a central vehicle registry by the next day: the buyer and seller each file a record with the same contract number, and the registry checks that both records agree.

**Key takeaways**

- Following the 2009 G20 commitments, derivatives must be reported to trade repositories: EMIR in the EU, Dodd-Frank in the US.
- EMIR is dual-sided and covers all derivatives with T+1 deadlines; Dodd-Frank uses a single reporting counterparty and adds real-time public reporting.
- LEI, UTI and UPI make reports combinable across repositories; matching UTIs on both sides is essential.
- Lifecycle events, valuations and collateral must be reported, and reconciliation breaks must be managed actively.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Who reports under EMIR when an EU bank enters an FX forward with an EU corporate that is a small non-financial counterparty (NFC-)?
> 2. **Intermediate:** In the example, the swap is cleared 30 minutes after execution. List the reports the bank must make under EMIR for the original trade and the cleared trade, and explain why both counterparties must use the same UTI.
> 3. **Interview:** "The trade repository reports that 3% of our trades are unmatched with our counterparties. How would you reduce it?" *Hint:* analyse breaks by field and counterparty; check UTI generation and sharing, LEI mapping, notional and date conventions, timing of lifecycle events and clearing; agree data conventions with frequent counterparties; and add pre-submission validation and daily break monitoring with owners.

#### Record-Keeping Obligations

**Why it matters.** Supervisors, auditors, prosecutors and courts often need to reconstruct what happened months or years later: why a trade was executed, what a customer was told, who approved a limit breach, what the trader said on the phone. Record-keeping rules require banks to keep complete, accurate, unalterable and retrievable records for defined periods. Failures are punished even without any other misconduct: between 2021 and 2024, US regulators fined banks and brokers more than USD 2bn in total for letting staff discuss business on WhatsApp and other unmonitored "off-channel" messaging apps.

**Main obligations relevant to treasury.**

| Regime | What must be kept | Minimum retention |
|---|---|---|
| MiFID II (EU) | Records of all services, orders and transactions; telephone conversations and electronic communications that relate to (or are intended to lead to) transactions | 5 years, up to 7 if requested by the regulator |
| EMIR (EU) | Records of every derivative concluded and any modification | 5 years after termination of the contract |
| MAR (EU) | Insider lists; records supporting STORs and surveillance decisions | 5 years |
| AML (EU and US) | Customer due diligence documents and transaction records | 5 years after the end of the relationship or transaction |
| CFTC (US) | Swap dealers: full records of each swap; oral communications | Life of the swap plus 5 years; oral records 1 year |
| SEC Rule 17a-4 (US broker-dealers) | Books, records and business communications, in non-rewriteable form or with a complete audit trail | 3 to 6 years depending on record type |
| Basel / prudential | Data and documentation supporting capital, liquidity and model calculations, regulatory reports | Set by national rules and internal policy (often 7 to 10 years) |

**Properties of a compliant record.**

- **Complete:** all relevant channels captured, including voice, chat, email and mobile devices used for business.
- **Immutable:** records cannot be altered or deleted before the end of the retention period (WORM storage, object lock, or an audit trail of every change).
- **Accurate timestamps:** MiFID II requires business clocks synchronized to UTC, with a maximum divergence of 100 microseconds for high-frequency trading and 1 second for voice trading.
- **Retrievable:** records must be found and produced within short deadlines when the regulator asks, which requires indexing and search, not just storage.
- **Deleted when no longer needed:** data protection law (the GDPR in the EU) requires personal data not to be kept longer than necessary. Legal retention obligations override the right to erasure while they last, but records must be deleted once retention ends, unless a **legal hold** applies due to litigation or investigation.

**Example: a retention schedule implemented as code.**

```text
  record_class                trigger_event           retention    legal_basis
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  OTC_DERIVATIVE_TRADE        trade_termination_date  5y           EMIR Art. 9
  TRADER_VOICE_RECORDING      recording_date          5y (7y opt)  MiFID II Art. 16(7)
  KYC_FILE                    relationship_end_date   5y           AMLR
  LIMIT_BREACH_APPROVAL       approval_date           7y           internal policy
  REGULATORY_REPORT_SNAPSHOT  reference_date          10y          internal policy

  Daily job:
    for each record:
      if legal_hold(record): skip                       # litigation / investigation
      expiry = trigger_event_date + retention
      if today > expiry: delete record and log deletion (who, what, when, under which rule)
```

Example: a swap traded on 3 March 2026 and terminated early on 15 September 2028 must be kept until at least 15 September 2033 under EMIR, even though the trade itself was alive for only two and a half years.

**Engineering view.** Record-keeping touches almost every treasury system: trade capture must keep a full audit trail of amendments (who changed what, when and why), reporting systems must keep the exact data snapshot used for each submitted report, and communications must be captured from approved channels only. Event-sourced designs, append-only logs and storage with retention locks map naturally onto these requirements.

**Analogy.** Record-keeping is like a flight data recorder: it must capture everything relevant, it must be tamper-proof, and it is only valuable if investigators can retrieve and read it quickly after an incident.

**Key takeaways**

- Banks must keep complete, immutable, accurately timestamped and retrievable records of transactions, communications and decisions.
- Retention periods differ by regime (typically at least 5 years) and are often counted from an event such as trade termination or end of relationship.
- Data protection requires deletion after retention ends, except under legal hold; retention schedules should be implemented as rules, not manual processes.
- Off-channel communications are a major enforcement focus; only monitored channels may be used for business.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Under EMIR, until when must a 10-year swap traded on 1 June 2026 be kept if it runs to maturity?
> 2. **Intermediate:** A customer asks the bank to delete all their personal data under the GDPR, two years after closing their accounts and one year after a dispute over an FX trade reached the courts. Which records can be deleted, and which must be kept? Explain.
> 3. **Interview:** "Design the audit trail for a treasury trade capture system so that any trade can be reconstructed as of any point in time." *Hint:* event-sourced or bitemporal model (valid time and system time), append-only storage with retention locks, user, timestamp and reason for each change, linkage to approvals and communications, and query APIs that rebuild the trade and its reports as of a given date.

---

<a id="10-corporate-treasury-and-cash-management-services"></a>
## 10. Corporate Treasury and Cash Management Services

The previous chapters looked at treasury from inside the bank. This chapter looks at the bank's customers: the treasury departments of large companies, who manage working capital, cash and payments across dozens of entities, currencies and banks, and the cash management and trade finance products banks sell them to do so. For a bank, these services bring fee income and stable operational deposits, which are valued highly in funding and liquidity metrics. For engineers, they bring some of the largest flows a bank processes: millions of payments, statements, sweeps, virtual account postings and trade documents that must be routed, reconciled and reported correctly every day.

<a id="101-corporate-treasury-operations"></a>
### 10.1 Corporate Treasury Operations

This subchapter explains what a corporate treasurer is trying to achieve (enough cash in the right place at the lowest cost) and the operating models used to get there: working capital management, cash visibility, payment factories, in-house banks and intercompany netting.

#### Working Capital Management

**Why it matters.** A company can be profitable on paper and still run out of cash. It pays suppliers and staff before customers pay it, and it holds stock in warehouses that has already been paid for but not yet sold. The money tied up in this gap must be financed, either from the company's own cash or from borrowing. Working capital management tries to shrink the gap, so that the business needs less financing for the same level of sales. It is the first question a corporate treasurer asks, and most bank cash management and trade finance products exist to help answer it.

**What it is.** **Net working capital** is the operating part of the balance sheet that turns over in the normal course of business:

```text
  Net working capital = Accounts receivable + Inventory - Accounts payable
                        (owed by customers)  (stock)     (owed to suppliers)
```

Treasurers measure it in days, because days are comparable across companies of different size and translate directly into cash:

| Metric | Formula | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| DSO (days sales outstanding) | Receivables / Revenue x 365 | How long customers take to pay |
| DIO (days inventory outstanding) | Inventory / Cost of goods sold x 365 | How long goods sit in stock |
| DPO (days payables outstanding) | Payables / Cost of goods sold x 365 | How long the company takes to pay suppliers |
| CCC (cash conversion cycle) | DSO + DIO - DPO | Days between paying for inputs and collecting cash from sales |

**The cash conversion cycle.**

```text
  Day 0           Day 40               Day 50                 Day 100
   |                |                    |                       |
   Goods received   Supplier paid        Goods sold              Customer pays
   |<---- DPO 40 -->|                    |                       |
   |<-------- DIO 50 ------------------->|<------ DSO 50 ------->|
                    |<----------- CCC = 50 + 50 - 40 = 60 days ->|
                    cash out                                  cash in
```

**Example: what a day is worth.** A distributor has annual revenue of EUR 365 million (EUR 1 million per day) and cost of goods sold of EUR 292 million (EUR 0.8 million per day).

```text
  Receivables  EUR 50m  -> DSO = 50 / 365 x 365 = 50 days
  Inventory    EUR 40m  -> DIO = 40 / 292 x 365 = 50 days
  Payables     EUR 32m  -> DPO = 32 / 292 x 365 = 40 days
  CCC = 50 + 50 - 40 = 60 days       Net working capital = 50 + 40 - 32 = EUR 58m

  Reduce DSO by 10 days   -> releases 10 x EUR 1.0m = EUR 10m of cash
  Extend DPO by 10 days   -> releases 10 x EUR 0.8m = EUR  8m of cash
  At a 5% borrowing rate, EUR 18m less debt saves EUR 0.9m interest per year
```

**Levers and the bank products behind them.**

| Lever | Corporate action | Typical bank product |
|---|---|---|
| Collect faster (lower DSO) | Electronic invoicing, direct debits, automatic matching of incoming payments, dunning | Virtual accounts, direct debit collection, lockbox, receivables finance (factoring) |
| Hold less stock (lower DIO) | Better demand planning, just-in-time supply | Inventory finance |
| Pay later (higher DPO) | Negotiate longer payment terms | Supply chain finance (Chapter 10.3), commercial cards |
| Finance the remaining gap | Short-term borrowing | Overdrafts, revolving credit facilities, commercial paper programmes |

**Early payment discounts.** A supplier offering "2/10 net 30" gives 2% off if the invoice is paid within 10 days instead of 30. Skipping the discount means paying 2% to keep the money 20 extra days, an annualized cost of:

```text
  Cost = d / (1 - d) x 365 / (N - D) = 0.02 / 0.98 x 365 / 20 = 37.2% per year
```

Unless the company's cash is worth more than 37% a year, taking the discount is the better choice. These trade-offs are why treasury, procurement and sales argue about payment terms.

**Tension between levers.** Every day gained by one company is lost by its counterparty. Extending DPO from 40 to 90 days helps the buyer and hurts small suppliers, who may fail or raise prices. This is why aggressive payment terms are often combined with supply chain finance, which lets suppliers get paid early at the buyer's credit cost.

**Engineering view.** Working capital metrics are computed from ERP data: receivables and payables ledgers, ageing reports (invoices grouped by days past due) and inventory valuations. Treasury systems pull these for cash forecasting (Chapter 5.2). Common data issues are average versus period-end balances (period-end figures are often "window-dressed" by delaying payments around the reporting date), intercompany invoices that must be excluded, and multiple currencies.

**Analogy.** Working capital is like the water sitting in a long pipe between a reservoir and a tap. The longer the pipe (the cash conversion cycle), the more water is stuck in it at any time, and the more you must pump in before anything comes out.

**Key takeaways**

- Net working capital = receivables + inventory - payables; it is cash tied up in operations that must be financed.
- The cash conversion cycle (DSO + DIO - DPO) measures that gap in days; each day multiplied by daily sales or costs gives cash released.
- Banks sell a product for each lever: collections and receivables finance, inventory finance, supply chain finance and short-term credit.
- Gains for one company are losses for its counterparty; payment terms are a negotiation, not a free lunch.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** A company has revenue of EUR 730 million, receivables of EUR 120 million, cost of goods sold of EUR 500 million, inventory of EUR 70 million and payables of EUR 90 million. Compute DSO, DIO, DPO and the cash conversion cycle.
> 2. **Intermediate:** A supplier offers "1/10 net 45". The company can borrow at 6% per year. Should it take the discount? Show the implied annual cost of not taking it.
> 3. **Interview:** "Our treasury wants a dashboard that shows how much cash would be released by improving working capital in each subsidiary. What data do you need and what pitfalls do you foresee?" *Hint:* per-entity receivables, payables and inventory from the ERP, revenue and COGS on the same period basis, currency conversion, removal of intercompany balances, averaging versus period-end, and translating days into cash using daily sales and costs.

#### Cash Visibility

**Why it matters.** A treasurer cannot manage what they cannot see. A multinational may hold several hundred bank accounts at twenty or more banks in forty countries. If treasury does not know each morning how much cash sits where, it borrows in one place while idle cash sits in another, misses payments, and cannot answer basic questions from the board or rating agencies. Cash visibility is the ability to see, at a defined time each day, the balances and transactions of all accounts in the group, in one place.

**What it involves.** Visibility is built by collecting bank statements from every bank and loading them into a treasury management system (TMS) or a data platform:

```text
  Bank A (DE)  --EBICS-------> camt.053 / camt.052  --+
  Bank B (US)  --SWIFT FileAct--> BAI2 / MT940       --+
  Bank C (UK)  --Host-to-host SFTP--> camt.053       --+-->  Normalize --> TMS cash position
  Bank D (SG)  --API (REST)--> JSON balances          --+     dedupe,       by entity, currency,
  Bank E (BR)  --manual portal download--> CSV        --+     convert FX    bank, account
```

**Types of statement.**

| Report | Timing | Content | Formats |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prior-day (end-of-day) statement | Early morning, for the previous day | Opening and closing booked balance, all booked transactions | MT940, camt.053, BAI2 |
| Intraday report | Several times per day or on request | Interim balances and transactions booked so far | MT942, camt.052, BAI2 intraday |
| Debit/credit notification | Per transaction, near real time | Single booking on an account | camt.054, webhooks |
| API balance query | On demand | Current booked and available balance | Bank-specific JSON, open banking APIs |

ISO 20022 statements carry typed balances, for example `OPBD` (opening booked), `CLBD` (closing booked), `CLAV` (closing available) and `ITBD` (interim booked). The difference between booked and available balance matters: a cheque credited today may be booked but not yet available for use. Message formats are covered in Chapter 12.2.

**Connectivity channels.** Corporates reach their banks through SWIFT (as a corporate member, often through a service bureau), EBICS (a file transfer standard widely used in Germany, France, Austria and Switzerland), host-to-host links over SFTP (Chapter 12.4), bank APIs and, as a last resort, downloads from the bank's web portal. A company with many banks often uses several channels at once.

**Example: a morning cash position.**

```text
  Group cash position, 19 Oct 2026, 08:00 CET, reporting currency EUR

  Entity   Bank     Account    Ccy   Closing booked   FX rate    EUR equiv.   Status
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  DE GmbH  Bank A   DE..0011   EUR      12,400,000    1.0000   12,400,000   received 06:10
  DE GmbH  Bank A   DE..0029   EUR      -1,800,000    1.0000   -1,800,000   received 06:10
  US Inc   Bank B   ..4471     USD       8,250,000    0.9150    7,548,750   received 07:45
  UK Ltd   Bank C   GB..9920   GBP       2,100,000    1.1600    2,436,000   received 05:30
  SG Pte   Bank D   ..7713     SGD       3,000,000    0.7000    2,100,000   received 02:15
  BR Ltda  Bank E   ..0505     BRL      15,000,000    0.1650    2,475,000   MISSING (last: 17 Oct)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Visible today                                                22,684,750
  Visibility ratio = visible balances / total known balances = 22.68 / 25.16 = 90%
```

The Brazilian statement did not arrive, so the position uses a stale balance or excludes it. Treasury must decide which, and the report must say so clearly.

**Common problems.**

- **Time zones:** "end of day" in Singapore is early morning in Europe and the previous evening in New York, so a group position mixes balances taken at different moments.
- **Missing or late statements:** connections fail, banks change formats, holidays differ by country.
- **Format variety:** the same MT940 field is filled differently by different banks; camt.053 has many optional elements.
- **Duplicates and gaps:** a statement may be resent, or one day may be skipped.
- **Restricted countries:** some markets (with capital controls) allow balance reporting but not moving the cash, so visible cash is not always usable cash.

**Engineering view.** A robust statement-loading pipeline checks **continuity** (today's opening balance must equal yesterday's closing balance, and statement sequence numbers must have no gaps), **balance arithmetic** (opening balance plus the sum of transactions equals closing balance), and **duplicates** (by statement ID, account and date). It records the time each statement was received, flags stale accounts and keeps the raw file for audit. Intraday reports should be replaced, not added, when the final end-of-day statement arrives, otherwise transactions are counted twice.

**Analogy.** Cash visibility is like air traffic control. Each bank is a radar station reporting the aircraft it sees; the controller needs one screen combining all stations, with a clear mark on any area where a radar has gone silent.

**Key takeaways**

- Cash visibility means seeing all group balances and transactions in one place at a defined time each day; it is the basis of every other treasury decision.
- Data arrives as prior-day statements (MT940, camt.053, BAI2), intraday reports (MT942, camt.052) and notifications or API calls, over SWIFT, EBICS, host-to-host and APIs.
- Visibility ratio, statement timeliness and continuity checks are the key quality measures.
- Visible cash is not always usable cash: time zones, value dates and capital controls matter.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** What is the difference between a camt.053 and a camt.052 message, and when would a treasurer use each?
> 2. **Intermediate:** Yesterday's closing balance on an account was EUR 4,000,000. Today's statement shows an opening balance of EUR 3,950,000, credits of EUR 1,200,000, debits of EUR 900,000 and a closing balance of EUR 4,250,000. Which checks fail, and what could explain each failure?
> 3. **Interview:** "Design the ingestion service that loads bank statements from 30 banks into our TMS." *Hint:* channel adapters per bank, a canonical statement model, parsers per format and per bank variant, continuity and balance arithmetic checks, idempotent loading keyed on statement identity, handling of intraday versus final statements, monitoring of late statements per bank cut-off, and retention of raw files.

#### Payment Factories

**Why it matters.** In a decentralized group, every subsidiary runs its own payments: its own bank accounts, its own e-banking tokens, its own formats and its own approval rules. The result is hundreds of bank connections, inconsistent controls, duplicated fees and payments that headquarters only discovers on the statement. Fraud often enters through the weakest subsidiary. A **payment factory** centralizes the processing of outgoing payments for the whole group into one hub with one set of controls and connections.

**What it is.** A payment factory receives payment files from the ERP systems of all group entities, validates, enriches and approves them centrally, and sends them to the banks in standard formats. Two models exist:

| Model | How payments are made | Accounts needed | Bank sees as debtor |
|---|---|---|---|
| **In the name of** (routing model) | The factory sends payments from each subsidiary's own bank account | Each subsidiary keeps local accounts | The subsidiary |
| **On behalf of** (POBO) | The factory pays from its own (or the in-house bank's) account on behalf of the subsidiary | Subsidiaries can close most accounts | The central entity, with the subsidiary as ultimate debtor |

The mirror image for receipts is **collections on behalf of** (COBO): customers pay into a central account, and the receipts are allocated to the subsidiary that issued the invoice.

**Flow.**

```text
  ERP DE ---+                       Payment factory
  ERP FR ---+--> pain.001 / CSV --> 1. Validate format, mandatory fields, IBAN/BIC
  ERP US ---+                       2. Enrich (bank routing, charges, purpose codes)
  ERP SG ---+                       3. Sanctions and fraud screening, duplicate check
                                    4. Approval workflow (four-eyes, limits)
                                    5. Netting / POBO conversion where applicable
                                    6. Route to bank and channel, respect cut-offs
                                           |
                       +-------------------+-------------------+
                       v                   v                   v
                    Bank A (EUR)        Bank B (USD)        Bank D (SGD)
                       |                   |                   |
                       +---- pain.002 status reports ----------+--> back to factory and ERPs
```

**Example: POBO payment in ISO 20022.** The French subsidiary owes a supplier EUR 25,000. Under POBO, the payment factory pays it from the group's central account in Germany:

```text
  pain.001 (simplified)
    Debtor:            Group Treasury GmbH       <- account holder
    DebtorAccount:     DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130 00
    UltimateDebtor:    Group France SAS          <- on whose behalf
    Creditor:          Fournisseur SARL
    CreditorAccount:   FR76 3000 6000 0112 3456 7890 189
    Amount:            EUR 25,000.00
    RemittanceInfo:    INV-2026-4471

  Booking: Group Treasury pays external supplier;
           Group France's internal account at the in-house bank is debited EUR 25,000.
```

The `UltimateDebtor` field lets the supplier and its bank see who the payment is really from, which helps reconciliation and satisfies payment transparency rules.

**Benefits and constraints.**

| Benefits | Constraints |
|---|---|
| Fewer bank connections and accounts, lower fees | Some countries restrict or forbid POBO (for example markets with capital controls or local currency rules) |
| One set of controls: segregation of duties, sanctions screening, fraud rules | Tax and legal questions: who is the payer for VAT, withholding tax and invoices |
| Standard formats (pain.001) instead of many local ones | Suppliers and authorities may reject payments not coming from the invoiced entity |
| Better cash visibility and forecasting, since all payments pass through one point | Central cut-off management across time zones is complex |
| Enables netting and in-house banking | Single point of failure: the factory needs high availability |

**Engineering view.** A payment factory is a high-volume, high-risk workflow system. Key design points are: a canonical payment model mapped to and from many input and output formats; idempotency and duplicate detection (the same invoice must not be paid twice if an ERP resends a file, Chapter 12.4); routing rules by currency, amount, urgency and country; bank cut-off calendars; immutable audit trails of approvals; and end-to-end status tracking by matching pain.002 status reports and bank statements back to the original instruction.

**Analogy.** A payment factory is like a central post office for a company: instead of each department buying its own stamps and driving to different post offices, all letters go to one mailroom that checks addresses, applies postage and hands them to the right carrier.
