- **Store results at the right grain.** Keeping results per trade and scenario enables drill-down and incremental runs, at the cost of storage. Many banks store vectors of P&L per trade (one value per scenario) and aggregate on demand.

**Key takeaways**

- Risk engines revalue portfolios under many scenarios to produce sensitivities, VaR, stress results, PFE and XVA.
- Counterparty exposure and XVA are the most compute-intensive measures because they simulate paths over time for every netting set.
- Banks combine TMS-native risk, specialised vendor engines and in-house quant libraries; front-to-risk consistency is a regulatory concern.
- Completeness checks, deterministic simulations and consistent snapshots are essential for trustworthy results.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain why calculating PFE for a portfolio of interest rate swaps takes far more computation than calculating its DV01.
> 2. **Intermediate:** A historical VaR run has 500 scenarios and 20,000 trades. Calculate the number of trade revaluations for full revaluation. Then estimate the reduction if 15,000 linear trades are handled with sensitivities (one revaluation per sensitivity bump, with 40 buckets) and only the other 5,000 are fully revalued.
> 3. **Interview:** "The risk report shows VaR dropping 30% overnight with no significant change in positions. What do you check first?" *Hint:* consider completeness of tasks and trade population, a missing or stale market data snapshot, scenario set changes, failed trade mappings that drop trades silently, and how you would build controls that detect these automatically.

#### Build vs Buy Decisions

**Why it matters.** Every system described above can be bought from a vendor, built in-house, or assembled from a mix of both. These decisions lock a bank in for ten years or more and cost tens or hundreds of millions. They are rarely pure technology decisions: they involve cost, regulation, differentiation, skills and risk. Engineers are often asked to contribute to them, and knowing the trade-offs helps you both in the decision and in the years of living with it.

**The basic trade-off.**

| Factor | Buy (vendor package) | Build (in-house) |
|---|---|---|
| Time to first value | Faster for standard functions | Slower: everything must be built |
| Functional coverage | Broad, proven on many clients | Only what you build |
| Fit to the bank's processes | The bank adapts to the package, or customises it at a cost | Exact fit |
| Differentiation | Same capabilities as competitors | Can be a competitive advantage |
| Regulatory change | Vendor delivers updates for common rules (Basel, FRTB, ISO 20022) | Bank must implement each change |
| Total cost of ownership | Licences, implementation, upgrades, customisation | Engineering team for the system's lifetime |
| Control and roadmap | Vendor's priorities, vendor lock-in | Full control |
| Key risks | Over-customisation, painful upgrades, vendor viability | Key-person dependency, under-investment over time |

**What usually ends up bought, and what built.** A common pattern in banks is "buy the commodity, build the differentiator, own the data":

```text
   Commodity (buy)                      Differentiator (build or extend)
   ---------------------------------    ---------------------------------
   Trade capture and lifecycle (TMS)    Proprietary pricing models
   Swift / payment connectivity         Client-facing digital channels
   Core banking ledgers                 Liquidity optimisation, funding decisions
   Regulatory reporting templates       Internal analytics and dashboards
   Reconciliation tools                 Integration layer and data platform
```

The integration layer and data platform are almost always the bank's own, whatever is bought. They are where the bank's knowledge of its own data lives, and they make it possible to replace a vendor later.

**A structured evaluation.** A defensible decision compares options on weighted criteria rather than on opinion. For example, for a new intraday liquidity monitoring capability:

| Criterion (weight) | Vendor A (score 1-5) | In-house build (score 1-5) |
|---|---|---|
| Functional fit (25%) | 4 | 5 |
| Time to deliver regulatory requirement (20%) | 4 | 2 |
| 10-year TCO (20%) | 3 | 3 |
| Integration with existing data platform (15%) | 2 | 5 |
| Vendor/key-person risk (10%) | 3 | 2 |
| Regulatory change support (10%) | 4 | 1 |
| **Weighted score** | **3.40** | **3.30** |

The scores are close, which is common. The decision then depends on non-scored factors: whether the regulatory deadline is fixed, whether the bank has the engineering capacity, and whether the capability is strategic.

**Total cost of ownership.** The licence is usually a minority of a vendor package's cost. A realistic TCO includes:

- implementation (integration, data migration, configuration, testing), often several times the first-year licence;
- annual maintenance and licence fees;
- infrastructure and environments (production, DR, several test environments);
- upgrades every few years, each a project in itself;
- the internal team that configures, supports and integrates the package;
- for builds, the full engineering team for the life of the system, not just the first release.

**The customisation trap.** Banks often buy a package and then customise it until it behaves like their old system. Each customisation makes upgrades harder, until the bank is stuck on an unsupported version. The usual guidance is to adopt the package's standard processes where they are not differentiating, and to put unavoidable custom logic outside the package, in the integration layer or in separate services.

**Key takeaways**

- Build-vs-buy decisions weigh time to value, fit, differentiation, regulatory change support, TCO, control and risk.
- Banks tend to buy commodity functions, build differentiating ones and always own their integration layer and data.
- TCO must include implementation, upgrades, infrastructure and the internal team, not just licences.
- Heavy customisation of a package combines the costs of buying and building; keep custom logic outside the package where possible.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Give two reasons why a bank might build its own intraday liquidity dashboard rather than buying one, and two reasons why it might buy.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Estimate a 10-year TCO for a vendor TMS with a licence of 1.5M per year, an implementation of 8M, an internal support team of 10 people at 150k each per year, and a major upgrade of 3M every four years. Compare it with an in-house build requiring 25 engineers for three years and 12 engineers afterwards, at the same cost per person.
> 3. **Interview:** "The business wants a new FX hedging product that our TMS cannot model. The vendor says it will be supported in 18 months. What options do you present?" *Hint:* consider waiting, a tactical side system with strict controls and a decommission plan, extending the TMS through a supported extension point, or modelling the product as a combination of supported products, and compare them on risk, time and cost.

<a id="132-data-architecture"></a>
### 13.2 Data Architecture

This subchapter covers how treasury data is structured and governed: the models for trades and positions, the management of reference and market data, the principle of a single authoritative source for each data item, and two techniques (bitemporal modelling and event sourcing) that let systems answer "what did we know, and when?".

#### Trade and Position Data Models

**Why it matters.** A trade is the basic fact of a treasury system: two parties agreed to exchange cash flows on certain terms. Almost everything else is derived from it: cash flows, settlements, positions, P&L, risk and accounting. If the trade model is wrong or ambiguous, every downstream system inherits the error. A **position** answers a different question: "how much of something do we hold, or owe, right now or on a given date?" Mixing up the two, or deriving positions inconsistently, is one of the most common sources of breaks between systems.

**Trade versus position.**

| Aspect | Trade | Position |
|---|---|---|
| What it records | An agreement at a point in time, with its terms | The net holding or exposure resulting from many trades |
| Granularity | One record per deal (plus versions) | One record per aggregation key (book, instrument, currency, date...) |
| Lifecycle | Created, amended, cancelled, partially terminated, matured | Recalculated whenever trades or market data change |
| Typical source | Captured in the TMS | Derived by a position keeping engine (Chapter 13.3) |
| Authority | Primary data | Derived data: must be reproducible from trades |

**Anatomy of a trade model.** Treasury products vary, but most models share a common structure: a header with economic and organisational attributes, one or more legs, and generated cash flows.

```text
  Trade (header)
  +------------------------------------------------------------+
  | trade_id, version, status (LIVE, CANCELLED, MATURED)       |
  | trade_date, entry_timestamp, trader, book, legal_entity    |
  | counterparty_id, product_type, external refs (UTI, USI)    |
  +------------------------------------------------------------+
        |
        +-- Leg 1 (e.g. fixed leg of a swap)
        |     notional, currency, start_date, end_date,
        |     rate or index (fixed 3.10% / EURIBOR 6M + spread),
        |     day count, payment frequency, calendars, BDC
        |       |
        |       +-- Cash flow 1: pay date, accrual period, amount (or "to be fixed")
        |       +-- Cash flow 2 ...
        |
        +-- Leg 2 (e.g. floating leg)
              ...
  Lifecycle events: NEW, AMEND, PARTIAL_TERMINATION, FIXING, NOVATION, CANCEL, MATURE
```

The leg structure lets one model cover many products: an FX forward has two currency legs with single cash flows, a deposit has one leg with principal and interest flows, and an interest rate swap has a fixed and a floating leg. Standards such as FpML (Chapter 12.3) and ISDA's Common Domain Model (CDM) use the same idea.

**Versioning.** Trades change: a trader corrects the rate, a counterparty asks for a different settlement date, a swap is partially terminated. Two fundamentally different changes must be modelled differently:

| Change | Meaning | Correct modelling |
|---|---|---|
| Correction (amendment of an error) | The trade was always meant to have the new terms | New version replaces the old one from the start; downstream systems restate |
| Lifecycle event (economic change) | The trade's terms change from an effective date onward | Event with an effective date; history before that date remains valid |

Never update trade rows in place. Each change creates a new version with a reason code, user and timestamp, so that the trade can be reconstructed as of any time (see bitemporal modelling below).

**Positions.** A position is an aggregate over trades, defined by an **aggregation key** and a **measure**.

```text
  Trades                                            Positions (key -> measure)
  FX-1 BUY  EUR 10M / SELL USD 11.65M  val 22-Oct   (BOOK_FX, EUR, 22-Oct) -> +10M
  FX-2 SELL EUR  4M / BUY  USD  4.67M  val 22-Oct   (BOOK_FX, EUR, 22-Oct) ->  -4M
  FX-3 BUY  EUR  2M / SELL USD  2.33M  val 24-Oct                   ==> net  +6M
                                                    (BOOK_FX, EUR, 24-Oct) -> +2M
                                                    (BOOK_FX, USD, 22-Oct) -> -6.98M
                                                    (BOOK_FX, USD, 24-Oct) -> -2.33M
```

Typical position types in treasury:

- **Cash positions** by account, currency and value date (the cash ladder, Chapter 5.2);
- **Securities positions** by instrument and account, on a trade-date or settlement-date basis;
- **Risk positions** by risk factor (for example DV01 by currency and tenor bucket);
- **Exposure positions** by counterparty or netting set, for limits.

**Engineering view.**

- Use stable, immutable trade identifiers, plus a version number. Downstream systems should reference `(trade_id, version)` when they need to know exactly what they processed.
- Carry the regulatory identifiers (UTI, LEI) and external references (confirmation IDs, platform IDs) on the trade; matching and reporting need them.
- Make positions reproducible: given the trades and the position rules, you must be able to recompute a position for any date and get the same answer.
- Model "who owns this position" explicitly: book, desk, legal entity and portfolio hierarchy are part of the position key, and hierarchy changes (book moves) are a common source of breaks.

**Key takeaways**

- Trades are primary facts; positions are derived aggregates that must be reproducible from trades.
- A header-legs-cash flows structure lets one model cover deposits, FX, swaps and bonds.
- Distinguish corrections (restate from the start) from lifecycle events (change from an effective date); never update trades in place.
- Positions are defined by an aggregation key and a measure; cash, securities, risk and exposure positions use different keys.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Model a 3-month EUR 25M term deposit placed with another bank as a trade with header, leg and cash flows. Which cash flows does it generate?
> 2. **Intermediate:** A swap's fixed rate was captured as 3.01% instead of 3.10% and corrected two weeks later. A month after that, the swap is partially terminated by 40%. Describe the versions and events stored, and what the P&L system must restate in each case.
> 3. **Interview:** "Design the tables for trades and positions in a new treasury platform supporting deposits, FX forwards and interest rate swaps." *Hint:* consider a generic header/leg/cash flow structure versus product-specific tables, versioning and lifecycle events, the position key, and which data is stored versus recomputed.

#### Reference and Static Data Management

**Why it matters.** A trade record usually contains identifiers only: counterparty `C-10442`, instrument `XS2411234567`, calendar `TARGET`. Everything needed to process it (the counterparty's legal name, LEI, credit limits and settlement instructions, the bond's coupon schedule, the holidays of the calendar) lives in **reference data**, also called **static data** because it changes much less often than trades and prices. Industry studies have repeatedly found that a large share of failed trades and settlement breaks come from poor reference data, especially wrong or outdated settlement instructions. Reference data errors spread to every trade that uses the record.

**Main reference data domains in treasury.**

| Domain | Examples | Typical external source |
|---|---|---|
| Legal entities and counterparties | Name, LEI, parent/ultimate parent, country, sector, credit rating, KYC status | GLEIF, rating agencies, internal KYC |
| Settlement instructions (SSIs) | Account, correspondent bank, BIC per currency and product | Counterparty notices, SWIFT SSI databases, DTCC ALERT |
| Instruments | ISIN, CUSIP, issuer, coupon, maturity, day count, call schedule | Bloomberg, LSEG, ANNA (ISIN), exchanges |
| Calendars | Holidays per city or settlement system (TARGET2, New York, London) | Vendor calendar services, central banks |
| Currencies and conventions | ISO 4217 codes, decimals, spot lag, day count conventions | ISO, market conventions |
| Indices | EURIBOR, SOFR, ESTR: tenor, fixing time, publication lag | Administrators (EMMI, Federal Reserve, ECB) |
| Internal hierarchies | Books, desks, legal entities, cost centres, portfolios | Internal (finance, front office) |

**Lifecycle of a reference data record.**

```text
  Request            Validate                 Approve            Publish             Use
  (operations,  -->  (format, external   -->  (checker,     -->  (distribution  -->  (trade capture,
   front office)      sources, duplicates)     second person)     to systems)         settlement,
                                                                                      risk...)
       ^                                                                                 |
       |                     Periodic review and external updates                        |
       +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

The maker-checker step is mandatory for sensitive data such as SSIs: changing a counterparty's account number is a classic fraud vector. Many banks also require a **call-back** to the counterparty, using a phone number already on file, before an SSI change is activated.

**Distribution patterns.**

| Pattern | Description | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Point-to-point copies | Each system keeps its own copy, maintained by hand or by file | Simple to start | Copies drift; no single version of truth |
| Central hub, scheduled distribution | Central master publishes daily or intraday files to consumers | Consistent at each publication | Latency between change and use |
| Central hub, event publication | Changes published as events on a message bus; consumers update caches | Near real-time, auditable | Consumers must handle ordering and replay |
| Central service, query at use | Consumers call an API when they need the data | Always current | Runtime dependency, latency, availability |

Most banks combine these: an event feed for systems that need to react to changes, plus API lookup for occasional queries.

**Example: a counterparty hierarchy.** Credit limits and large exposure reporting (Chapter 9) aggregate exposure up to the ultimate parent. If one subsidiary is not linked to its parent, the group's exposure is understated.

```text
  Global Bank Holding plc (LEI 5493...A1)          <- ultimate parent
      |
      +-- Global Bank plc (London)      LEI 5493...B2
      |       +-- Global Bank plc, NY branch  (same LEI, different BIC)
      +-- Global Bank AG (Frankfurt)    LEI 5299...C3
      +-- Global Securities LLC (NY)    LEI 2549...D4  <- missing link = understated exposure
```

**Engineering view.**

- Give each reference entity an internal immutable ID, and store external identifiers (LEI, BIC, ISIN) as attributes with validity dates. External identifiers change (corporate actions, mergers) and are sometimes reused.
- Make reference data effective-dated: a holiday added next year, an SSI valid from 1 November, a book moved to another desk at month-end.
- Add data quality rules at the source (mandatory fields, format checks such as LEI check digits and ISIN checksums) and dashboards for completeness and staleness.
- Treat reference data changes as high-risk operations: they need approval, audit trails and, for SSIs, out-of-band verification.

**Key takeaways**

- Reference data describes the entities that trades refer to: counterparties, SSIs, instruments, calendars, indices and internal hierarchies.
- Errors in reference data affect every trade that uses the record; poor SSIs are a leading cause of settlement failures.
- Changes go through request, validation, maker-checker approval and controlled distribution; SSI changes need out-of-band verification.
- Use internal IDs, effective dating and data quality rules; distribute via events or APIs rather than uncontrolled copies.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** List five reference data items needed to settle an FX forward and say where each comes from.
> 2. **Intermediate:** A counterparty sends an email asking to change its USD settlement account from next Monday. Design the process and system controls before the change becomes active.
> 3. **Interview:** "Ten systems each hold their own copy of the counterparty list, and they disagree. How would you introduce a counterparty master without a big-bang migration?" *Hint:* consider building the master from the best existing source, a cross-reference table mapping each system's IDs to master IDs, publishing changes as events, migrating consumers one at a time, and measuring convergence with reconciliation reports.

#### Market Data Management

**Why it matters.** Every valuation, risk figure and many limits depend on market data: FX rates, interest rate fixings, bond prices, volatilities and credit spreads. Wrong market data produces wrong numbers silently: a stale USD/JPY rate or a mistyped swap rate flows straight into P&L, VaR and capital, and nothing crashes. Market data is also expensive (vendor licences are among a bank's largest IT costs) and governed by redistribution rules. **Market data management** covers sourcing, validating, storing and distributing this data, and building derived data such as curves and surfaces from it.

**Raw versus derived market data.**

```text
  Raw (observed)                      Derived (calculated)               Consumers
  +---------------------------+       +----------------------------+     +-----------------+
  | Quotes: deposit rates,    |       | Discount and forward       |     | Pricing         |
  |  futures, swap rates      +------>+ curves (Chapter 11.2)      +---->+ P&L             |
  | FX spot and forward points|       | FX forward curves          |     | VaR / stress    |
  | Bond prices               +------>+ Bond yield / spread curves +---->+ ALM / FTP       |
  | Option quotes             +------>+ Volatility surfaces        +---->+ Limits          |
  | Fixings (SOFR, ESTR,      |       | Historical scenario sets   |     | Accounting (FV) |
  |  EURIBOR)                 |       |  (returns time series)     |     | Collateral      |
  +---------------------------+       +----------------------------+     +-----------------+
```

**Real-time versus end-of-day.**

| Aspect | Real-time (streaming) | End-of-day (official snapshot) |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Trading, pre-trade pricing, intraday risk | Official valuation, P&L, risk, accounting, regulatory reports |
| Source | Vendor streams (Bloomberg B-PIPE, LSEG Real-Time), venues, brokers | Snapshot of streams at a fixed cut-off, vendor closing prices, broker quotes |
| Volume | Thousands of updates per second | One record per instrument per day |
| Validation | Light: filtering, spike detection | Full: tolerance checks, cross-source comparisons, sign-off |
| Storage | Usually not stored at full tick level by treasury | Stored permanently, versioned, used for history and VaR |

**The official end-of-day snapshot.** Banks define a **close** for each region (for example 17:00 London for EUR and GBP products, 17:00 New York for USD products). At the close, the market data system takes a snapshot, validates it, builds curves and publishes an official set that all end-of-day processes use. Using one official set is what makes P&L, risk and accounting consistent.

**Validation rules.** Typical checks before a snapshot is released:

| Check | Example | Action on failure |
|---|---|---|
| Staleness | Quote not updated for 3 days on a liquid instrument | Flag for review, use alternate source |
| Day-on-day jump | 10Y EUR swap rate moves 40bp, threshold 15bp | Require analyst confirmation |
| Cross-source comparison | Bloomberg and LSEG differ by more than tolerance | Investigate, choose source per hierarchy |
| Arbitrage/consistency | Negative forward rates where not plausible, crossed bid/ask, vol surface with calendar arbitrage | Reject or smooth |
| Completeness | Missing tenor points for a curve | Interpolate per policy or use previous with flag |

Each override (manual price, alternate source) is recorded with user, reason and approval. Product control later performs **independent price verification (IPV)**: comparing the prices used for valuation against independent sources and adjusting P&L if needed.

**Example: a market data record.**

```text
  instrument_id : EUR_SWAP_10Y
  field         : MID_RATE
  value         : 0.02745
  as_of_date    : 2026-10-19
  snapshot      : LDN_CLOSE
  source        : VENDOR_A (primary)
  status        : VALIDATED
  overridden    : false
  loaded_at     : 2026-10-19T17:02:13Z
  validated_by  : md_ops_user_17 at 2026-10-19T17:21:40Z
```

Storing `as_of_date` and `snapshot` together lets the same instrument have several official values on one day (London close, New York close, Tokyo close), each used by the processes of that region.

**Licensing.** Vendor contracts restrict who may see data, how it may be redistributed and how derived data may be used. A market data platform must record which users and applications consume which data and report usage to vendors. Building curves from licensed quotes and publishing them to clients, for example, may require separate rights.

**Engineering view.**

- Keep raw quotes, validated values and derived objects (curves, surfaces) as separate layers with lineage between them, so you can explain any curve point from its inputs.
- Make snapshots immutable once published. Corrections create a new snapshot version, and consumers can be told to rerun.
- Separate the time a value applies to (`as_of_date`, snapshot) from the time it was loaded or changed; this is bitemporal data (below).
- Monitor consumers: know which processes used which snapshot version, so you can target reruns after a correction.

**Key takeaways**

- Market data drives valuations, risk and limits; errors propagate silently.
- Distinguish raw observed quotes from derived curves and surfaces, and real-time streams from official end-of-day snapshots.
- The official snapshot is validated (staleness, jumps, cross-source, consistency, completeness), and overrides are recorded and approved.
- Published snapshots are immutable and versioned; licensing rules restrict use and redistribution.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain why a bank uses one official end-of-day market data snapshot for P&L, risk and accounting rather than each system taking its own prices.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Design validation rules for an EUR swap curve snapshot with 15 tenors. Include thresholds, how they differ by tenor, and what happens when a rule fails at 17:30 with the EOD batch due to start at 19:00.
> 3. **Interview:** "After the official snapshot was published and the EOD batch completed, someone finds that the GBP 5Y swap rate was wrong by 20bp. What happens next?" *Hint:* consider who decides whether to correct, creating a new snapshot version, identifying all consumers of the old version, rerunning valuations and P&L, restating reports already sent, and documenting the incident.

#### Golden Source and Data Ownership

**Why it matters.** In a typical bank, the same fact is stored in many places. The counterparty's rating appears in the credit system, the TMS, the risk engine and the reporting warehouse. A trade's notional exists in front office, back office, risk and finance. When the copies disagree, which one is right? Without a clear answer, reports from different departments contradict each other and every disagreement becomes a manual investigation. After the 2008 crisis, regulators found that many banks could not aggregate their exposures quickly or reliably. The Basel Committee responded with **BCBS 239** (Principles for effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, 2013), which requires banks to have clear data ownership, accuracy, completeness and timeliness of risk data. The **golden source** principle is central to meeting it.

**Key concepts.**

| Concept | Definition |
|---|---|
| Golden source (authoritative source) | The single system designated as the authoritative origin of a data item. All other copies are derived from it |
| Data owner | A business role (not IT) accountable for the definition, quality and correct use of a data domain |
| Data steward | The person or team that manages the data day to day: fixing errors, maintaining rules |
| Data lineage | The documented path of a data item from its golden source through transformations to reports |
| Critical data element (CDE) | A data item whose errors materially affect key reports or decisions; gets stricter controls |

**Example: golden sources for treasury data.**

| Data domain | Golden source | Data owner | Main consumers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Treasury trades | TMS | Head of treasury front office | Back office, risk, finance, regulatory reporting |
| Customer loans and deposits | Core banking system | Retail/commercial banking operations | ALM, liquidity, finance |
| Counterparties and LEIs | Counterparty master | Client onboarding / KYC | All |
| SSIs | Settlement instruction master | Operations | TMS, payment hub |
| EOD market data | Market data platform | Product control or market data team | Valuation, risk, finance |
| GL balances | General ledger | Finance (financial control) | Reporting, reconciliations |
| Behavioural model parameters | Model inventory / ALM engine | ALM / treasury | ALM, FTP, liquidity stress |

**Copies are allowed, edits are not.** Consumers may cache or copy golden-source data for performance, but they must not change it locally. If a consumer finds an error, it is corrected at the source and flows back down. A common anti-pattern is fixing data in the reporting warehouse to make a report correct: the report is right this month, but the source is still wrong, and other consumers still see the error.

```text
  Wrong:                                     Right:
  TMS (rate 3.01%) --> Warehouse             TMS (rate 3.01%)  <-- error raised to owner
                       (patched to 3.10%)        | corrected to 3.10%
                       --> Report OK             v
  Risk engine still uses 3.01%               Warehouse, risk engine, finance
                                             all receive 3.10%
```

**Data lineage.** For every critical number in a regulatory report or ALCO pack, the bank should be able to trace back through every transformation to the source records. Lineage is documented at two levels: **design-time lineage** (which tables and jobs feed which reports) and **run-time lineage** (which file, snapshot and run produced this particular figure).

**Engineering view.**

- Record the golden source of every data item in a data catalogue, and enforce it in architecture reviews: new systems may not become an additional source for an existing domain.
- Propagate source identifiers and versions through every transformation (source system, source record ID, extract timestamp) to make run-time lineage possible.
- Build data quality checks at the source and at each handover: completeness (record counts, control totals), validity (formats, ranges) and consistency (reconciliation with the source).
- Avoid "local fixes" in downstream systems. If a temporary adjustment is unavoidable, record it as an explicit, approved adjustment with an expiry date, not as a silent change.

**Analogy.** A golden source is like the master copy of a legal contract: you may make photocopies to work with, but if a clause is wrong, you amend the master, not a photocopy.

**Key takeaways**

- Each data item has one golden source; all other copies derive from it and must not be edited locally.
- Data owners are business roles accountable for definition and quality; stewards manage the data day to day.
- BCBS 239 requires accurate, complete, timely and traceable risk data, which depends on golden sources and lineage.
- Fix errors at the source; record downstream adjustments explicitly, with approval and expiry.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain the difference between a data owner and a data steward, with an example from the SSI domain.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Both the TMS and the collateral system store the margin agreement terms (thresholds, minimum transfer amounts) for each counterparty, and they disagree for 5% of counterparties. Propose how to decide the golden source and how to fix the situation.
> 3. **Interview:** "A regulator asks you to show how the LCR figure for last quarter was calculated, from source data to the reported number. What must exist in your architecture to answer within days?" *Hint:* consider a data catalogue with design-time lineage, run identifiers propagated through every layer, retained input snapshots, recorded adjustments and their approvals, and reconciliations at each handover.

#### Bitemporal Data Modeling

**Why it matters.** Financial data has two separate timelines. The first is when something is true in the business world: a trade was effective from 1 March, a rate fixed on 15 April. The second is when the bank's systems knew about it: the trade was booked on 3 March, a wrong fixing was corrected on 20 April. Auditors and regulators often ask questions that need both: "What did the risk report you submitted on 31 March show, and why is it different from what you would calculate today for 31 March?" A system that only overwrites values, or only keeps one timeline, cannot answer. **Bitemporal modelling** stores both timelines explicitly.

**The two time dimensions.**

| Dimension | Also called | Question it answers | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Valid time | Business time, effective time, application time | When is this fact true in the real world? | The swap's notional is 100M from 1 Mar to 15 Jun, then 60M after a partial termination |
| Transaction time | System time, knowledge time, record time | When did the system record this fact, and until when was it believed? | The 60M notional was recorded on 16 Jun at 09:12 |

**Example.** A bank holds a term deposit of EUR 50M. On 10 October it books the deposit with a rate of 2.40%, effective from 1 October. On 14 October it discovers the correct rate was 2.45%.

```text
  Table: deposit_terms (bitemporal)
  +---------+-------+------------+------------+---------------------+---------------------+
  | deal_id | rate  | valid_from | valid_to   | recorded_from       | recorded_to         |
  +---------+-------+------------+------------+---------------------+---------------------+
  | D-1001  | 2.40% | 2026-10-01 | 9999-12-31 | 2026-10-10 08:30    | 2026-10-14 11:05    |  superseded
  | D-1001  | 2.45% | 2026-10-01 | 9999-12-31 | 2026-10-14 11:05    | 9999-12-31          |  current
  +---------+-------+------------+------------+---------------------+---------------------+
```

The table now answers different questions:

| Question | Query condition | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| What is the rate on 12 Oct, as we know it today? | valid time contains 12 Oct, transaction time = now | 2.45% |
| What did we believe on 12 Oct about the rate on 12 Oct? | valid time contains 12 Oct, transaction time contains 12 Oct | 2.40% |
| What did the 12 Oct accrual report use? | Rerun "as known at" the report's run time | 2.40%, explaining the difference in accrued interest |

Visualised as a two-dimensional grid:

```text
  transaction time (when we knew)
     ^
     |              +------------------------------------------
  14 Oct  ----------|  2.45% (corrected; applies back to 1 Oct)
     |   +----------+------------------------------------------
  10 Oct |  2.40% (original booking)
     |   +-------------------------------------------------------
     +---+-------------------------------------------------------> valid time
       1 Oct                                                      (when it is true)
```

**Implementation options.**

| Option | Description | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Four timestamp columns | `valid_from/to`, `recorded_from/to` on each table; rows never updated except closing `recorded_to` | Portable; queries must always filter both dimensions |
| SQL:2011 temporal tables | `PERIOD FOR` application time plus `SYSTEM_TIME` versioning, supported to different degrees by Db2, SQL Server, MariaDB, Oracle (Flashback/temporal validity), and PostgreSQL extensions | System time maintained by the database; less custom code |
| Bitemporal databases | Databases designed around both timelines (for example XTDB) | Native "as of" queries, less mainstream |
| Event log plus projections | Store events with effective and recorded times; build bitemporal views from them | Combines with event sourcing (next topic) |

**SQL example (four-column approach).**

```sql
-- Rate as known at a given moment, effective on a given business date
SELECT rate
FROM   deposit_terms
WHERE  deal_id       = 'D-1001'
  AND  valid_from   <= DATE '2026-10-12'
  AND  valid_to      > DATE '2026-10-12'
  AND  recorded_from <= TIMESTAMP '2026-10-12 18:00:00'
  AND  recorded_to   > TIMESTAMP '2026-10-12 18:00:00';
-- returns 2.40%: the value used by the 12 October EOD run

-- A correction never updates the old row's data; it closes it and inserts a new one
UPDATE deposit_terms SET recorded_to = :now
 WHERE deal_id = 'D-1001' AND recorded_to = TIMESTAMP '9999-12-31 00:00:00';
INSERT INTO deposit_terms VALUES ('D-1001', 0.0245, DATE '2026-10-01', DATE '9999-12-31',
                                  :now, TIMESTAMP '9999-12-31 00:00:00');
```

**Where bitemporality matters in treasury.**

- Trade corrections and back-dated lifecycle events, to explain P&L restatements;
- Reference data (SSIs, ratings, hierarchies), to show what a payment or limit check used at the time;
- Market data corrections after a snapshot was published;
- Regulatory reports, which must be reproducible as submitted and also restatable with corrected data.

**Engineering view.**

- Decide per table whether it needs one dimension (most audit needs: transaction time), both, or neither (pure caches).
- Use half-open intervals `[from, to)` consistently; this avoids gaps and overlaps at boundaries.
- Enforce non-overlap constraints per key in both dimensions; overlapping rows make "as of" queries return two answers.
- Index for the common queries ("current", "as of business date", "as known at") and consider current-state views, because bitemporal tables grow quickly.

**Key takeaways**

- Bitemporal data tracks valid time (when a fact is true) and transaction time (when the system knew it).
- It lets you reproduce what a report showed when it was produced and explain differences with today's view.
- Corrections close the old record's transaction period and insert a new record; nothing is overwritten.
- Use half-open intervals, non-overlap constraints and suitable indexes; apply bitemporality where audit and restatement need it.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** A bond's rating changes from A to BBB, effective 5 May, but it is loaded on 7 May. Write the rows of a bitemporal rating table before and after the load.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Write a SQL query that returns, for each deal, the rate effective on the last business day of September as known at the time the September regulatory report was submitted (2026-10-15 16:00).
> 3. **Interview:** "Our risk report for 30 June showed a counterparty exposure of 120M. Today, recalculating 30 June gives 95M. The regulator asks why. How would your data design let you answer?" *Hint:* consider rerunning "as known at" the report's run time, then changing one input at a time (trades, reference data, market data) to "as known today", and attributing the 25M difference to the specific corrections and their timestamps.

#### Event Sourcing for Ledgers

**Why it matters.** Accounting has used an append-only model for centuries: a ledger is a sequence of entries, and an error is corrected by a new, reversing entry, never by erasing the old one. Many software systems do the opposite: they store current state and overwrite it. For treasury ledgers (cash positions, securities holdings, accounting subledgers), overwriting loses exactly the information auditors, reconcilers and investigators need. **Event sourcing** applies the ledger principle to software: the system stores the sequence of events that happened, and derives current state by replaying them.

**State-based versus event-sourced.**

```text
  State-based (CRUD)                          Event-sourced
  +--------------------------+                +-------------------------------------------+
  | account | balance        |                | seq | event               | amount      |
  | NOSTRO1 | 7,250,000      |                |  1  | OpeningBalanceSet   | 10,000,000  |
  +--------------------------+                |  2  | PaymentSent (P-881) | -5,000,000  |
  Only the latest value is kept.              |  3  | FundsReceived (R-4) |  2,500,000  |
  How did it get there?  Unknown.             |  4  | PaymentReturned     | -   250,000 |
                                              |     |  (R-4 partly)       |             |
                                              +-------------------------------------------+
                                              balance = replay(events) = 7,250,000
                                              History, cause and order are preserved.
```

**Core concepts.**

| Concept | Description |
|---|---|
| Event | An immutable fact in the past tense: `TradeBooked`, `PaymentSettled`, `CouponReceived`. Contains the data, the effective time and the recorded time |
| Event store | Append-only log of events, ordered per stream (for example per account or per trade) |
| Stream | The events of one aggregate, such as one account or one trade |
| Projection (read model) | A view derived from events, such as current balances, positions by value date, or a GL trial balance |
| Snapshot | A saved state at a point in the stream to avoid replaying from the beginning |
| Compensating event | A new event that reverses or corrects an earlier one; the earlier event remains |

**Example: an event-sourced cash ledger in Python.**

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from decimal import Decimal
from datetime import date, datetime

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class LedgerEvent:
    seq: int                 # position in the account's stream
    account: str
    kind: str                # "CREDIT", "DEBIT", "REVERSAL"
    amount: Decimal
    value_date: date         # valid time: when the cash moves
    recorded_at: datetime    # transaction time: when we learned about it
    ref: str                 # payment or trade reference
    reverses: int | None = None

def balance(events: list[LedgerEvent], on: date, known_at: datetime) -> Decimal:
    """Value-dated balance as known at a given moment (bitemporal projection)."""
    relevant = [e for e in events if e.value_date <= on and e.recorded_at <= known_at]
    total = Decimal("0")
    for e in sorted(relevant, key=lambda e: e.seq):
        if e.kind == "CREDIT":
            total += e.amount
        else:                # DEBIT, or REVERSAL of a credit
            total -= e.amount
    return total
```

Because each event carries both a value date and a recorded time, the same log answers "what is the balance for value 22 October?" and "what did we think the balance was at 10:00 yesterday?". The event log is naturally bitemporal.

**Appending safely.** An event store must prevent two writers from appending conflicting events to the same stream. The usual technique is **optimistic concurrency**: the writer states which sequence number it expects to be last, and the append fails if another event was added in between.

```sql
-- Event store table with a uniqueness constraint per stream position
CREATE TABLE ledger_events (
    account      TEXT        NOT NULL,
    seq          BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    kind         TEXT        NOT NULL,
    amount       NUMERIC(20,2) NOT NULL,
    value_date   DATE        NOT NULL,
    recorded_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    ref          TEXT        NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (account, seq),
    UNIQUE (account, ref, kind)          -- idempotency: the same payment is not booked twice
);
-- Writer read seq 41 as last; it appends seq 42. A concurrent writer that also
-- appends seq 42 violates the primary key and must reload and retry.
```

**Benefits and costs.**

| Benefits | Costs |
|---|---|
| Complete audit trail by construction | More complex than CRUD; teams need to learn the model |
| Any past state can be reconstructed | Projections must be rebuilt when their logic changes |
| New read models can be built from history | Event schema evolution must be managed (versioned events, upcasters) |
| Natural fit for streaming and integration (events published to other systems) | Queries need projections; ad hoc queries on the event log are slow |
| Corrections are explicit and traceable | Personal data in immutable logs needs care (crypto-shredding, separation) |

**Where it fits in treasury.** Event sourcing is a strong fit for ledgers and positions (cash, nostro, securities, subledger postings) and for trade lifecycles (booked, amended, confirmed, settled). It is usually not worth it for reference data screens or report configuration. Many modern core banking and payment platforms are built on an append-only posting log with projected balances, which is event sourcing under another name.

**Engineering view.**

- Name events after business facts in the past tense, and include all data needed to understand them later, including references to the triggering message or user.
- Make event handlers and projections idempotent; events are delivered at least once in most infrastructures (Chapter 12.4).
- Reconcile projections against the event log regularly: the balance projection must equal the sum of events.
- Plan for schema evolution from day one: version event types and keep the code to read old versions.

**Key takeaways**

- Event sourcing stores the sequence of immutable events and derives current state by replaying them, as accounting ledgers have always done.
- Corrections are compensating events; nothing is deleted or overwritten.
- Events with value dates and recorded times give bitemporal answers naturally.
- Optimistic concurrency, idempotent handlers, projection reconciliation and event versioning are the essential engineering practices.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** For a securities account, list the events (in past tense) generated by buying a bond, receiving two coupons and selling half the position.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Extend the Python `balance` function so that a `REVERSAL` event correctly reverses the specific event it references, whether that event was a credit or a debit.
> 3. **Interview:** "The business wants a new report showing nostro balances by hour for the last two years. The system is event-sourced. How do you build it, and what can go wrong?" *Hint:* consider building a new projection by replaying history, the cost of replay at this volume, snapshots, handling old event schema versions, and checking the new projection against existing end-of-day balances.

<a id="133-processing-models"></a>
### 13.3 Processing Models

This subchapter covers how treasury systems turn data into results: the nightly batch that produces official figures, intraday and real-time processing for decisions that cannot wait, position keeping, distributed compute grids for heavy calculations, and engines that run portfolios through scenarios.

#### End-of-Day Batch Processing

**Why it matters.** Banks produce official numbers once a day: the P&L the desk is judged on, the risk figures checked against limits, the accounting entries in the general ledger, the liquidity figures reported to regulators. These numbers must be consistent with each other, which means they must be calculated from the same trades, the same market data and the same reference data, as of the same moment. The **end-of-day (EOD) batch** does this: after the business day closes, it freezes the inputs and runs a chain of dependent jobs that produce the official results. In many banks the EOD batch is still the backbone of treasury processing, even where real-time systems exist alongside it.

**The shape of an EOD batch.**

```text
  17:00  Business close (per region)
    |
    v
  [1] Cut-off: stop or tag new trades for today; freeze trade population
    |
  [2] Market data snapshot validated and published (Chapter 13.2)
    |
  [3] Lifecycle processing: fixings, resets, coupon and maturity events,
    |   option expiries, accruals for today
    |
  [4] Revaluation: mark-to-market of all trades, positions
    |
    +------------------+------------------+--------------------+
    |                  |                  |                    |
  [5a] P&L and       [5b] Risk runs     [5c] Accounting      [5d] Liquidity /
       P&L explain        (sensitivities,     events and          ALM extracts
                          VaR, PFE)           postings
    |                  |                  |                    |
    +------------------+--------+---------+--------------------+
                                |
  [6] Reconciliations and controls (positions, GL, completeness)
                                |
  [7] Reports published; date roll to next business day
                                |
  07:00  Results available for the morning: P&L, risk, limits, liquidity
```

The interval between business close and morning publication is the **batch window**. Global banks often run several regional batches (Asia, Europe, Americas) or one global batch timed after the New York close, which leaves a short window before Asia opens.

**Scheduling and dependencies.** EOD batches have hundreds or thousands of jobs. They are managed by enterprise schedulers such as Control-M, Autosys or Tivoli Workload Scheduler, or by modern orchestrators such as Airflow. The scheduler holds the dependency graph: a job runs when its predecessors have completed successfully and its input conditions (files arrived, snapshot published) are met.

| Concept | Description |
|---|---|
| Dependency graph (DAG) | Jobs and the "must finish before" relationships between them |
| Critical path | The longest chain of dependent jobs; it determines when the batch finishes |
| Business date | The date being processed, which differs from the calendar date once processing passes midnight |
| Date roll | The step that moves systems to the next business date, after which new trades belong to the new day |
| Checkpoint/restart | The ability to restart a failed job without rerunning everything before it |

**Example: critical path.** Suppose these jobs and durations:

| Job | Duration | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| A: trade cut-off | 10 min | - |
| B: market data snapshot | 30 min | - |
| C: lifecycle processing | 40 min | A |
| D: revaluation | 60 min | B, C |
| E: P&L | 20 min | D |
| F: VaR | 120 min | D |
| G: accounting | 45 min | D |
| H: reports | 15 min | E, F, G |

The critical path is A, C, D, F, H: 10 + 40 + 60 + 120 + 15 = 245 minutes. Speeding up accounting (G) does not shorten the batch. Speeding up VaR (F) does, until another path becomes critical (A, C, D, G, H takes 170 minutes).

**Failure handling.** A batch failure at 02:00 puts the morning's figures at risk. Good batch design includes:

- **Idempotent, restartable jobs.** A job rerun with the same business date and inputs produces the same result and does not double post.
- **Completeness and control totals.** Each job checks record counts and totals against its input before passing control.
- **Clear status.** A failed job stops its dependants; it does not let them run on partial data.
- **Runbooks and support rotas.** Operators know which failures can be fixed by a rerun and which need developers or business sign-off.
- **Fallback.** If a non-critical step cannot finish, decide in advance whether reports are published with yesterday's values and a clear flag.

**Engineering view.**

- Make the business date an explicit parameter of every job, never the system clock. This is what makes reruns of past dates possible.
- Separate "today's official run" from reruns and what-if runs in storage, with run IDs, so that corrections never overwrite published results silently.
- Monitor the critical path daily and track batch duration trends; volume growth slowly pushes completion time toward the morning deadline.
- Keep batch jobs small and well defined; a single monolithic job that takes four hours cannot be restarted halfway.

**Key takeaways**

- The EOD batch freezes inputs and produces consistent official figures for P&L, risk, accounting and liquidity.
- It is a dependency graph of jobs run by a scheduler; the critical path determines completion time.
- Jobs must take the business date as a parameter, be idempotent and restartable, and check completeness.
- Batch windows shrink as banks become global and volumes grow, which pushes processing toward intraday and incremental models.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain the difference between the business date and the calendar date in an EOD batch that finishes at 03:00.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Using the critical path example, the VaR job is split into four parallel jobs of 35 minutes each, followed by a 10-minute aggregation. What is the new batch duration, and which path is now critical?
> 3. **Interview:** "The EOD batch fails at 01:30 in the accounting step because of a bad trade. P&L and risk have already completed. What do you do, and how should the system be designed to make this easier?" *Hint:* consider isolating the bad trade (exception queue) versus fixing and rerunning, whether P&L and risk need rerunning if the trade is corrected, idempotent postings, and communication with finance before the GL deadline.

#### Intraday and Real-Time Processing

**Why it matters.** A batch tells you tomorrow morning what happened today. Many treasury decisions cannot wait. A payments treasurer must know now whether the bank has enough central bank reserves to release a large payment (Chapter 5.3). A trader needs the current position before hedging. A limit system must reject a trade that would breach a counterparty limit before it is executed, not the next morning. Regulators also expect banks to monitor intraday liquidity in real time (BCBS 248 monitoring tools). **Intraday and real-time processing** produce results continuously as events arrive.

**Spectrum of processing models.**

| Model | Latency | Typical treasury use |
|---|---|---|
| End-of-day batch | Hours (once a day) | Official P&L, risk, accounting, regulatory reports |
| Intraday batch (micro-batch) | Minutes (every 5-30 minutes) | Intraday risk refresh, liquidity dashboards, cash forecasts |
| Event-driven (streaming) | Seconds or less | Real-time cash positions, payment release decisions, position updates |
| Synchronous request/response | Milliseconds, inside a user or system transaction | Pre-trade limit checks, pricing requests, payment authorisation |

**A typical event-driven architecture.**

```text
  Sources                       Event backbone                 Processors                Consumers
  +-----------------+          +----------------+          +-------------------+     +-----------------+
  | TMS: trades     +--------->+                +--------->+ Position engine   +---->+ Trader blotters |
  | Payment hub:    +--------->+  Message bus / +--------->+ (cash, securities)|     +-----------------+
  |  sent, settled  |          |  event log     |          +-------------------+     +-----------------+
  | Swift: camt.054,+--------->+  (e.g. Kafka,  +--------->+ Liquidity monitor +---->+ Liquidity       |
  |  MT900/910      |          |   MQ)          |          |  (reserve balance,|     | dashboard,      |
  | RTGS: balance   +--------->+                |          |   queued payments)|     | alerts          |
  |  notifications  |          |                +--------->+ Limit engine      +---->+ Payment release |
  | Market data     +--------->+                |          +-------------------+     +-----------------+
  +-----------------+          +----------------+
```

**Example: real-time reserve position.** A treasurer starts the day with EUR 2.0bn at the central bank. During the day, the liquidity monitor processes settlement events:

| Time | Event | Amount (EUR m) | Balance (EUR m) | Queued outgoing (EUR m) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 07:00 | Opening balance | | 2,000 | 0 |
| 08:15 | Incoming RTGS credit | +350 | 2,350 | 0 |
| 09:30 | Outgoing payment settled | -900 | 1,450 | 0 |
| 10:05 | Large payment queued (waiting for release) | | 1,450 | 1,200 |
| 10:06 | Alert: balance minus queue below threshold of 500 | | | |
| 10:40 | Incoming repo cash | +600 | 2,050 | 1,200 |
| 10:41 | Treasurer releases queued payment | -1,200 | 850 | 0 |

The batch view would only show the end-of-day balance; the real-time view makes the 10:06 decision possible.

**Batch and real-time together.** Most banks run a **hybrid**: a real-time layer for operational decisions and an EOD layer for official, reconciled figures. The two views must be reconciled at the end of the day, because real-time processing can miss or duplicate events, and late corrections arrive after the stream has moved on.

| Concern | Real-time layer | EOD layer |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | Best available now; may be incomplete | Complete and reconciled |
| Market data | Live prices | Official snapshot |
| Corrections | Applied as new events, may arrive late | Included in rerun |
| Use | Decisions during the day | Official reporting, P&L, accounting |

**Engineering view.**

- **Ordering and duplicates.** Events can arrive late, duplicated or out of order. Use idempotency keys and sequence numbers per source, and decide how to handle late events (apply and recompute, or apply as a correction).
- **State recovery.** A streaming processor holds state (current balances). It must be able to rebuild that state after a restart, from a snapshot plus the event log (see event sourcing in Chapter 13.2).
- **Start-of-day alignment.** Initialise real-time positions from the reconciled EOD positions every morning, so errors do not accumulate over days.
- **Latency budgets.** For synchronous checks, such as pre-trade limits, define a maximum response time and a policy for timeouts (fail open or fail closed). For payments and limits, fail closed is the usual default.

**Key takeaways**

- Intraday and real-time processing support decisions that cannot wait for the batch: payment release, limit checks, hedging.
- Models range from micro-batches to event streaming to synchronous checks, with different latency and complexity.
- Banks run a hybrid: real-time for operations, EOD for official figures, reconciled daily.
- Ordering, duplicates, state recovery and start-of-day alignment are the main engineering concerns.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** For each of these, say whether EOD batch, intraday batch, streaming or synchronous processing fits best: (a) regulatory LCR report, (b) pre-trade counterparty limit check, (c) central bank reserve balance dashboard, (d) intraday VaR refresh for the trading desk.
> 2. **Intermediate:** A streaming position engine receives a settlement confirmation for a payment before the event saying the payment was sent, because the two come from different systems. How should the engine handle this?
> 3. **Interview:** "The real-time cash position for a nostro account shows 15M more than the EOD reconciled position for the same day. How would you design the system so that such differences are detected and explained?" *Hint:* consider an automatic end-of-day comparison by account, keeping event-level detail on both sides so differences can be matched, typical causes (missing events, duplicates, late back-valued entries), and resetting the real-time state from EOD positions.

#### Position Keeping Engines

**Why it matters.** "How much do we have?" sounds simple, but treasury needs many versions of the answer: how much EUR cash will be on the nostro account at Deutsche Bank for value tomorrow, how many units of a bond the desk holds today on a trade-date basis, and how much the bank owes a counterparty across all its FX forwards. A **position keeping engine** maintains these positions by applying trade, settlement and cash events to aggregated balances, and it is the basis for cash management, funding decisions, limits and risk.

**Position bases.** The same trades produce different positions depending on which date is used.

| Basis | Position changes on | Answers | Used by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trade-date | The day the trade is agreed | What have we committed to? | Traders, market risk, P&L |
| Settlement-date (contractual) | The day the trade is due to settle | What should we hold or have on the account on date X? | Cash management, funding |
| Actual settlement | The day settlement is confirmed | What do we actually hold now? | Operations, reconciliation |
| Projected (forecast) | Expected flows including forecasts | What will the balance probably be? | Liquidity management (Chapter 5.2) |

**Example: a cash ladder.** The engine projects cash by currency, account and value date. On Monday 19 October, for the USD nostro:

```text
  USD nostro at Correspondent X        Mon 19   Tue 20   Wed 21   Thu 22   Fri 23
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Opening (actual / projected)          120.0    105.0    135.0     85.0     85.0
  FX trades settling                    -40.0    +30.0    -50.0    -10.0
  Money market maturities               +25.0
  Customer payments (forecast)                                     +10.0
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Closing projected                     105.0    135.0     85.0     85.0     85.0
  (USD millions)
```

As each settlement is confirmed, the engine moves the flow from "projected" to "actual". If a flow fails to settle, the projected balance for the following days changes, and the treasurer must fund or invest the difference.

**Processing model.** Position engines apply incremental updates and avoid recalculating from all trades on every event.

```text
  Event (trade booked, amended, cancelled, settled, cash received)
     |
     v
  1. Determine affected keys: (account, currency, value date), (book, instrument)...
  2. Compute delta: new contribution minus old contribution of this trade version
  3. Apply delta to position aggregates (atomically, with the event's sequence)
  4. Record the delta with a reference to the event (audit, drill-down)
  5. Publish position-changed events for dashboards and limit engines
```

Step 2 matters for amendments. If a trade's amount changes from 10M to 12M, the engine must remove the old 10M contribution and add the new 12M, not add 12M. Storing each trade's last contribution per key makes this possible.

**Python sketch: applying a trade amendment.**

```python
from collections import defaultdict
from decimal import Decimal

positions = defaultdict(Decimal)          # (account, ccy, value_date) -> balance
contrib = {}                              # trade_id -> {key: amount} of current version

def apply_trade_version(trade_id: str, flows: dict) -> None:
    """flows: {(account, ccy, value_date): amount} for the new trade version.
    A cancellation passes an empty dict."""
    old = contrib.get(trade_id, {})
    for key in set(old) | set(flows):
        delta = flows.get(key, Decimal("0")) - old.get(key, Decimal("0"))
        if delta:
            positions[key] += delta
    contrib[trade_id] = flows
```

**Engineering view.**

- **Recompute to verify.** Incremental positions can drift because of missed or duplicated events. Recompute positions from the full trade population regularly (for example in the EOD batch) and compare with the incremental results.
- **Concurrency.** Many events update the same popular keys (the main USD nostro). Use per-key ordering (partitioning by key in a stream) or database-level atomic updates to avoid lost updates.
- **Drill-down.** Users always ask "what makes up this number?". Keep the per-trade contributions so any position can be broken down.
- **Multiple bases from one event stream.** Derive trade-date, settlement-date and actual positions from the same events with different rules, rather than separate feeds that can disagree.

**Key takeaways**

- A position keeping engine maintains aggregated holdings and cash balances from trade and settlement events.
- Trade-date, contractual settlement, actual settlement and projected positions answer different questions.
- Incremental updates must apply the difference between old and new trade versions; per-trade contributions make this and drill-down possible.
- Periodic full recomputation and per-key ordering protect against drift and lost updates.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** A desk buys a bond on Monday for settlement on Wednesday. Show its securities position on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday on a trade-date basis and on a settlement-date basis.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Using the Python sketch, trace the `positions` dictionary for: an FX trade booked with USD -10M for value 21 Oct, amended to USD -12M for value 22 Oct, then cancelled. Confirm that all positions return to zero.
> 3. **Interview:** "The cash ladder for value tomorrow in the position engine differs from the sum of trades in the TMS by 3M. How do you investigate?" *Hint:* compare at trade level using per-trade contributions, look for trades missing on either side, amendments applied twice or as additions, value date or account mapping differences, and timing of the TMS extract compared with the engine's last event.

#### Calculation Grids and Distributed Compute

**Why it matters.** Some treasury calculations are too heavy for a single machine. A counterparty exposure simulation with 5,000 netting sets, 2,000 Monte Carlo paths and 100 time steps needs a billion netting set valuations. A historical VaR on 50,000 trades with 500 scenarios needs 25 million revaluations, before any sensitivities. These calculations must finish within the batch window, and some must also run on demand during the day. **Calculation grids** spread these calculations across hundreds or thousands of CPU cores.

**Why risk calculations parallelise well.** Most risk calculations are "embarrassingly parallel": the valuation of trade A under scenario 17 does not depend on the valuation of trade B under scenario 18. The work can be split into independent tasks, computed in parallel and aggregated at the end.

```text
                      Portfolio x Scenarios
            scen 1   scen 2   scen 3   ...   scen 500
  trade 1  [ task  |  task  |  task  | ... |  task  ]
  trade 2  [ task  |  task  |  task  | ... |  task  ]
  ...
  trade N  [ task  |  task  |  task  | ... |  task  ]

  Partitioning options:
   - by trade (each task: one block of trades, all scenarios)   -> good cache reuse of trade data
   - by scenario (each task: all trades, one block of scenarios) -> good reuse of market data
   - by both (blocks of trades x blocks of scenarios)           -> most flexible
```

**Grid architecture.**

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| Client / job submitter | Defines the job (portfolio, scenarios, measures) and submits it |
| Scheduler / broker | Splits jobs into tasks, assigns tasks to workers, tracks status, retries failures |
| Workers (engines) | Load the pricing library, market data and trades, run tasks, return results |
| Data distribution | Delivers market data, trade data and static data to workers (shared cache, object storage, pre-loaded) |
| Result aggregation | Collects and combines task outputs (sums, vectors, cubes) |

Products and platforms used for this include IBM Spectrum Symphony and TIBCO GridServer in many banks, and increasingly Kubernetes-based schedulers, cloud batch services and frameworks such as Ray or Dask. GPUs are used for Monte Carlo workloads such as XVA, where the same calculation runs on many paths.

**Example: sizing a grid.** A nightly PFE run needs 1.2 billion netting-set valuations, each taking on average 0.5 ms of CPU time. The batch window for this job is 90 minutes.

```text
  Total CPU time    = 1.2e9 x 0.5 ms = 6.0e5 s = ~167 CPU-hours
  Window            = 1.5 hours
  Cores (ideal)     = 167 / 1.5 = ~111 cores
  With 70% efficiency (data loading, stragglers, retries):
  Cores needed      = 111 / 0.7 = ~160 cores
```

**Practical issues.**

| Issue | Description | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Data distribution | Shipping market data and trades to thousands of workers can dominate runtime | Pre-load and cache, ship references not data, locality-aware scheduling |
| Stragglers | A few slow tasks delay the whole job | Smaller tasks, speculative re-execution, balanced partitioning by cost |
| Failures | Workers crash or are pre-empted | Idempotent tasks, automatic retries, checkpointing |
| Determinism | Results depend on task split or random seeds | Seeds per path, order-independent aggregation (Chapter 11.4) |
| Completeness | Missing task results produce plausible but wrong totals | Expected task manifest, aggregation refuses to publish incomplete results |
| Cost | Large grids sit idle outside the batch | Elastic or cloud capacity, sharing with other workloads |

**Engineering view.**

- Design tasks to be pure functions of their inputs (trades, market data snapshot ID, scenario IDs, model version). This makes retries, caching and reproducibility straightforward.
- Make the pricing library identical on all workers, versioned and recorded with each result.
- Use floating-point aggregation that does not depend on the order in which results arrive, or sort before summing; otherwise reruns differ in the last digits and reconciliations fail.
- Measure task duration distributions, not just averages; the slowest tasks determine job completion.

**Key takeaways**

- Grids spread embarrassingly parallel risk calculations (trades x scenarios x time steps) over many cores.
- A scheduler splits jobs into tasks, workers compute them, and an aggregation layer combines results.
- Data distribution, stragglers, failures, determinism and completeness are the main practical problems.
- Tasks should be pure, idempotent functions of versioned inputs, with order-independent aggregation.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain why a historical VaR calculation is "embarrassingly parallel", and name one step in the process that is not.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Using the sizing example, the bank adds 40% more netting sets and wants to halve the window to 45 minutes. How many cores are needed at the same efficiency? Suggest two ways to reduce this number without changing the methodology.
> 3. **Interview:** "Rerunning yesterday's XVA calculation on the grid gives a CVA that differs from the original by 0.3%. Nothing changed in the inputs. What could cause this?" *Hint:* consider random seeds tied to worker or task order, non-deterministic floating-point aggregation, different library versions on some workers, missing or duplicate tasks, and how to detect each one.

#### Scenario and Stress Engines

**Why it matters.** Treasury constantly asks "what if?": what happens to NII if rates rise 200bp, to the LCR if 20% of corporate deposits leave in a month, to the bond portfolio if credit spreads widen like in 2008, to collateral calls if the bank is downgraded by two notches. Regulators ask the same questions in prescribed formats (Chapter 16.1 covers regulatory stress tests and scenario design). A **scenario engine** is the infrastructure that defines scenarios, applies them consistently to the bank's portfolios and models, and stores the results so they can be compared and explained.

**What a scenario is, technically.** A scenario is a set of changes to the inputs of a calculation, with a horizon and possibly a path over time.

| Scenario element | Examples |
|---|---|
| Market shocks | Parallel +200bp shift, steepener, EUR/USD -15%, credit spreads +150bp, equity -30% |
| Behavioural assumptions | Deposit run-off rates, prepayment speeds, drawdown of committed facilities |
| Counterparty and rating events | Default of the largest counterparty, two-notch downgrade of the bank |
| Business assumptions | New business volumes, margins, funding mix |
| Time structure | Instantaneous shock, or a path over 1, 3, 12 or 36 months |

**Shock definition.** Shocks are usually applied to risk factors, not directly to prices, so that one scenario definition applies to every product.

| Shock type | Formula | Typical risk factors |
|---|---|---|
| Absolute | new = base + shock | Interest rates, spreads (in bp) |
| Relative | new = base x (1 + shock) | FX rates, equity prices, volatilities |
| Replacement | new = specified value | Fixings, specific prices |

**Engine architecture.**

```text
  +----------------------+      +-------------------------+      +------------------------+
  | Scenario library     |      | Scenario application    |      | Calculation            |
  | - definitions        +----->+ - expand to risk factor +----->+ - full revaluation     |
  | - versions, approval |      |   level shocks          |      |   (grid)               |
  | - historical,        |      | - build shocked curves, |      | - or sensitivity-based |
  |   hypothetical,      |      |   surfaces, FX          |      |   approximation        |
  |   regulatory         |      | - apply behavioural     |      | - ALM / liquidity      |
  +----------------------+      |   overrides             |      |   projections          |
                                +-------------------------+      +-----------+------------+
                                                                             |
                                +-------------------------+      +-----------v------------+
                                | Analysis and reporting  |<-----+ Result store           |
                                | - base vs scenario      |      | (portfolio x scenario  |
                                | - attribution by driver |      |  x measure x horizon)  |
                                +-------------------------+      +------------------------+
```

**Full revaluation versus sensitivity-based.**

| Approach | How | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full revaluation | Reprice every trade with the shocked market data | Captures non-linearity (options, convexity) exactly | Expensive: trades x scenarios valuations |
| Sensitivity-based (Taylor) | Approximate P&L = delta x shock + 1/2 gamma x shock^2 + ... | Fast; scenarios can be applied instantly | Inaccurate for large shocks and non-linear products |
| Hybrid | Sensitivities for linear products, full revaluation for options | Balances cost and accuracy | Two methods to maintain and reconcile |

**Example: sensitivity-based versus full revaluation.** A bond portfolio has a DV01 of -EUR 85,000 (it loses 85,000 per +1bp) and a convexity contribution of +EUR 30 per bp squared.

```text
  Shock +200bp
  Linear:        -85,000 x 200                     = -17,000,000
  With convexity: -17,000,000 + 30 x 200^2          = -17,000,000 + 1,200,000 = -15,800,000
  Full revaluation (from the pricing engine)        =  -15,750,000 (for example)

  The linear approximation overstates the loss by about 1.25M (8%); adding
  convexity reduces the error to 50k. For options, the error can be much larger.
```

**Engineering view.**

- **Scenarios as versioned data.** Store scenario definitions as data with IDs, versions, owners and approval status, not as code or spreadsheet formulas. Every result must reference the exact scenario version.
- **Consistent application.** One scenario expansion service should produce shocked market data for all consumers (market risk, ALM, liquidity, capital). Different teams applying "the same" +200bp shock differently is a common source of inconsistent ALCO and risk reports.
- **Base run first.** Every scenario result is compared with a base run on the same data. Store base and scenario results together with the same input snapshot.
- **Explainability.** Management asks why a scenario result changed from last quarter. Design for attribution: change one input at a time (portfolio, market data, scenario definition, model version) and record each step.

**Key takeaways**

- A scenario is a versioned set of changes to market, behavioural, counterparty and business inputs, applied instantly or over a time path.
- Shocks are defined on risk factors (absolute, relative, replacement) so one definition applies to all products.
- Full revaluation is accurate but expensive; sensitivity-based methods are fast but miss non-linearity in large shocks.
- Store scenarios as approved, versioned data, apply them through one shared service, and keep base and scenario results together for attribution.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Define a scenario "EUR rates +100bp parallel, EUR/USD -10%, deposit outflow 5%" as a structured record with risk factor shocks and behavioural overrides.
> 2. **Intermediate:** A portfolio has DV01 = -EUR 40,000 per bp and a convexity term of EUR 12 per bp squared. Estimate the P&L for shocks of +50bp, +200bp and -200bp with and without convexity. For which shock is the linear approximation least reliable, and why?
> 3. **Interview:** "Market risk and treasury ALM both report the impact of a +200bp shock on the banking book bond portfolio, and their numbers differ by 20%. How would you investigate, and how would you prevent this?" *Hint:* compare portfolio scope, shock definitions (instantaneous vs over a horizon, which curve is shocked, floors), valuation method (full revaluation vs sensitivities), and market data snapshot; consider a shared scenario expansion service.

<a id="134-reconciliation-and-controls"></a>
### 13.4 Reconciliation and Controls

This subchapter covers the mechanisms that let a bank trust its numbers: reconciling cash and positions against external and internal sources, the algorithms that match records, the workflows that resolve breaks, the four-eyes principle, and the audit trails that show who did what and when.

#### Cash and Nostro Reconciliation

**Why it matters.** A bank holds accounts with other banks, called **nostro** accounts ("ours", held with you), in every currency it deals in (Chapter 1.4). The bank keeps its own record of what should be on each nostro account, based on its trades and payments. The correspondent bank keeps the real account and sends statements. If the two disagree, something is wrong: a payment failed, a counterparty paid the wrong amount, a fee was charged, a fraudulent payment left the account, or a trade was booked incorrectly. Unreconciled differences are real money at risk, so **nostro reconciliation** is one of the oldest and most important controls in bank operations. Regulators and auditors check that it is done daily and that differences are resolved promptly.

**The two sides.**

```text
  Internal side ("our books")                  External side ("their books")
  +--------------------------------+          +--------------------------------+
  | Expected flows from TMS,       |          | Correspondent's statement:     |
  | payment hub, core banking      |          | MT950 / MT940 / camt.053 (EOD) |
  | (ledger entries on the nostro  |          | MT900/910, camt.054 (intraday  |
  |  mirror account)               |          |  debit/credit notifications)   |
  +---------------+----------------+          +----------------+---------------+
                  |                                            |
                  +--------------------+-----------------------+
                                       v
                          +---------------------------+
                          | Reconciliation engine     |
                          | - load and normalise      |
                          | - match (rules)           |
                          | - generate breaks         |
                          +-------------+-------------+
                                        v
                  Matched items          Breaks (unmatched or partially matched)
                  (closed)               -> investigation workflow
```
