3. The effectiveness requirements are met: an economic relationship exists, credit risk does not dominate the value changes, and the hedge ratio is consistent with how risk is actually managed.

**What the documentation contains.**

| Element | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Risk management objective and strategy | Why the hedge exists | Convert a fixed-rate bond to floating to stay within IRRBB limits |
| Hedging instrument | Specific trade(s) and proportion | Swap SWP-55871, 100% of notional |
| Hedged item | Asset, liability, firm commitment, highly probable forecast transaction or portfolio | Bond XS0000000000, EUR 100m nominal |
| Hedged risk | The risk component being hedged | Fair value changes due to the EUR benchmark rate |
| Hedge type | Fair value, cash flow or net investment | Fair value hedge |
| Hedge ratio | Quantity of instrument per quantity of item | 1:1 |
| Effectiveness assessment | Prospective method and ineffectiveness measurement | Critical terms and regression; cumulative dollar offset for measurement |
| Sources of ineffectiveness | Expected differences | Discount curve basis, floating leg, counterparty credit |
| Designation date | On or before the start of hedge accounting | 2026-10-19 |

**Example: a designation record.**

```yaml
hedge_relationship:
  id: HR-2026-0412
  version: 1
  type: FAIR_VALUE
  framework: IFRS9
  designation_timestamp: 2026-10-19T14:32:05Z
  designated_by: alm_desk_user_014
  approved_by: accounting_policy_user_007
  objective: >
    Convert the fixed-rate exposure on a EUR 100m 5-year bond held at amortized cost
    to floating, in line with the IRRBB hedging strategy approved by ALCO.
  hedged_risk: EUR benchmark interest rate (ESTR-discounted swap curve)
  hedged_items:
    - instrument: XS0000000000
      nominal: 100000000
      proportion: 1.0
  hedging_instruments:
    - trade_id: SWP-55871
      proportion: 1.0
  hedge_ratio: 1.0
  effectiveness:
    prospective: critical_terms_and_regression
    measurement: dollar_offset_cumulative
  expected_ineffectiveness: [discount_curve_basis, floating_leg, counterparty_credit]
  status: DESIGNATED
```

**Lifecycle.**

```text
  DRAFT --approve--> DESIGNATED --period-end assessment--> passes --> stays DESIGNATED
                        |    ^                                |
                        |    |                                | criteria no longer met
                        |    +-- REBALANCED (new hedge ratio, |
                        |        same objective; IFRS 9)      v
                        |                                DISCONTINUED
                        +--- instrument expires, is sold or terminated;
                             hedged item derecognized; forecast no longer expected ---^
```

- **Rebalancing (IFRS 9):** if the hedge ratio drifts but the risk management objective is unchanged, the ratio is adjusted and the relationship continues.
- **Discontinuation:** under IFRS 9, a bank cannot voluntarily de-designate a relationship that still meets the risk management objective. Under IAS 39 it can.
- **Macro hedges:** banks using the IAS 39 portfolio fair value hedge (Chapter 6.3) designate an *amount* of a portfolio per repricing time bucket rather than specific items. Because the portfolio changes all the time, they de-designate and re-designate it every period, often monthly, and track the basis adjustments of each closed designation separately.

**Engineering view.**

- The designation timestamp must be on or before the start of hedge accounting. The system should block backdated designations or route them to accounting policy as exceptions.
- Hedge relationships are immutable once approved. Rebalancing creates a new version that links to the previous one, with maker-checker approval.
- Subscribe to trade lifecycle events from the treasury system for every trade used in a hedge. An amendment or termination of a hedging swap that the hedge accounting team does not see is one of the most common hedge accounting failures.
- A trade can be partly designated in several relationships. Check that the designated proportions of each trade never sum to more than 100%.
- Generate the documentation from the record itself, so the document and the data cannot diverge.

**Analogy.** Designating a hedge is like filing a patent: you must file before showing the invention to the world, and the filing defines exactly what is protected. A filing made after the fact protects nothing.

**Key takeaways**

- Hedge accounting requires formal designation and documentation at inception, before the results are known.
- Documentation covers objective, instrument, item, hedged risk, type, ratio, effectiveness method and expected ineffectiveness.
- Relationships go through designation, assessment, rebalancing and discontinuation; macro hedges are re-designated periodically.
- Systems must prevent backdating, version relationships, watch hedging trades for lifecycle events and control designated proportions.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** List five items that hedge documentation must contain under IFRS 9.
> 2. **Intermediate:** A trader asks to designate a swap traded three weeks ago as a hedge of a bond, effective from the swap's trade date, because the swap has since lost value. Explain the problem and what the system should allow instead.
> 3. **Interview:** "How would you detect that a hedging swap has been amended or terminated in the treasury system without the hedge accounting team being informed?" *Hint:* subscribe to lifecycle events filtered on designated trade IDs, block or alert on changes, run a daily reconciliation between the hedge relationship inventory and live trades, and check designated proportions against current notionals.

#### Fair Value vs Cash Flow Hedges

**Why it matters.** Chapter 6.3 introduced the hedge types. Choosing between them is a design decision with long-lasting consequences. The same pay-fixed swap could be documented as a fair value hedge of a fixed-rate asset or as a cash flow hedge of floating-rate funding, depending on how risk management describes the exposure. The choice decides where volatility appears (P&L, OCI or capital), which balances the system must track, and what happens when the hedge ends.

**Mechanics compared.**

| Aspect | Fair value hedge (FVH) | Cash flow hedge (CFH) |
|---|---|---|
| Hedged exposure | Fair value changes of a recognized fixed-rate item or firm commitment | Variability of cash flows of floating-rate items or highly probable forecast transactions |
| Hedging instrument | Fair value change to P&L | Effective part to OCI (cash flow hedge reserve), ineffective part to P&L |
| Hedged item | Carrying amount adjusted for the hedged risk (basis adjustment), through P&L | Measurement unchanged |
| Ineffectiveness | Net of the derivative and the basis adjustment, both in P&L | Over-hedge to P&L; under-hedge not recognized (lower-of test) |
| Effect on equity | Through P&L only | Through the OCI reserve; the reserve is filtered out of CET1 (CRR Article 33) |
| Balances the system tracks | Cumulative basis adjustment per hedged item or portfolio | Cumulative changes of the hedge and the hypothetical derivative; reserve balance |
| On discontinuation | Basis adjustment amortized to P&L over the item's remaining life | Reserve kept and recycled when the hedged cash flows affect P&L; to P&L at once if the forecast transaction is no longer expected |

**Where a value change ends up.**

```text
  A pay-fixed swap gains 10.0 when rates rise.

  FAIR VALUE HEDGE                                  CASH FLOW HEDGE
  (hedged item: fixed-rate bond)                    (hedged item: floating-rate funding)

  Swap                  +10.0  --> P&L              Swap                  +10.0 --> OCI reserve
  Bond basis adjustment  -9.6  --> P&L                                            (effective part)
  ----------------------------------------          Funding               no entry today
  Net P&L                +0.4  (ineffectiveness)    Later: the reserve is recycled to P&L as the
                                                    higher floating interest is paid, offsetting it
```

**Choosing the hedge type.**

| Balance sheet exposure | Usual hedge | Swap |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed-rate assets (bonds, mortgages) | Fair value hedge: convert fixed to floating | Pay fixed, receive floating |
| Issued fixed-rate debt | Fair value hedge: convert fixed to floating | Receive fixed, pay floating |
| Floating-rate loans | Cash flow hedge: lock in income | Receive fixed, pay floating |
| Floating-rate funding, rolled over | Cash flow hedge: lock in cost | Pay fixed, receive floating |
| Forecast bond issuance | Cash flow hedge: lock in the future coupon | Forward-starting pay-fixed swap |

**Example: forecast issuance (cash flow hedge).** In January, treasury plans to issue a EUR 500m 5-year fixed-rate bond in June. To lock in today's rates, it enters a forward-starting pay-fixed swap and designates it as a CFH of the forecast coupons.

1. **January to June:** rates rise. The swap gains EUR 12.0m and the hypothetical derivative EUR 12.3m. Under the lower-of test, EUR 12.0m goes to the CFH reserve and nothing to P&L.
2. **June:** the bond is issued at a higher coupon, and the swap is closed for EUR 12.0m in cash. The reserve stays in equity.
3. **The next 5 years:** the reserve is recycled to interest expense as the coupons are paid, about EUR 2.4m per year (following the EIR pattern in practice). This offsets the higher coupon, so the effective cost of the bond is close to the January rate.
4. **If the issuance is cancelled** and no longer expected to happen, the whole EUR 12.0m is reclassified to P&L immediately. If it is only delayed but still expected, the reserve remains.

**Example: discontinuing a fair value hedge.** A fixed-rate bond has a cumulative basis adjustment of EUR -1.35m when its hedging swap is terminated, three years before the bond matures. The bond's carrying amount stays 1.35m lower, and the adjustment is amortized into interest income over the remaining three years: about EUR 0.45m per year, following the EIR method.

**Engineering view.**

- A fair value hedge needs a valuation of the hedged item *for the hedged risk only*, which the bank does not otherwise compute for an amortized-cost item. The hedge system needs its own pricing of hedged items on the benchmark curve.
- A cash flow hedge needs **hypothetical derivatives**: synthetic swaps with terms frozen at designation, valued by the pricing library but never booked as real trades.
- Basis adjustments and reserves outlive the hedges that created them, sometimes by decades for long mortgages. Design for years of tracking after the derivative has gone.
- Capital reporting needs the CFH reserve broken down, because it is removed from CET1.

**Analogy.** A fair value hedge is like putting a protective case on a phone you own: the case and the phone are valued together. A cash flow hedge is like fixing the price of next year's holiday today: nothing changes in your possessions now, but the saving is kept aside and released when you actually pay for the trip.

**Key takeaways**

- Fair value hedges adjust the hedged item's carrying amount through P&L; cash flow hedges store the effective part of the derivative's change in OCI.
- Under the CFH lower-of test, over-hedging goes to P&L but under-hedging does not.
- On discontinuation, FVH basis adjustments are amortized; CFH reserves are recycled when the hedged cash flows affect P&L, or immediately if the forecast transaction is no longer expected.
- The hedge type determines which long-lived balances and synthetic valuations the system must maintain.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** A bank issues a 7-year fixed-rate bond and swaps it to floating. Which hedge type fits, and where do the swap's fair value changes go?
> 2. **Intermediate:** In the forecast issuance example, the issuance is first delayed by three months but remains highly probable, and is later cancelled. Describe the accounting at each step.
> 3. **Interview:** "Why might a bank prefer cash flow hedge accounting for some exposures even when a fair value hedge could also work?" *Hint:* consider which balance sheet items are available as hedged items, P&L volatility versus OCI volatility, the CET1 filter, the operational effort of basis adjustments on large portfolios compared with hypothetical derivatives, and what happens on discontinuation.

#### Effectiveness Calculations

**Why it matters.** Chapter 6.3 described the effectiveness tests and their thresholds. In a system, effectiveness is a calculation pipeline that runs every reporting period for every relationship: obtain the right valuations, compute cumulative changes, assess, measure ineffectiveness and produce postings. Most failures come from the inputs, not from the test formula: the wrong curve, dirty instead of clean values, or a hedged item valued with risks that were never hedged.

**The pipeline.**

```text
  Hedge relationship inventory (designation records)
         |
         v
  [1] Period-end valuations per relationship
        - hedging instrument: clean fair value, full market curves
        - FVH: hedged item valued for the hedged risk only
        - CFH: hypothetical derivative, clean value
         |
         v
  [2] Changes since designation (cumulative) and since the last period
         |
         v
  [3] Assessment: prospective (regression on rate scenarios); retrospective where required
         |                                          fail --> discontinuation workflow
         v
  [4] Ineffectiveness measurement and split: P&L / OCI / basis adjustment
         |
         v
  [5] Accounting events --> rules engine (14.1) --> postings
      All inputs and results stored per run for audit
```

**Getting the inputs right.**

- **Clean values:** use values excluding accrued interest. Otherwise accruals and coupon payments appear as value changes and create artificial ineffectiveness. Accruals are booked separately in net interest income.
- **Isolating the hedged risk (FVH):** value the hedged item's cash flows on the benchmark curve with the credit spread frozen at its designation level. Many banks hedge only a **benchmark component**: the cash flows at the swap rate prevailing at designation. Changes in the issuer's credit spread are not part of the hedged risk and must not enter the calculation.
- **Hypothetical derivative (CFH):** a swap whose terms match the hedged cash flows, priced at market at designation (zero value at inception) and without counterparty credit adjustments. It models a perfect hedge, so its value moves in the same direction as the actual hedge.
- **Cumulative measurement:** measure ineffectiveness on a cumulative basis since designation. The period amount is the cumulative amount now minus the cumulative amount already booked.

**Worked example: fair value hedge (EUR m).**

| | Q1 | Q2 | Cumulative to Q2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Swap clean fair value change | +2.40 | -0.90 | +1.50 |
| Hedged item change for hedged risk | -2.30 | +0.95 | -1.35 |
| Dollar offset (cumulative) | 104.3% | | 111.1% |
| Ineffectiveness to P&L | +0.10 | +0.05 | +0.15 |

Both cumulative ratios are inside 80-125%, and the cumulative ineffectiveness of +0.15 equals the sum of the two quarters.

**Worked example: cash flow hedge lower-of test (EUR m).** A pay-fixed swap hedges floating-rate funding. The reserve holds the smaller of the cumulative change in the swap and the cumulative change in the hypothetical derivative.

| Period | Cumulative swap | Cumulative hypothetical | Reserve balance | OCI movement | Swap change in period | P&L ineffectiveness |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 | +3.0 | +3.2 | +3.0 | +3.0 | +3.0 | 0.0 (under-hedge) |
| Q2 | +4.5 | +4.2 | +4.2 | +1.2 | +1.5 | +0.3 (over-hedge) |
| Q3 | -1.0 | -0.8 | -0.8 | -5.0 | -5.5 | -0.5 (over-hedge) |

After Q3, cumulative P&L ineffectiveness is -0.2, which equals the cumulative swap change minus the reserve: -1.0 - (-0.8).

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from decimal import Decimal

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CfhResult:
    reserve: Decimal          # cumulative balance of the cash flow hedge reserve
    oci_movement: Decimal     # posting to OCI this period
    ineffectiveness: Decimal  # posting to P&L this period

def cfh_lower_of(cum_hedge: Decimal, cum_hypothetical: Decimal,
                 prev_reserve: Decimal, period_hedge_change: Decimal) -> CfhResult:
    if cum_hedge * cum_hypothetical <= 0:   # no offset: nothing qualifies for the reserve
        reserve = Decimal(0)
    else:
        sign = 1 if cum_hedge > 0 else -1
        reserve = sign * min(abs(cum_hedge), abs(cum_hypothetical))
    oci = reserve - prev_reserve
    return CfhResult(reserve, oci, period_hedge_change - oci)

cfh_lower_of(Decimal("4.5"), Decimal("4.2"), Decimal("3.0"), Decimal("1.5"))
# CfhResult(reserve=Decimal('4.2'), oci_movement=Decimal('1.2'), ineffectiveness=Decimal('0.3'))
```

**Prospective assessment.** A regression test revalues the hedging instrument and the hedged item under a set of rate scenarios (parallel shifts, twists, or historical changes) and regresses one series of value changes on the other. Store the scenario set and results with the relationship, because auditors will ask how the test was performed at each date. Under IFRS 9 there is no 80-125% bright line, so a weak result leads to a review of the hedge ratio (rebalancing) rather than automatic discontinuation.

**Engineering view.**

- Use the same curves, cut-off times and model versions as the official valuations, and store the inputs (curve snapshots, model versions, trade versions) so any period can be reproduced exactly.
- Keep hypothetical derivatives and hedged-risk valuations inside the hedge accounting module as synthetic instruments. Booking them as trades in the treasury system lets them leak into risk and P&L.
- Run a dry run a few days before period end so failing relationships are found while there is still time to act.
- Macro hedges can involve thousands of relationships and time buckets. Batch the valuations and parallelize per relationship.
- Guard ratio tests against very small denominators, and report ratios together with absolute amounts (the "small numbers problem" of Chapter 6.3).

**Analogy.** An effectiveness run is like a monthly bank reconciliation. The arithmetic is trivial; the work lies in making sure both sides are measured on the same basis and at the same moment.

**Key takeaways**

- Effectiveness is a periodic pipeline: valuations, cumulative changes, assessment, ineffectiveness split and postings.
- Use clean values, isolate the hedged risk with frozen credit spreads, and model CFH hedged items with hypothetical derivatives.
- Fair value hedge ineffectiveness is the net of the derivative and the basis adjustment; CFH ineffectiveness follows the lower-of test.
- Reproducibility requires storing all valuation inputs per run.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain why effectiveness calculations use clean rather than dirty values.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Extend the cash flow hedge table with Q4: the cumulative swap change is +0.5 and the cumulative hypothetical change is +0.6. Compute the reserve balance, the OCI movement and the P&L ineffectiveness, then check your answer with `cfh_lower_of`.
> 3. **Interview:** "After a change in curve methodology, 40 hedge relationships fail the effectiveness test in March. How do you investigate?" *Hint:* reproduce the results with stored inputs before and after the change; check whether the hedged item and the hedging instrument were both moved to the new curve set; compare values for each relationship one at a time; and consider whether the change went through model governance.

#### Accounting Entries for Hedges

**Why it matters.** The final output of hedge accounting is journal entries. They use accounts that do not exist elsewhere (basis adjustments, the CFH reserve, hedge results), they must be traceable to a relationship and a period, and some of them continue long after the hedge has ended. Errors here appear directly in reported profit and equity.

**Accounts used.**

| Account | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Derivative assets and liabilities: hedging | Fair value of hedging derivatives, shown separately from trading derivatives |
| Hedge basis adjustment (per hedged item) | FVH adjustment to the carrying amount of the hedged item |
| Fair value changes of hedged items in portfolio hedges | Separate balance sheet line for IAS 39 macro fair value hedges |
| Cash flow hedge reserve (OCI) | Effective portion of CFH derivatives |
| Hedge result (P&L) | Fair value changes of hedging instruments and hedged items, and ineffectiveness |
| Interest income and expense: hedging derivatives | Net swap accruals, presented within net interest income |

**Fair value hedge entries (EUR m).** Using the effectiveness example: a EUR 100m fixed-rate bond at amortized cost hedged with a pay-fixed swap.

```text
  Q1: rates rise
  Dr  Derivative assets: hedging                         2.40
      Cr  Hedge result: hedging instrument (P&L)                    2.40
  Dr  Hedge result: hedged item (P&L)                    2.30
      Cr  Debt securities at AC: hedge basis adjustment             2.30

  Q2: rates fall partially
  Dr  Hedge result: hedging instrument (P&L)             0.90
      Cr  Derivative assets: hedging                                0.90
  Dr  Debt securities at AC: hedge basis adjustment      0.95
      Cr  Hedge result: hedged item (P&L)                           0.95

  Q3: swap terminated for its fair value of 1.50; hedge discontinued
  Dr  Nostro                                             1.50
      Cr  Derivative assets: hedging                                1.50
  Each quarter for the remaining 3 years (straight-line shown; EIR in practice):
  Dr  Debt securities at AC: hedge basis adjustment      0.1125
      Cr  Interest income: securities                               0.1125
```

**Interest on the hedging swap.** The swap's accruals are booked in net interest income next to the interest on the hedged item, so NII shows the hedged result. Suppose the bond pays 3.00%, the swap pays 2.60% fixed and receives 3-month Euribor fixed at 2.10%:

```text
  Quarterly accruals on EUR 100m
  Dr  Accrued interest receivable: bond          0.750
      Cr  Interest income: securities                       0.750
  Dr  Interest expense: hedging derivatives      0.650
      Cr  Accrued interest payable: swap                    0.650
  Dr  Accrued interest receivable: swap          0.525
      Cr  Interest income: hedging derivatives              0.525

  Net interest income = 0.750 - 0.650 + 0.525 = 0.625
                      = (Euribor 2.10% + 0.40%) x 100m / 4  -> the bond now earns floating
```

**Cash flow hedge entries (EUR m).** Using the lower-of example:

```text
  Q1: Dr  Derivative assets: hedging       3.00
          Cr  Cash flow hedge reserve (OCI)               3.00
  Q2: Dr  Derivative assets: hedging       1.50
          Cr  Cash flow hedge reserve (OCI)               1.20
          Cr  Hedge result: ineffectiveness (P&L)         0.30
  Q3: Dr  Cash flow hedge reserve (OCI)    5.00
      Dr  Hedge result: ineffectiveness    0.50
          Cr  Derivative assets / liabilities: hedging    5.50
```

**Recycling.** For a forecast transaction such as the bond issuance in the previous topic, recycling is an explicit entry each period:

```text
  Swap closed at issuance:   Dr  Nostro                        12.0
                                 Cr  Derivative assets: hedging          12.0
  Each year, for 5 years:    Dr  Cash flow hedge reserve (OCI)  2.4
                                 Cr  Interest expense: issued debt        2.4
  If the issuance is cancelled and no longer expected:
                             Dr  Cash flow hedge reserve (OCI) 12.0
                                 Cr  Hedge result (P&L)                  12.0
```

For a cash flow hedge of an ongoing floating-rate exposure, the swap's periodic net settlements are booked in net interest income in the same period as the hedged interest. The reserve, which holds the effective part of the swap's clean value, unwinds as the swap approaches maturity. Banks implement this either with explicit reclassification entries each period or through their accrual booking design. The method must be documented in the accounting policy and applied consistently.

**Engineering view.**

- Post hedge entries through the same rules engine as other events, with the relationship ID as an attribute. This allows reconciliation and audit per relationship.
- By default, a treasury system posts every swap revaluation to trading P&L. For hedging swaps, the hedge accounting module must redirect these postings, either through a hedge clearing account that it allocates or through reclassification entries. If the treasury system and the hedge module both post the same fair value change, P&L is double counted: a classic defect.
- Reconcile basis adjustment and reserve balances in the GL to the hedge module every period, per relationship.
- Generate amortization schedules for basis adjustments and reserves at discontinuation, and keep running them after the derivative has gone.

**Analogy.** Hedge entries are like keeping two halves of a matched receipt in the same folder. Each half alone looks like a gain or a loss; filed together, they show the protection that was bought.

**Key takeaways**

- FVH entries post the derivative's change and the basis adjustment to P&L; the net is ineffectiveness.
- CFH entries split the derivative's change between the OCI reserve and P&L under the lower-of test.
- Swap accruals are booked in net interest income so that NII reflects the hedged position.
- Reserves and basis adjustments must be recycled or amortized after discontinuation, and hedge postings must not duplicate the treasury system's default derivative postings.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Write the fair value hedge entries for a period in which the swap loses 0.80 and the hedged item gains 0.75 for the hedged risk. What is the ineffectiveness?
> 2. **Intermediate:** The treasury system automatically posts every swap revaluation to "Trading P&L". Explain what happens to reported results if the hedge accounting module also posts the change of the same swap to "Hedge result", and design a posting flow that prevents it.
> 3. **Interview:** "Walk me through the journal entries over the life of a forward-starting swap used to hedge a forecast bond issuance." *Hint:* cover the periods before issuance (OCI versus ineffectiveness), the settlement of the swap at issuance, recycling over the life of the bond, and what happens if the issuance is delayed or cancelled.

<a id="143-management-reporting"></a>
### 14.3 Management Reporting

Financial statements serve outside readers and arrive monthly or quarterly; management needs faster, more granular and forward-looking views. This subchapter covers the main treasury management reports and the data quality controls that make them trustworthy.

#### Liquidity and ALM Dashboards

**Why it matters.** At 08:30 the treasurer needs to know two things: whether the bank is safe today, and whether it is moving in the right direction. Liquidity can change within hours (Chapter 5.3; Silicon Valley Bank faced USD 42bn of withdrawal requests in a single day), while interest rate risk changes more slowly. A dashboard brings the key metrics, limits and trends together, and a good one makes a breach or an adverse trend impossible to miss.

**Audiences.**

| Audience | Question | Frequency | Typical content |
|---|---|---|---|
| Treasury desk | Can we settle everything today? What must we fund? | Intraday or real time | Central bank balance, intraday usage, payment queue, today's maturities |
| Treasurer, head of ALM | Are we within limits? Where are we heading? | Daily | LCR, survival horizon, buffer, funding concentration, deposit flows |
| ALCO, CFO | Is the strategy working? | Monthly | Trends, forecasts, plan versus actual (ALCO packs, below) |
| Board risk committee | Are we within risk appetite? | Quarterly | Risk appetite metrics with status |

**Metric catalogue.**

| Metric | Defined in | Typical frequency |
|---|---|---|
| LCR | Chapter 9.2 | Daily (internal), monthly (regulatory) |
| NSFR | Chapter 9.2 | Monthly or quarterly |
| Survival horizon under stress | Chapter 5.1 | Daily |
| Liquidity buffer size and composition | Chapter 5.4 | Daily |
| Intraday liquidity usage | Chapter 5.3 | Intraday |
| Maturity ladder and cash flow gaps | Chapter 5.2 | Daily |
| NII and EVE sensitivity | Chapter 6.2 | Monthly, some banks daily |
| Funding concentration and deposit flows | Chapter 7.1 | Daily or weekly |
| Asset encumbrance | Chapter 5.4 | Monthly |

**Example: a daily dashboard.**

```text
  LIQUIDITY AND ALM DASHBOARD - GROUP            As of 2026-10-16 EOD | Run 20261016-03 | Data completeness 99.8%
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Metric                       Value      Appetite / early warning   Status   1-day     20-day trend
  LCR (internal)               148%       >= 120% / 130%             GREEN    -3 pp     falling
  Survival horizon (stress)    67 days    >= 60 / 70 days            AMBER    -5 days   falling
  NSFR (last month end)        126%       >= 110% / 115%             GREEN    n/a       stable
  HQLA buffer (EUR bn)         21.4       >= 18.0 / 19.5             GREEN    -0.6      falling
  Peak intraday usage          38%        <= 60% / 50%               GREEN    +4 pp     stable
  Top-10 depositor share       14.2%      <= 20% / 17%               GREEN    +0.1 pp   rising
  NII sensitivity, -200bp      -6.1%      >= -10% / -8%              GREEN    n/a       stable
  EVE sensitivity (SOT)        -11.3%     >= -15% / -13%             GREEN    n/a       stable
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  LCR drivers (1-day): retail deposit outflows -1.2 pp, settled bond purchases -1.0 pp,
                       wholesale maturities -0.8 pp
  Alert: survival horizon below early warning level (70 days) since 2026-10-15
```

**Design principles.**

- **One metric, one definition.** Metrics are calculated in a governed calculation layer, never in the dashboard tool.
- **Context for every number.** Show the as-of date, run ID and data completeness, and place the limit and early warning level next to the value. Status is derived by rule, not set by hand.
- **Trends and drivers, not only levels.** A falling LCR at 148% may matter more than a stable one at 135%.
- **Drill-down** by entity, currency, product and counterparty.
- **Consistency with regulatory figures.** On regulatory reporting dates, the internal LCR must reconcile to the reported LCR, with documented differences.

**Architecture.**

```text
  Liquidity engine ---+
  ALM engine ---------+--> results store -----------> metric layer -------------> dashboard
  Payments / RTGS ----+    (versioned snapshot        (definitions, limits,        (presentation,
  Limits system ------+     per run, run ID)           status rules, drivers)       drill-down)
```

**Engineering view.**

- Tie every published number to a run ID. A restatement creates a new version; it never overwrites the original.
- Monitor delivery against the agreed deadline (for example, the daily dashboard available by 07:30) and show data freshness on the screen.
- Support a stress mode: during a crisis, management will ask for refreshes every hour or more often. BCBS 239 expects banks to produce risk data quickly in stress (see the last topic of this subchapter).
- Restrict access: liquidity data can be highly sensitive, and for listed banks it may be inside information.

**Analogy.** A good dashboard is like a car's instrument panel: a few gauges that matter, each with a red zone, and warning lights that come on before the engine fails, not after.

**Key takeaways**

- Different audiences need different metrics at different frequencies, from intraday to quarterly.
- Core metrics include LCR, NSFR, survival horizon, buffer, intraday usage, gaps, NII and EVE sensitivity, and concentration.
- Show limits, early warning levels, trends, drivers, as-of dates and data completeness next to each metric.
- Calculate metrics in a governed layer, version every run, and be ready for frequent refreshes in stress.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Choose five metrics for a treasurer's daily liquidity dashboard and justify each choice in one sentence.
> 2. **Intermediate:** The dashboard shows an LCR of 148%, while the regulatory report for the same date shows 141%. List possible reasons and describe how you would design the system so that the difference can be explained.
> 3. **Interview:** "Design the data architecture for a liquidity dashboard that must refresh every 15 minutes during a stress event." *Hint:* incremental position updates from payment and trading events (Chapter 13.3), cached HQLA valuations, a stress mode with reduced scope, completeness indicators per source, versioned snapshots, and graceful degradation when a source is late.

#### P&L Explain Reports

**Why it matters.** Chapter 8.1 described P&L attribution for trading desks. Treasury also owns the banking book, whose income is mostly accrual-based net interest income, and management asks a different question there: why is NII different from last month, from budget, or from forecast? P&L explain reports answer both questions. Without a credible explanation, reported numbers are not trusted and decisions are delayed.

**Two kinds of explain.**

| Report | Scope | Measure | Frequency | Main components |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Daily P&L explain | Fair-valued treasury positions, derivatives, hedge results | Fair value P&L and OCI | Daily | Carry, rates, spreads, FX, new trades, amendments, unexplained (Chapter 8.1) |
| NII variance analysis | Banking book: loans, deposits, funding, hedges | Net interest income | Monthly, versus prior period, budget or forecast | Volume, rate, mix, day count, hedges, one-off items |

**Volume and rate effects.**

```text
  Income = average balance (V) x rate (r)

  Change = V1 x r1 - V0 x r0
         = (V1 - V0) x r0      volume effect: change in balance at the old rate
         + (r1 - r0) x V1      rate effect:   change in rate on the new balance
```

The order matters. Some banks use a three-way split with a separate joint term (V1 - V0) x (r1 - r0). Choose one convention, document it and apply it everywhere.

**Example (annualized, EUR m).**

| Line | V0 (bn) | r0 | V1 (bn) | r1 | NII before | NII after | Volume effect | Rate effect | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mortgages (income) | 10.0 | 3.00% | 10.5 | 3.20% | 300.0 | 336.0 | +15.0 | +21.0 | +36.0 |
| Retail deposits (expense) | 8.0 | 1.00% | 8.2 | 1.25% | -80.0 | -102.5 | -2.0 | -20.5 | -22.5 |
| **Net** | | | | | **220.0** | **233.5** | **+13.0** | **+0.5** | **+13.5** |

NII grew by EUR 13.5m, almost entirely because of mortgage volume. The higher mortgage rates (+21.0m) were almost fully absorbed by higher deposit rates (-20.5m), so the margin gain from higher rates has nearly disappeared. This is a typical late-cycle pattern, in which deposit rates catch up with market rates (deposit beta, Chapter 6.1).

**Other components of an NII explain.**

- **Day count:** February has 28 days and March 31, so monthly NII changes even when balances and rates do not.
- **Hedges:** net swap accruals from Section 14.2, shown separately so that management sees what hedging contributed.
- **One-off items:** EIR catch-up adjustments (Section 14.1), prepayment fees, corrections of prior periods.
- **Business split:** through FTP (Chapter 6.4), the NII change is allocated to lending, deposits and treasury.

**Workflow.**

```text
  Flash P&L        Official P&L            Explain                Commentary            Sign-off
  (T+0 evening, -> (T+1, product control -> (components +      -> (items above        -> (product control,
   front office)    after IPV and           unexplained)           threshold,             desk head)
                    adjustments)                                   by desk)
```

Thresholds decide what needs commentary, for example unexplained amounts above 5% of the day's P&L or above EUR 100k.

**Engineering view.**

- The explain must add up: explained plus unexplained must equal the official P&L or NII exactly, using the same positions and cut-off.
- Store the inputs for both dates (positions, market data, rates, balances) so any explain can be re-run.
- Make the separation of effects deterministic, with a documented order of steps.
- Capture commentary as structured data attached to the report version, so it becomes part of the audit trail rather than an email.
- Keep the explain additive across levels: the sum of desk explains must equal the total explain.

**Analogy.** A P&L explain is like a household comparing this month's spending with last month's: more people at dinner (volume), higher grocery prices (rate), and one extra day in the month (day count). If a large difference remains unexplained, something was missed or wrongly recorded.

**Key takeaways**

- Daily explains cover fair-valued positions; NII variance analysis covers the accrual banking book.
- Volume and rate effects split NII changes; the decomposition convention must be documented and consistent.
- Day count, hedges, one-off items and FTP allocation complete the NII explain.
- Explains must reconcile exactly to official figures and be reproducible from stored inputs.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** A deposit balance falls from EUR 5.0bn at 0.50% to EUR 4.6bn at 0.90%. Compute the volume and rate effects on annual interest expense.
> 2. **Intermediate:** NII in February is 4% lower than in January, although balances and rates did not change. What explains this, and how should the report present it?
> 3. **Interview:** "Product control complains that the daily explain for treasury's FVOCI portfolio shows 15% unexplained P&L every day. How would you debug it?" *Hint:* compare position sets and cut-off times between the explain and the official figures; look for missing risk factors (basis spreads, issuer-specific credit curves); check how new trades and amendments are classified, clean versus dirty value treatment, FX translation and sign conventions.

#### ALCO Reporting Packs

**Why it matters.** Chapter 4.1 described ALCO's mandate and the metrics it reviews. The ALCO pack is the evidence of how the bank governs its balance sheet, and supervisors read packs and minutes during inspections. Producing it is a monthly process with hard deadlines, many contributors and high stakes. Traditionally it was a large spreadsheet assembled by hand, which is an operational risk in itself.

**Typical structure.**

| Section | Content | Main source |
|---|---|---|
| Executive summary | Key messages, breaches, decisions requested | Treasury and ALM commentary |
| Balance sheet and plan | Balance sheet versus plan, loan and deposit growth | GL (finance), planning |
| Liquidity | LCR, NSFR, survival horizon, buffer, stress results, funding plan | Liquidity engine |
| Interest rate risk | NII and EVE sensitivities, repricing gaps, hedging activity, outlier test | ALM engine |
| NII and margins | NII versus plan, volume and rate explain, FTP results | Finance, FTP engine |
| Capital (in some banks) | CET1, leverage ratio, RWA | Regulatory reporting |
| Market outlook | Rate scenarios, competitor pricing | Economics, business lines |
| Limits and breaches | Utilization, breaches, remediation | Limits system (Chapter 8.4) |
| Decisions and actions | Proposals, open actions from previous meetings | ALCO secretary |

**Production timeline (working days after month end).**

```text
  M+1   Month-end data final; ALM and liquidity engines run on month-end positions
  M+3   GL close complete; balance sheet reconciled to finance figures
  M+4   Metrics frozen (data lock); tables and charts generated
  M+5   Commentary by treasury, ALM and risk; review by heads of function
  M+6   Pack signed off by the treasurer and a risk delegate; distributed to members
  M+8   ALCO meeting; decisions and actions minuted
  M+9   Pack, data snapshot and minutes archived (immutable, retained per policy)
```

**Production pipeline.**

```text
  GL -----------+
  ALM engine ---+--> reporting data mart ---> metric layer ---------> pack generator ---> draft pack
  Liquidity ----+    (frozen snapshot per     (definitions, limits,   (templates,            |
  FTP engine ---+     month end)               status rules)           tables, charts)       v
  Limits -------+                                                                commentary and review
                                                                                          |
                                                                                sign-off --> archive
```

**Quality principles.**

- **Consistency across sections.** Total deposits in the balance sheet section and in the liquidity section should match, or the difference (for example, accounting versus behavioural views) should be explained in the pack.
- **Reconciliation to finance.** Balance sheet figures reconcile to the GL (Section 14.1), and remaining differences are listed.
- **Versioning.** The pack shown at the meeting is archived together with its data snapshot. Later corrections are documented as restatements, never applied silently.
- **Less end-user computing.** Replace manual spreadsheet steps with generated tables. Inventory and control any spreadsheets that remain.
- **Action tracking.** Decisions are recorded as structured items with an owner and a due date, and reported on at the next meeting.

**Engineering view.**

- Generate the pack from templates that read the frozen snapshot, and print the snapshot or run ID on every page.
- After the data lock, route late corrections through a controlled restatement process instead of regenerating the pack quietly.
- Keep chart scales and definitions stable from month to month so that members can compare packs.
- Use reconciliation checks as gates in the pipeline: if the balance sheet does not reconcile to the GL within tolerance, the pack is not generated without an explicit override.
- Restrict distribution. For listed banks, ALCO packs can contain inside information under market abuse rules.

**Analogy.** An ALCO pack is like a flight's pre-departure briefing pack: compiled to a fixed deadline from many sources, read by the people who decide, and kept afterwards as evidence of what they knew when they decided.

**Key takeaways**

- The ALCO pack documents balance sheet governance and is read by supervisors.
- It covers the balance sheet, liquidity, interest rate risk, NII, limits and decisions, and draws on several engines and the GL.
- Production follows a fixed timeline with a data lock, commentary, sign-off and archiving.
- Automation should generate figures from a frozen snapshot with reconciliation gates; commentary and judgment remain human.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Name four sections of an ALCO pack and the source system for each.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Deposits are EUR 52.3bn in the balance sheet section and EUR 51.1bn in the liquidity section of the same pack. Give possible reasons and explain how the pack should present the difference.
> 3. **Interview:** "Today the ALCO pack is 60 linked spreadsheets that two analysts assemble over five days. How would you automate it, and what would you not automate?" *Hint:* a data mart with month-end snapshots, governed metric definitions, generation from templates, reconciliation checks as gates, human commentary, judgment and sign-off, incremental migration and a parallel run against the manual pack.

#### Data Quality Controls in Reporting

**Why it matters.** A report is only as good as its data. During the 2008 crisis, many banks could not aggregate their exposures quickly or accurately. In response, the Basel Committee published **BCBS 239** (2013), its principles for risk data aggregation and risk reporting, and supervisors still list data quality among banks' most persistent weaknesses. For treasury, a wrong LCR or a missing deposit feed can lead to wrong funding decisions or to incorrect regulatory reports.

**BCBS 239 in engineering terms.**

| Principles | Requirement | Engineering implication |
|---|---|---|
| 1-2: Governance and infrastructure | Clear ownership, integrated architecture, common taxonomy | Data owners, data dictionary, shared reference data |
| 3: Accuracy and integrity | Data reconciled and largely automated | Reconciliations, minimal manual steps |
| 4: Completeness | All material risk data captured | Completeness controls per feed and entity |
| 5: Timeliness | Data available when needed, including in stress | Deadlines, monitoring, alerting |
| 6: Adaptability | Ad hoc and stress requests can be met | Flexible data model, self-service queries |
| 7-11: Reporting | Reports accurate, comprehensive, clear, frequent enough and distributed properly | Report-level controls, distribution lists, sign-off |

**Data quality dimensions.**

| Dimension | Question | Example control in treasury reporting |
|---|---|---|
| Completeness | Is everything there? | Record counts and control totals from source match what was loaded; every entity and feed arrived |
| Accuracy | Is it correct? | Balances reconcile to the GL; prices pass IPV |
| Validity | Does it follow the rules? | Maturity date after start date; valid ISO currency code; valid HQLA level |
| Consistency | Do sources agree? | Liquidity and ALM engines show the same deposit totals |
| Timeliness | Is it current? | Feeds arrive before cut-off; market data date equals the reporting date |
| Uniqueness | Are there duplicates? | One record per trade ID and version |
| Plausibility | Does it look reasonable? | Day-on-day change in an LCR outflow category above a threshold is flagged |

**Where controls sit.**

```text
  Source systems
     | [C1] Ingestion: record counts, control totals, schema, arrival time
     v
  Staging
     | [C2] Validation: validity rules, referential integrity, duplicates
     v
  Calculation engines
     | [C3] Reconciliation: to the GL and between engines
     v
  Results
     | [C4] Plausibility: variance against the previous day and thresholds
     v
  Reports
       [C5] Sign-off: data owner attestation, data quality scorecard attached

  Failed control --> severity --> critical: block publication
                                  major:    publish with caveat and approval
                                  minor:    log and track
```

**Example: a plausibility check.** A day-on-day variance check flags items that moved by more than both a relative and an absolute threshold, and also reports items that appeared or disappeared:

```python
from decimal import Decimal

def variance_breaches(today: dict[str, Decimal], yesterday: dict[str, Decimal],
                      rel_threshold: Decimal, abs_threshold: Decimal) -> list[str]:
    issues = []
    for key in sorted(today.keys() | yesterday.keys()):
        if key not in today:
            issues.append(f"{key}: missing today (was {yesterday[key]})")
        elif key not in yesterday:
            issues.append(f"{key}: new today ({today[key]})")
        else:
            change = today[key] - yesterday[key]
            base = abs(yesterday[key]) or Decimal(1)
            if abs(change) > abs_threshold and abs(change) / base > rel_threshold:
                issues.append(f"{key}: {yesterday[key]} -> {today[key]} ({change:+})")
    return issues

# LCR outflows by category, EUR m
today = {"retail_stable": Decimal("1210"), "retail_less_stable": Decimal("2950"),
         "wholesale_operational": Decimal("4100")}
yesterday = {"retail_stable": Decimal("1205"), "retail_less_stable": Decimal("2380"),
             "wholesale_operational": Decimal("4090"),
             "wholesale_non_operational": Decimal("3600")}
variance_breaches(today, yesterday, Decimal("0.10"), Decimal("100"))
# ['retail_less_stable: 2380 -> 2950 (+570)',
#  'wholesale_non_operational: missing today (was 3600)']
```

Using two thresholds avoids noise from small lines with large percentage moves and from large lines with small percentage moves. The second finding is the dangerous one: a missing feed of EUR 3.6bn of outflows would make the LCR look *better*. Missing data often flatters liquidity metrics, so completeness controls must block publication rather than merely warn.

**Issue management.** Every failed control creates an issue with a severity, an owner and a root cause. Fix issues at the source, because fixes applied in the report come back every month. Manual adjustments ("overlays") are recorded with a reason, an approver and an expiry, and are reversed in the next period unless renewed.

**Engineering view.**

- Write controls as versioned code that runs automatically in the pipeline. Store each result (control ID, run ID, status, measured values) as data that can be shown to auditors.
- Do not allow controls to be disabled or thresholds changed without approval and an audit record.
- Maintain lineage from each report cell back to source fields, so that an issue can be traced and its impact assessed.
- Attach a data quality scorecard to each report version, so readers know which caveats apply.

**Analogy.** Data quality controls are like an airline's pre-flight checklist: almost every item passes on almost every day, which is exactly why the list must be run in full every time.

**Key takeaways**

- BCBS 239 sets expectations for accurate, complete, timely and adaptable risk data aggregation and reporting.
- Controls cover completeness, accuracy, validity, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness and plausibility, at ingestion, validation, reconciliation, results and sign-off.
- Missing data often makes liquidity metrics look better, so completeness failures must block publication.
- Controls should be automated, versioned and auditable, with issues fixed at the source and overlays approved and time-limited.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Assign each control to a data quality dimension: (a) record count from source equals record count loaded; (b) no trade ID appears twice; (c) the market data date equals the reporting date; (d) deposit totals agree between the liquidity and ALM engines.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Explain why missing data often makes the LCR look better, and design a completeness control that would catch a missing feed of wholesale deposits even if the feed file arrives empty.
> 3. **Interview:** "A supervisor's BCBS 239 review finds that your liquidity reports depend on 40 manual adjustments each month. What is your remediation plan?" *Hint:* inventory the adjustments and group them by root cause; fix them at the source in order of materiality; turn recurring ones into governed rules; put controls on the remaining overlays; track the reduction as a metric; document lineage.

---

<a id="15-engineering-reliable-and-secure-treasury-software"></a>
## 15. Engineering Reliable and Secure Treasury Software

Treasury software moves real money, feeds regulatory reports and runs against hard deadlines. A defect can mean a payment sent twice, a missed CLS pay-in or a wrong liquidity ratio sent to the supervisor. This chapter covers the engineering practices that keep such systems correct, available and secure: how to test financial calculations, how to design for resilience and run incidents against cut-offs, how to protect payments and keys, and how change is governed in a regulated bank.

<a id="151-correctness-and-testing"></a>
### 15.1 Correctness and Testing

This subchapter covers how to model the treasury domain so that errors are hard to write, and how to prove that calculations are right: golden datasets, property-based tests, regression against vendor systems, and parallel runs before go-live.

#### Domain-Driven Design for Financial Systems

**Why it matters.** Many serious defects in treasury systems are not algorithm errors. They come from misunderstanding the domain: adding EUR to USD, treating a trade date as a value date, or assuming that "position" means the same thing to the dealer and to the accountant. Domain-driven design (DDD) puts the business language and its rules into the structure of the code, so that misunderstandings show up as compile errors, failed invariants or explicit translations instead of wrong numbers.

**Core ideas.**

- **Ubiquitous language:** developers and the business use the same terms with the same meaning, in conversations, documents and code. If treasury says "value date", the code says `value_date`, not `date2` or `settle_dt`.
- **Bounded context:** a part of the system inside which each term has exactly one meaning. Treasury needs several, because the same word legitimately means different things in different departments.
- **Value object:** an immutable object defined by its values, with its rules built in, such as `Money`, `CurrencyPair`, `Tenor`, `BusinessDate` or `Rate`.
- **Entity and aggregate:** an entity has an identity that persists through changes (a trade with its trade ID). An aggregate is a cluster of objects that changes as a unit through one root, which enforces the invariants (rules that must always hold).
- **Domain event:** a record of something that happened in business terms, such as `TradeBooked`, `TradeAmended` or `SettlementConfirmed`. Other contexts react to events rather than reading each other's tables.
- **Anti-corruption layer (ACL):** a translation layer at the boundary with external systems (a vendor TMS, SWIFT, a core banking system), so that their model does not leak into yours.

**One word, several meanings.**

| Term | Front office context | Settlement context | Accounting context | Liquidity context |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade | The deal agreed with a counterparty, with price and economics | A set of settlement obligations with SSIs | A source of postings over its lifecycle | A set of future cash flows |
| Position | Net risk per instrument and book | Securities and cash expected per account | Carrying amount per lot and category | Inflows and outflows per time bucket |
| Date | Trade date | Settlement or value date | Trade date or settlement date accounting (Chapter 14.1) | Cash flow date, adjusted to business days |
| Cancel | Deal never existed | Instruction must be recalled | Reversal postings needed | Cash flows removed from the ladder |

Trying to make one shared `Trade` class that serves all four meanings usually produces a large object with fields that are only valid in some states. Each context should have its own model, linked by trade ID and events.

```text
  +--------------------+  TradeBooked / TradeAmended   +---------------------+
  | Front office       |------------------------------>| Settlement          |
  | deals, pricing,    |                               | instructions, SSIs, |
  | counterparties     |                               | nostro positions    |
  +--------------------+                               +---------------------+
       |  TradeBooked                                          |  SettlementConfirmed
       v                                                       v
  +--------------------+                               +---------------------+
  | Accounting         |                               | Liquidity           |
  | IFRS 9, postings,  |                               | cash ladder, LCR,   |
  | GL feeds           |                               | intraday positions  |
  +--------------------+                               +---------------------+
       ^                                                       ^
       |                 +---------------------------+         |
       +-----------------| Anti-corruption layer     |---------+
                         | vendor TMS / SWIFT models |
                         +---------------------------+
```

**Example: value objects and an aggregate.** A value object makes an invalid operation impossible to write. Chapter 11.4 builds a `Money` type that refuses to add amounts in different currencies. The same idea applies to aggregates:

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal
from enum import Enum

class Status(Enum):
    LIVE = "LIVE"
    SETTLED = "SETTLED"
    CANCELLED = "CANCELLED"

@dataclass
class FxForward:
    trade_id: str
    buy: Money
    sell: Money
    value_date: date
    status: Status = Status.LIVE
    events: list = field(default_factory=list)

    def __post_init__(self):
        if self.buy.currency == self.sell.currency:
            raise DomainError("an FX forward needs two different currencies")
        if self.buy.amount <= 0 or self.sell.amount <= 0:
            raise DomainError("amounts must be positive; direction is given by buy/sell")

    def amend_value_date(self, new_date: date, today: date) -> None:
        if self.status is not Status.LIVE:
            raise DomainError(f"cannot amend a {self.status.value} trade")
        if new_date < today:
            raise DomainError("value date cannot be moved into the past")
        old, self.value_date = self.value_date, new_date
        self.events.append(TradeAmended(self.trade_id, "value_date", old, new_date))
```

The rules (two currencies, positive amounts, no amendment after settlement) live in one place. No other code can put an `FxForward` into an invalid state, and every change produces an event that settlement, accounting and liquidity can consume.

**Common pitfalls.**

| Pitfall | Consequence | DDD remedy |
|---|---|---|
| Primitive obsession: amounts as `float`, currencies as free strings | Mixed currencies, rounding errors, typos such as "EUT" | Value objects (`Money`, `Currency`) validated at construction |
| Anemic model: data classes with rules spread across services | The same rule implemented differently in three places | Rules in the aggregate root |
| Vendor model used directly everywhere | A vendor upgrade or replacement touches the whole code base | Anti-corruption layer |
| One canonical model for all contexts | A large, ambiguous object that nobody fully understands | Separate bounded contexts with explicit translation |

**Engineering view.**

- Build a glossary with treasury and operations and keep it in the repository. Review new terms in code review.
- Map bounded contexts to services, teams and data ownership (Chapter 13.2), so that each term has an owner.
- Keep calculations (pricing, accruals, bucketing) as pure functions over value objects. They are then easy to test with golden and property-based tests.
- Use event storming workshops with dealers, operations and finance to discover events and rules before writing code.

**Analogy.** Bounded contexts are like departments in a hospital. "Discharge" means one thing to the ward, another to billing and another to pharmacy. Each department keeps its own records and they coordinate through well-defined forms, not by sharing one giant patient file that everyone edits.

**Key takeaways**

- DDD puts the business language and rules into the code, so that domain errors become hard to write.
- Value objects (`Money`, `Tenor`, `BusinessDate`) remove whole classes of bugs, such as mixed currencies.
- Aggregates enforce invariants and emit domain events on every change.
- The same term means different things in front office, settlement, accounting and liquidity; model them as separate bounded contexts.
- Protect your model from vendor and network models with anti-corruption layers.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** List four invariants that a `Deposit` aggregate (a fixed-term interbank deposit) should enforce at creation and on amendment.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Your team is building a cash ladder service that consumes trades from a vendor TMS. Sketch the anti-corruption layer: which vendor fields it maps, which it rejects, and which domain events it publishes. What happens when the vendor adds a new product type?
> 3. **Interview:** "Our codebase has a 180-field `Trade` class used by every service. What would you do?" *Hint:* identify bounded contexts and which fields each one uses; extract context-specific models and translate at the boundaries; migrate one consumer at a time using events; do not attempt a big-bang rewrite.

#### Golden Test Datasets

**Why it matters.** Unit tests check that code does what the developer intended. They do not check that the developer intended the right thing. A swap valuation can pass every unit test and still use the wrong day count convention. A golden test dataset is a fixed set of inputs with expected outputs that come from an independent, trusted source and have been approved by someone who understands the business. It is the reference that every release is compared against.

**What a golden dataset contains.**

- **Inputs:** a frozen as-of date, market data (curves, FX rates, fixings, volatilities), reference data (calendars, instruments, counterparties) and trades or positions.
- **Expected outputs:** cash flows, accruals, present values, sensitivities, regulatory buckets, accounting entries, whatever the system produces.
- **Provenance:** where each expected value came from (hand calculation in a spreadsheet reviewed by a quant, a vendor system, a term sheet, a regulator's worked example) and who approved it.
- **Tolerances:** how close is close enough, per measure.

```text
golden/
  v2026.09/
    manifest.yaml            # owner, approver, as-of date, sources, change log
    market_data/
      curves_2026-06-30.json
      fx_fixings_2026-06-30.json
    reference_data/
      calendars.json         # TARGET, NYSE/Fed, London, including 2028 leap year
    trades/
      fx_forward_001.json ... irs_045.json ... deposit_120.json
    expected/
      cashflows.csv          # exact to the minor unit
      pv.csv                 # tolerance per measure, see manifest
      lcr_buckets.csv
      postings.csv
```

**Coverage: edge cases matter most.** Most production defects occur at boundaries, so a good golden set is built product by product against a checklist of edge cases.

| Edge case | Example trade | What it catches |
|---|---|---|
| Month-end roll | 1M deposit starting 31 January | Modified following and end-of-month rules |
| Holiday on payment date | Swap coupon falling on 25 December | Business day adjustment, calendar joins |
| Leap year | ACT/365F accrual across 29 February 2028 | Day count implementation |
| Short or long stub | Swap with a 2-month first period | Schedule generation |
| Negative rates | EUR deposit at -0.50% (2019 market data) | Sign handling, floors |
| Same-day maturity | Trade maturing on the as-of date | Inclusive or exclusive date logic |
| Zero or tiny notional | 0.01 EUR position | Division and rounding |
| Large notional | EUR 10bn repo | Overflow, precision |
| Amended and cancelled trades | Trade with three versions | Versioning and event handling |

**Example: a golden test runner.**

```python
import csv
from decimal import Decimal
import pytest

TOLERANCE = {"cashflow": Decimal("0"),            # exact to the cent
             "pv": Decimal("0.01"),               # absolute, per trade
             "dv01": Decimal("0.0001")}           # absolute, per trade

def load_expected(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        return [(r["trade_id"], r["measure"], Decimal(r["value"])) for r in csv.DictReader(f)]

@pytest.mark.parametrize("trade_id,measure,expected",
                         load_expected("golden/v2026.09/expected/pv.csv"))
def test_golden(trade_id, measure, expected, engine):
    actual = engine.calculate(trade_id, measure)
    assert abs(actual - expected) <= TOLERANCE[measure], (
        f"{trade_id} {measure}: expected {expected}, got {actual}")
```

Each failure names the trade and the measure. Because the trades are small and documented, a developer can see immediately which edge case broke.

**Governance of the golden set.** The expected values are only useful if they cannot be changed casually. If a release changes a golden result, there are two possibilities: the code is wrong, or the old expected value was wrong. Updating the expected value ("re-baselining") must therefore be a reviewed change with a written reason and business approval, never an automatic "accept all new values". Keep the golden set versioned with the code, so that any historical release can be re-tested against the set that was valid at the time.

**Engineering view.**

- Make the golden suite part of every build. It should run in minutes, so keep it small and representative; full-portfolio comparisons belong in regression testing (see below).
- When a production defect is found, add a golden case that reproduces it before fixing it.
- Store market data in the same format as production snapshots, so that the golden set exercises the real loading code.
- Do not generate expected values with the code under test. That only proves the code agrees with itself.

**Analogy.** A golden dataset is like the reference weights kept by a standards office. You do not check a scale by weighing something with the same scale; you weigh an object whose mass has been certified independently.

**Key takeaways**

- A golden dataset is a frozen set of inputs and independently sourced, approved expected outputs.
- Edge cases (month-ends, holidays, leap years, stubs, negative rates) are where defects concentrate.
- Each measure needs an explicit tolerance; cash flows are usually exact to the minor unit.
- Changing an expected value is a reviewed business decision, not an automatic update.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Propose five golden test cases for a fixed-term deposit product, each targeting a different edge case. State the expected interest for one of them by hand.
> 2. **Intermediate:** After a library upgrade, 12 of 400 golden PVs differ by between 0.02 and 0.30 EUR, all on swaps with a stub period. Describe how you would decide whether the code or the golden values are wrong, and who must approve the outcome.
> 3. **Interview:** "How would you build a golden test set for an LCR engine?" *Hint:* small synthetic balance sheets covering each outflow and inflow category and each HQLA level; caps (Level 2 and inflow caps); expected values derived from the regulation and reviewed by regulatory reporting; edge cases at the 30-day boundary; version per rule change.

#### Property-Based Testing for Calculations

**Why it matters.** Example-based tests check the cases the developer thought of. Financial code fails in the cases nobody thought of: a negative amount, a single-element list, a date range crossing a holiday, an amount of 0.01 split three ways. Property-based testing (PBT) states general rules that must hold for *all* valid inputs, then lets a library generate hundreds or thousands of random inputs to look for a counterexample.

**How it works.**

1. Describe the input space with generators (strategies): amounts with two decimals, currencies from a list, dates within a range, lists of weights.
2. State a property: a rule that must hold for every generated input.
3. The framework runs the test many times with random inputs. If one fails, it **shrinks** the input to the smallest example that still fails, which makes debugging easy.

Libraries: Hypothesis (Python), jqwik and QuickTheories (Java), FsCheck (.NET), ScalaCheck (Scala), QuickCheck (Haskell, Erlang).

**Kinds of properties useful in treasury.**

| Property type | Treasury example |
|---|---|
| Invariant (conservation) | Allocating an amount across accounts preserves the total exactly; sum of bucketed cash flows equals sum of all cash flows |
| Round trip | Parsing a generated ISO 20022 message and serializing it again gives the same message; converting EUR to USD and back at the same mid rate returns the original within rounding |
| Monotonicity | For positive cash flows, PV decreases as the discount rate increases; LCR outflows do not decrease when a run-off rate increases |
| Bounds | Discount factors for positive rates are in (0, 1]; year fractions are non-negative; generated payment dates are business days |
| Symmetry or parity | A payer swap and a receiver swap with the same terms have opposite PVs; put-call parity for European options |
| Linearity (metamorphic) | Doubling the notional doubles PV and DV01; splitting a trade into two halves gives the same total |
| Oracle | A fast optimized engine agrees with a slow, simple reference implementation |

**Example: finding a bug with Hypothesis.** Chapter 11.4 shows a `Money.allocate` method that splits an amount by ratios and hands out leftover minor units, noting that the sketch handles positive amounts only. A property-based test finds this limitation without being told about it:

```python
from decimal import Decimal
from hypothesis import given, strategies as st

amounts = st.decimals(min_value=Decimal("-1000000"), max_value=Decimal("1000000"), places=2)
ratios = st.lists(st.integers(min_value=1, max_value=100), min_size=1, max_size=10)

@given(amount=amounts, ratios=ratios)
def test_allocation_preserves_total(amount, ratios):
    parts = Money(amount, "EUR").allocate(ratios)
    assert len(parts) == len(ratios)
    assert sum(p.amount for p in parts) == amount           # conservation
    assert max(p.amount for p in parts) - min(p.amount for p in parts) <= \
        abs(amount) + Decimal("0.01")                       # loose sanity bound
```

```text
Falsifying example: test_allocation_preserves_total(
    amount=Decimal('-0.01'), ratios=[1, 1])
AssertionError: assert Decimal('0.00') == Decimal('-0.01')
```

Hypothesis shrank thousands of possible failures to the simplest one. With -0.01 split in two, each share rounds toward zero to 0.00, the remainder is -1 minor unit, and `range(-1)` hands out nothing, so one cent disappears. In a ledger, a lost cent is a reconciliation break.

**Writing good properties.**

- Start with conservation and bounds. They are easy to state and catch many bugs.
- Generate realistic but adversarial inputs: include zero, negative values, the smallest unit, very large values, and dates around month-ends and holidays.
- Avoid restating the implementation inside the test. A property such as "PV equals sum of discounted cash flows" written with the same formula as the code proves nothing.
- Save failing examples as regular regression tests (Hypothesis does this automatically in its example database, but a named test in the repository is clearer).
- Use a fixed seed or derandomized mode in CI if reproducibility matters to your auditors, and run deeper randomized searches nightly.

**Engineering view.**

- PBT complements golden tests: golden tests answer "is it right for these known cases?", PBT answers "does it behave sensibly for everything?".
- Stateful PBT (Hypothesis `RuleBasedStateMachine`) is useful for position keepers and ledgers: generate random sequences of bookings, amendments and cancellations, and check after each step that the position equals the sum of live trades.
- Calculation code written as pure functions over value objects (see the DDD topic above) is much easier to test this way.

**Analogy.** Example-based tests are like checking that a bridge holds three particular trucks. Property-based tests are like a load-test machine that drives thousands of random combinations of vehicles across it and, when the bridge cracks, tells you the lightest combination that did it.

**Key takeaways**

- PBT checks rules that must hold for all valid inputs, using generated data.
- Shrinking reduces a failure to the smallest counterexample, which makes it easy to understand.
- Conservation, round trip, monotonicity, bounds, parity, linearity and oracle properties all apply to treasury calculations.
- Stateful PBT is well suited to ledgers and position keepers.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Write three properties for a function `year_fraction(start, end, convention)` that supports ACT/360 and ACT/365F.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Write a Hypothesis test for a function that assigns cash flows to LCR time buckets (0-30 days, over 30 days). Which properties would you check, and how would you generate dates around the 30-day boundary?
> 3. **Interview:** "Our Hypothesis test is flaky in CI: it passes locally and fails randomly on the build server. What is going on and what do you do?" *Hint:* random generation finds different inputs on each run, so the failure is probably a real bug; read the falsifying example, reproduce it as a fixed test, then fix the code; consider seeds and the example database for reproducibility, not for hiding the failure.

#### Regression Testing Against Vendor Systems

**Why it matters.** Banks rarely compute anything in isolation. An in-house liquidity engine reads cash flows from a vendor TMS such as Murex or Calypso (Chapter 13.1). A new pricing library replaces a vendor's. Front office checks valuations against Bloomberg. When two systems compute the same number, they must agree or the difference must be explained. Regression testing against a vendor system turns that comparison into a repeatable, automated process, both when building your own components and when the vendor releases a new version.

**Two common scenarios.**

| Scenario | Reference | Candidate | Goal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Building or replacing a calculation | Vendor system (or the system being replaced) | In-house component | Show that the new component agrees, or explain every difference |
| Vendor upgrade | Current vendor version | New vendor version | Show that the upgrade changes nothing unexpected |

**The process.**

```text
  1. Freeze inputs            same as-of date, same market data snapshot,
                              same trade population, same static data
             |
  2. Align conventions        day counts, calendars, interpolation, curve
                              set-up, rounding, sign conventions, units
             |
  3. Run both systems         full portfolio, ideally several dates
                              (including a month-end)
             |
  4. Compare and classify     per trade and measure, against tolerances
             |
  5. Explain every break      convention / market data / timing / data /
                              genuine defect (ours or vendor's)
             |
  6. Sign off                 business and risk accept the residual
                              differences with written explanations
```

Most of the effort goes into step 2. Two correct systems can disagree because one interpolates zero rates linearly and the other interpolates log discount factors, or because one applies the payment calendar and the other the fixing calendar.

**Example: a comparison report.**

| Trade | Measure | Vendor | In-house | Difference | Classification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| IRS-1043 | PV (EUR) | 1,204,331.18 | 1,204,331.18 | 0.00 | Match |
| IRS-1188 | PV (EUR) | -88,402.67 | -88,415.02 | -12.35 | Convention: vendor uses 2-day lag on fixing calendar, we used payment calendar; fixed in our config |
| DEP-2201 | Accrued interest | 4,166.67 | 4,166.66 | -0.01 | Rounding: vendor rounds per period, we round at end; accepted, documented |
| FXF-0917 | Cash flow date | 2026-12-28 | 2026-12-29 | 1 day | Data: vendor calendar missing a 2026 holiday; raised with vendor |
| BOND-0031 | PV (EUR) | 9,881,200.00 | 9,912,640.00 | 31,440.00 | Defect: our ex-coupon logic; fixed, golden case added |

Summary statistics are useful (number of matches, breaks by class, largest differences), but the rule is that every break above tolerance must have an explanation. "Small and probably fine" is not an explanation.

**Vendor upgrades.** Vendor TMS upgrades often change hundreds of components at once. A robust upgrade regression:

- Restores a copy of production (trades, static data, market data) into two environments, one on each version.
- Runs the full end-of-day batch on both, for at least one normal day and one month-end.
- Compares all outputs: cash flows, valuations, risk, accounting entries, confirmation and payment messages, regulatory feeds.
- Reviews the vendor's release notes against the differences found. Every difference should map to a documented change, or it is a regression.

**Engineering view.**

- Build the comparison as a tool, not a one-off spreadsheet: comparison keys, tolerance per measure, classification codes, and a report that can be attached to the change record (Section 15.4).
- Keep an "explained differences" register with an owner and an expiry, so that accepted differences are reviewed rather than forgotten.
- Compare at several levels: trade, position, aggregate. Aggregates can match while individual trades offset each other's errors.
- Reuse the reconciliation and matching machinery from Chapter 13.4.

**Analogy.** It is like two accountants independently preparing the same tax return. Where the totals differ, they go line by line until each difference is traced to a specific choice (one used a different depreciation method) or a mistake. They do not settle for "close enough".

**Key takeaways**

- Comparing with a vendor or legacy system is a repeatable process: freeze inputs, align conventions, run, compare, explain, sign off.
- Most differences come from conventions and data, not from algorithms.
- Every break above tolerance needs a written explanation and an owner.
- Vendor upgrades need full-portfolio regression covering a normal day and a period end.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** List five convention differences that could make two correct systems produce different PVs for the same interest rate swap.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Total portfolio PV matches between the vendor and your engine to within EUR 3, but 140 individual trades differ by up to EUR 2,000. Explain what this suggests and how you would investigate.
> 3. **Interview:** "The vendor ships a new major version of the TMS next quarter. Design the regression test plan." *Hint:* production copy in two environments; normal day and month-end; all outputs including messages and postings; automated comparison with tolerances; mapping differences to release notes; sign-off by business, risk and finance; time for a second cycle after fixes.

#### Parallel Runs and Shadow Mode

**Why it matters.** Golden and regression tests use frozen data. Production has messy data, unexpected volumes, late amendments and month-ends. Before a bank retires an old system and trusts a new one, it runs both on real production data for long enough to see the full range of business situations. Regulators and auditors usually expect evidence of this for systems that feed financial or regulatory reporting.

**Definitions.**

| Technique | What happens | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Parallel run | Old and new systems both process the same real inputs for a period; outputs are reconciled; the old system's results remain official | Replacing an ALM engine, GL interface or regulatory reporting system |
| Shadow mode | The new system receives a copy of live traffic in real time but its outputs are not used (no payments sent, no positions published) | Real-time payment engines, limit checks, position keepers |
| Canary release | A small share of real traffic is processed by the new system for real | Low-risk changes in high-volume flows, after shadow mode |
