| Dark launch | New code is deployed but switched off by a feature flag | Separating deployment from release |

```text
                          production inputs
                 (trades, payments, market data, statements)
                                  |
                       +----------+-----------+
                       |                      |
                       v                      v
              +-----------------+    +-------------------+
              | Current system  |    | New system        |
              | (official)      |    | (shadow)          |
              +--------+--------+    +---------+---------+
                       |                       |
                outputs used             outputs captured,
                (payments, reports)      egress blocked
                       |                       |
                       +----------+------------+
                                  v
                       +----------------------+
                       | Daily reconciliation |
                       | classify every break |
                       +----------------------+
```

**Example: exit criteria for a new liquidity engine.**

| Criterion | Threshold |
|---|---|
| Duration | At least three consecutive month-ends, including one quarter-end |
| LCR at consolidated level | Difference below 0.1 percentage points on every run |
| Line-level outflows and inflows | 99.5% of lines within EUR 100k; every larger break explained |
| Unexplained breaks | Zero open at go-live |
| Timeliness | New engine finishes at least 60 minutes before the reporting deadline on every run |
| Operations | Runbooks used by the operations team for the full parallel run; incidents logged and closed |
| Sign-off | Head of liquidity reporting, risk, finance, IT; internal audit informed |

**The biggest risk: a shadow that is not really a shadow.** A shadow payment engine that is accidentally connected to the real SWIFT gateway will send real payments twice. Protect against this in several layers:

- Configuration: the shadow instance has sending disabled and uses separate queue names.
- Network: no route from the shadow environment to payment gateways or external endpoints.
- Credentials: the shadow has no certificates or keys for the production network.
- Monitoring: an alert fires if any message leaves the shadow environment.

**Engineering view.**

- Design for comparability from the start: stable business keys, identical inputs, outputs in a comparable format.
- Automate the daily reconciliation and the break classification. A parallel run that relies on manual spreadsheet comparison usually stops being checked after a few weeks.
- Expect the old system to be wrong sometimes. A parallel run often finds long-standing defects in the legacy system, which then need a decision: replicate the old behaviour for continuity, or fix it and explain the change in reported numbers.
- Plan the cost: running two systems, two sets of operations and the reconciliation for months is expensive, so agree exit criteria before starting.

**Analogy.** A parallel run is like a new pilot flying alongside a training captain for many hours before being allowed to fly alone. The captain remains responsible, and every difference in judgment is discussed.

**Key takeaways**

- Parallel runs and shadow mode test a new system on real production data before it becomes official.
- Agree exit criteria up front: duration including period ends, tolerances, zero unexplained breaks, timeliness and sign-offs.
- A shadow system must be technically unable to send real payments or publish official numbers.
- Parallel runs often reveal defects in the legacy system as well.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain the difference between a parallel run and a canary release, and give a treasury example for which each is suitable.
> 2. **Intermediate:** During a parallel run, the new engine's NSFR is consistently 0.4 percentage points higher than the legacy engine's. Investigation shows the legacy system misclassifies some operational deposits. What decisions need to be made, and by whom, before go-live?
> 3. **Interview:** "How would you run a new real-time payment engine in shadow mode safely?" *Hint:* mirror inputs from the message bus; separate queues and configuration; no network route or credentials to gateways; compare outputs (routing, validation results, timing) per payment; alert on any egress; move to canary only after clean results over high-volume days.

<a id="152-resilience-and-operations"></a>
### 15.2 Resilience and Operations

This subchapter covers how treasury systems stay available and recover from failure: the regulatory expectations for operational resilience, high availability and disaster recovery design, running incidents against payment cut-offs, and monitoring financial flows end to end.

#### Operational Resilience Requirements (DORA)

**Why it matters.** Regulators used to focus on whether a bank had enough capital and liquidity. Since the late 2010s they have also asked whether a bank can keep delivering its critical services when technology fails, a supplier goes down or an attacker gets in. In the EU this is now law: the **Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)**, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554, applies from 17 January 2025 to banks, investment firms, payment institutions, insurers and other financial entities. For engineers, DORA turns many good practices (asset inventories, incident classification, resilience testing, vendor oversight) into obligations with evidence that supervisors can request.

**From availability to resilience.** Traditional IT thinking asks "how do we prevent outages?". Operational resilience assumes that disruptions will happen and asks "how do we keep critical services within tolerable impact when they do?".

| Concept | Meaning | Treasury example |
|---|---|---|
| Critical or important function (DORA) / important business service (UK) | A service whose disruption would materially harm clients, the firm or financial stability | Executing high-value payments; meeting CLS pay-ins; managing the intraday liquidity position |
| Impact tolerance (UK) | Maximum tolerable disruption, usually a time limit | Critical payments executed within 2 hours, and no later than the scheme cut-off |
| Mapping | Linking each function to the people, processes, technology, data and third parties it needs | Payment execution depends on the payment engine, SWIFT gateway, HSM, sanctions screening, the TMS and a cloud provider |
| Severe but plausible scenario | A disruption to test against | Ransomware encrypts the payment engine database on the morning of a quarter-end |

**The five pillars of DORA.**

| Pillar | Main requirements | What it means for engineers |
|---|---|---|
| 1. ICT risk management | Management body accountable; documented framework; inventory of ICT assets and dependencies; protection, detection, response, recovery, backup policies; learning and evolving | Maintain an accurate inventory of systems, data flows and dependencies; documented backup and recovery for each critical system |
| 2. ICT incident management and reporting | Detect, classify and log incidents; report major incidents to the competent authority; notify affected clients | Monitoring that detects incidents quickly; data to classify them (clients affected, duration, value, data loss, geographic spread) |
| 3. Digital operational resilience testing | Annual testing programme (vulnerability scans, scenario tests, performance tests, source code reviews, penetration tests); threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) at least every three years for significant entities | Testable systems, test environments, fixing findings with tracked remediation |
| 4. ICT third-party risk | Register of information on all ICT contracts; mandatory contract clauses; exit strategies; concentration risk; EU oversight of critical ICT third-party providers | Know which vendors and cloud services each critical function uses; be able to exit them (Section 15.4) |
| 5. Information sharing | Voluntary sharing of cyber threat intelligence among financial entities | Consume and contribute threat indicators |

**Major incident reporting timeline.** Under the DORA technical standards, once an incident is classified as major, the bank sends:

```text
  Incident detected ---> classified as major
                              |
                              +-- Initial notification: within 4 hours of classification
                              |   (and no later than 24 hours after becoming aware)
                              |
                              +-- Intermediate report: within 72 hours of the initial notification
                              |   (updated when the situation changes significantly)
                              |
                              +-- Final report: within 1 month of the latest intermediate report
                                  (root cause, impact, remediation)
```

Classification uses criteria such as the number of clients and counterparties affected, the value of transactions affected, duration and downtime, data losses, critical services affected, geographic spread, reputational impact and economic impact. These criteria need data that engineering must be able to produce during the incident: "how many payments, of what value, for how many clients, were delayed by how long?"

**Other regimes.** The UK PRA and FCA operational resilience rules (PRA SS1/21) require firms to identify important business services, set impact tolerances and be able to stay within them in severe but plausible scenarios, with full compliance from March 2025. The Basel Committee's Principles for Operational Resilience (2021) set the international baseline. For financial market infrastructures, the CPMI-IOSCO Principles (PFMI) expect critical systems to resume within two hours of a disruption (see Disaster Recovery and RTO/RPO below).

**Engineering view.**

- Keep a machine-readable dependency map from each critical function to services, databases, queues, HSMs, network links and third parties. It is the basis for impact analysis, testing and incident classification.
- Instrument systems so that incident impact can be quantified quickly (see Observability below).
- Make resilience testing routine: failover tests, restore tests and chaos experiments on non-production and, where safe, production.
- Treat findings from tests and incidents as tracked remediation items with owners and deadlines.

**Analogy.** Operational resilience is the difference between a building that has good locks and a building that has also planned its fire exits, drills the evacuation twice a year and knows how quickly it can reopen after a fire.

**Key takeaways**

- Operational resilience assumes disruptions will happen and focuses on keeping critical services within tolerable impact.
- DORA (applicable since 17 January 2025) has five pillars: ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing, third-party risk and information sharing.
- Major incidents have tight reporting deadlines (4 hours, 72 hours, 1 month), which require incident data to be available quickly.
- Engineers must maintain dependency maps, testable recovery and quantifiable impact data.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Map the "execute high-value outgoing payments" function to at least eight technical and third-party dependencies.
> 2. **Intermediate:** A database failure delays 2,300 outgoing payments with a total value of EUR 4.1bn for 95 minutes, and 14 miss the T2 customer payment cut-off. Which DORA classification criteria are relevant, and which data would you need to report within four hours?
> 3. **Interview:** "Your bank is preparing for its first threat-led penetration test of the treasury platform. What do you do as the lead engineer?" *Hint:* scope (critical functions, live production systems), asset and dependency inventory, logging and detection readiness, safe-testing rules with the red team, a control group that knows, remediation planning and retesting.

#### High Availability for Payment Systems

**Why it matters.** A payment engine that is down at 16:30 CET cannot release payments before the T2 customer cut-off. But for payments, availability is only half the problem. A highly available system that, during a failover, sends the same EUR 50m payment twice has turned a technical incident into a financial loss and a recovery effort with a counterparty. High availability (HA) for payments means staying up **without** ever losing or duplicating a payment.

**Availability in numbers.**

| Availability | Downtime per year | Downtime per month (30 days) |
|---|---|---|
| 99.9% ("three nines") | 8.76 hours | 43.2 minutes |
| 99.95% | 4.38 hours | 21.6 minutes |
| 99.99% ("four nines") | 52.6 minutes | 4.3 minutes |
| 99.999% ("five nines") | 5.3 minutes | 26 seconds |

When downtime happens matters as much as how much there is. Ten minutes at 03:00 may be harmless; ten minutes at 16:55 on a quarter-end can mean missed cut-offs. Treasury SLOs should be defined around business windows.

**Correctness first.** The CAP theorem says that during a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability. For payment execution the choice is clear: it is better to stop sending payments for a few minutes than to send them twice or from two nodes that disagree about balances. In practice:

- **Single writer per payment:** at any moment, exactly one node is allowed to release a given payment.
- **Durable state before side effects:** record "about to send payment X with message ID M" in a durable store before sending, so that a node taking over knows what may already have been sent.
- **Idempotency at every boundary:** each payment has a stable unique reference (end-to-end ID, UETR, message ID). Downstream systems reject duplicates (Chapter 12.4).
- **Fencing:** a node that has lost leadership must not be able to send, even if it does not yet know that it has lost it.

**Example: fencing tokens.** Leader election alone is not enough. A node can pause (for example during a long garbage collection), lose its lease, and then wake up still believing it is the leader. A fencing token is a number that increases with every new lease. The gateway rejects requests carrying an older token.

```text
  Time  Node A                         Lease service        Node B              SWIFT gateway
  ----  -----------------------------  -------------------  ------------------  ----------------------
  t0    acquires lease, token 41       holder=A, token=41
  t1    long GC pause ...
  t2                                   lease expires
  t3                                   holder=B, token=42   acquires lease
  t4                                                        sends PMT-9 (tok 42) accepts, last=42
  t5    wakes, sends PMT-9 (tok 41)                                             rejects: 41 < 42
```

Without the token check at step t5, PMT-9 would be sent twice.

**Typical architecture.**

```text
              Site A (primary)                       Site B (secondary)
   +-----------------------------------+    +-----------------------------------+
   | Payment engine nodes (active)     |    | Payment engine nodes (standby or  |
   |   leader per partition            |    |   active for other partitions)    |
   | Durable queue cluster  <----------+----+-> replicated synchronously        |
   | Database primary  ----------------+----+-> synchronous replica             |
   | SWIFT gateway + HSM               |    | SWIFT gateway + HSM               |
   +-----------------------------------+    +-----------------------------------+
            ^                                                  ^
            +------------ health checks, lease service --------+
```

| Pattern | How it works | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active-passive | One site processes, the other takes over on failure | Simple ownership; no conflicting writes | Failover takes time; standby may not work when needed unless tested |
| Active-active, partitioned | Both sites process, each owning a disjoint set of payments (for example by account or currency) | Uses all capacity; smaller blast radius | Rebalancing ownership on failure must be fenced |
| Active-active, shared | Any node can process any payment, coordinated through a consensus store | Highest availability | Hardest to get right; consensus latency on every payment |

**Graceful degradation.** When a dependency fails, a payment system should degrade rather than collapse:

- If sanctions screening is unavailable, hold payments (never skip screening) and alert.
- If the liquidity check is slow, prioritize critical payments (Chapter 5.3) and queue the rest.
- If one RTGS channel is down, switch to the contingency channel for critical payments.
- Accept incoming payment instructions into a durable queue even if execution is paused, so that nothing is lost.

**Engineering view.**

- Test failover regularly, in production, during business hours where possible. A failover that has only been tested in a weekend window will surprise you on a Tuesday afternoon.
- After any failover, reconcile what was sent (gateway logs, SWIFT acknowledgements, RTGS statements) against the payment engine's state before resuming.
- Avoid shared single points of failure hidden under redundant layers: one DNS server, one HSM cluster, one certificate that expires, one network link.

**Analogy.** A payment system's HA is like a relay race baton: having a second runner ready is useless if both runners can end up carrying a baton at the same time. The handover must be clean and unambiguous.

**Key takeaways**

- Payment HA means staying available without ever losing or duplicating a payment.
- Prefer consistency over availability for payment execution: pause rather than double-send.
- Use durable state before side effects, idempotency keys and fencing tokens.
- Define availability targets around business windows and cut-offs, not only annual percentages.
- Degrade gracefully: hold, queue and prioritize, but never skip mandatory controls.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Calculate the maximum monthly downtime for an SLO of 99.95%, and explain why the time of day of that downtime matters for a payment engine.
> 2. **Intermediate:** A node sends a payment to the SWIFT gateway, then crashes before recording the acknowledgement. Describe how the node that takes over decides whether to resend.
> 3. **Interview:** "Design an active-active payment engine across two data centres." *Hint:* partition ownership (by account or currency), leases with fencing tokens, synchronous replication of payment state, idempotent gateways, reconciliation after failover, behaviour during a network partition between the sites.

#### Disaster Recovery and RTO/RPO

**Why it matters.** High availability handles component failures within a site. Disaster recovery (DR) handles losing a whole site, a whole cloud region or, increasingly, the integrity of the data itself (ransomware, logical corruption). For each system the bank must decide, and prove through tests, how quickly it comes back and how much data it can afford to lose.

**Definitions.**

- **RTO (Recovery Time Objective):** the maximum acceptable time from disruption until the service is restored.
- **RPO (Recovery Point Objective):** the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in time. An RPO of 15 minutes means the bank accepts losing up to 15 minutes of transactions, which it must then recover from other sources.
- **MTD (Maximum Tolerable Downtime):** the point at which the business impact becomes unacceptable; the RTO must be shorter.

```text
          last good copy                  disruption                    service restored
               |                              |                                 |
  -------------+------------------------------+---------------------------------+------> time
               |<------------ RPO ----------->|<------------- RTO ------------->|
                  data that may be lost           time the service is unavailable
```

**Tiering systems.** Not every system needs the same RTO and RPO. Faster recovery and zero data loss are expensive, so banks assign tiers.

| Tier | Example treasury systems | RTO | RPO | Typical technique |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Payment engine, SWIFT connectivity, RTGS interface, intraday liquidity monitor | Minutes to 2 hours | 0 | Synchronous replication to a nearby site; hot standby; tested failover |
| 1 | TMS front office, limits, position keeping | 2-4 hours | Near 0 to 15 minutes | Synchronous or near-synchronous replication; warm standby |
| 2 | ALM engine, regulatory reporting, risk batch | 24 hours | 4-24 hours | Asynchronous replication or backups; rerun batch from inputs |
| 3 | Analytics, historical data marts | Days | 24 hours or more | Backups |

For financial market infrastructures, the PFMI (Principle 17) sets an expectation that critical systems resume within **two hours** of a disruption and can complete settlement by the end of the day. Banks that participate in these systems usually align their critical payment systems with that target.

**Replication is not backup.** Synchronous replication gives RPO 0 against hardware or site loss, but it faithfully replicates every logical error. If a faulty release or ransomware corrupts the primary database, the replica is corrupted within milliseconds.

| Threat | Protected by replication? | Protected by backups? |
|---|---|---|
| Server or disk failure | Yes | Yes, but slower |
| Loss of a data centre | Yes, if the replica is in another site | Yes, if backups are off-site |
| Faulty release corrupts data | No | Yes, restore to a point before the release |
| Ransomware encrypts data | No | Only if backups are immutable and isolated (a "cyber vault") |

**Recovering lost transactions.** With an RPO above zero, recovery is not finished when the database is back. Example: a payment engine fails over asynchronously with 3 minutes of lost data. Payments sent in those 3 minutes exist at SWIFT and at the RTGS but not in the recovered database. Before releasing anything new, the bank must:

1. Pull outgoing message logs from the SWIFT interface and statements or status reports from the RTGS for the gap.
2. Reconcile them against the recovered payment state and mark the missing payments as sent.
3. Re-request any client instructions received during the gap.
4. Only then resume processing, or the lost-but-sent payments will be sent again.

This is one reason tier 0 payment systems aim for RPO 0.

**DR testing.** A DR plan that has not been tested is only a hope. Good practice:

- Full failover tests at least annually for critical systems, ideally running production from the DR site for a period.
- Restore tests from backups, including from immutable backups, with integrity checks on the restored data.
- Tests that include people and procedures: who decides to invoke DR, how operations are told, how third parties (SWIFT, the RTGS operator) are informed.
- Record achieved RTO and RPO against targets, and track gaps as findings.

**Engineering view.**

- Make systems restartable from an input log: if the trade and payment events are durable (Chapter 13.2, event sourcing), derived state can be rebuilt.
- Keep configuration, certificates and secrets for the DR site current and tested; expired certificates at the DR site are a classic failure.
- Avoid DR sites that share hidden dependencies with the primary site (same identity provider, same DNS, same cloud control plane).

**Analogy.** RPO is how far back your last save point is in a video game; RTO is how long it takes to reload. Replication is like auto-saving every second, which does not help if you just walked off a cliff: the save already includes the fall.

**Key takeaways**

- RTO is how quickly a service must be restored; RPO is how much data loss is acceptable.
- Tier systems by criticality; tier 0 payment systems aim for RPO 0 and recovery within about two hours.
- Replication protects against site loss but not against corruption or ransomware; immutable backups are also needed.
- After failover with data loss, reconcile with external sources before resuming, or payments may be duplicated.
- DR must be tested, including people and procedures, and achieved RTO/RPO recorded.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain the difference between RTO and RPO using an ALM engine that runs a nightly batch.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Ransomware encrypts the payment engine's primary and replica databases at 10:40 on a Monday. The last immutable backup is from 02:00. Write the recovery sequence until payments can safely resume.
> 3. **Interview:** "The business asks for RPO 0 and RTO 15 minutes for every treasury system. How do you respond?" *Hint:* cost and complexity of synchronous replication and hot standby; tiering by business impact; which systems can be rebuilt from inputs; agree tiers with the business and document the residual risk.

#### Cut-Off Driven Incident Management

**Why it matters.** In most IT incident processes, severity depends on how many users are affected. In treasury, the clock matters most. A problem that delays all outgoing payments by 30 minutes is a minor nuisance at 09:00 and a severe incident at 16:40 CET, because T2's customer payment cut-off is at 17:00. Missing a CLS pay-in, a CCP margin call or a central bank repayment has consequences that cannot be fixed later in the day. Incident management in treasury therefore has to be driven by the time remaining to the next cut-off and by what is at stake before it.

**Severity is a function of time and value.**

| Time to next relevant cut-off | Value or criticality at risk | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| More than 4 hours | Any | Medium: fix in normal priority |
| 1 to 4 hours | Routine payments | High |
| 1 to 4 hours | Critical payments (CLS, CCP, central bank) | Critical |
| Less than 1 hour | Any material value | Critical: activate contingency in parallel with the fix |

The point of such a matrix is to escalate automatically as the clock runs, without waiting for someone to notice that the deadline is close.

**Decision points.** Runbooks for treasury incidents are written as a timeline with decision points rather than as a single procedure:

```text
  T2 customer payments cut-off 17:00 CET, payment engine stuck since 15:50

  15:50  Detection: payments in RELEASED state not acknowledged by gateway
  16:00  Incident declared; incident commander assigned; treasury informed
  16:15  DECISION 1: is a fix likely before 16:30?
           no  -> prepare contingency: export critical payments list
  16:30  DECISION 2: switch critical payments to manual channel?
           yes -> operations key critical payments directly in the
                  SWIFT interface (four-eyes), or use the central bank's
                  contingency channel
  16:40  DECISION 3: request cut-off extension from the central bank?
           only for systemic amounts; rarely granted, decided by treasury
  17:00  Cut-off: list payments that missed; inform clients and counterparties;
           arrange funding for positions that did not settle
  after  Reconcile manual payments against the engine BEFORE it is restarted,
           so that they are not sent a second time
```

The last step is easy to forget and causes duplicate payments: once the engine is fixed, it still holds the payments that were sent manually.

**Prioritizing what is at risk.** During an incident, operations needs to see quickly which payments are at risk and which to save first. A small helper that sorts by deadline and criticality is worth building in advance:

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime
from decimal import Decimal

PRIORITY = {"CLS": 0, "CCP_MARGIN": 0, "CENTRAL_BANK": 0, "INTERBANK": 1, "CLIENT": 2}

@dataclass
class PendingPayment:
    ref: str
    category: str
    amount_eur: Decimal
    cut_off: datetime

def at_risk(payments: list[PendingPayment], now: datetime, horizon_min: int = 60):
    """Payments whose cut-off is within the horizon, most urgent first."""
    soon = [p for p in payments if (p.cut_off - now).total_seconds() <= horizon_min * 60]
    return sorted(soon, key=lambda p: (PRIORITY[p.category], p.cut_off, -p.amount_eur))
```

**Roles.**

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Incident commander | Owns the timeline and decisions; keeps the team focused on the next decision point |
| Technical lead | Diagnoses and fixes; tells the commander honestly whether the fix will be ready in time |
| Treasury / operations lead | Decides on contingency, prioritization and cut-off extension requests; talks to counterparties |
| Communications | Updates management, affected business lines and, if needed, regulators (DORA reporting) |

**After the incident.** A blameless post-incident review records the timeline, root cause, impact in business terms (payments delayed or missed, value, cost of overnight funding, penalties) and actions. Repeated contingency use should lead to automation of the contingency path itself.

**Engineering view.**

- Store cut-off calendars as reference data (per scheme, per currency, per payment type) and use them in monitoring, so that alerts carry "minutes to cut-off".
- Build contingency tooling before it is needed: export of critical payments, manual-release reconciliation, idempotent restart.
- Rehearse: run incident drills late in the afternoon, not only in the morning.

**Analogy.** It is like an airport when the baggage system fails. A failure at 04:00 is an inconvenience. A failure 40 minutes before a full departure wave means staff start loading bags by hand immediately, before anyone knows the root cause, because the departure time will not move.

**Key takeaways**

- In treasury, incident severity depends on time to cut-off and the value and criticality at stake.
- Runbooks should be timelines with decision points, including when to switch to manual or contingency channels.
- Contingency starts in parallel with the fix, not after the fix fails.
- Reconcile manually sent payments before restarting the system, or they will be duplicated.
- Cut-off calendars should drive alerting and escalation automatically.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain why the same 30-minute outage of a payment engine can be "medium" at 09:00 and "critical" at 16:30.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Extend the `at_risk` function so that it also returns the total value at risk per category and flags payments whose cut-off has already passed.
> 3. **Interview:** "At 16:20 the payment engine is down and the fix needs one more hour. Walk me through what you do." *Hint:* declare critical, assign roles, identify critical payments and cut-offs, switch them to a manual or contingency channel under four-eyes, consider an extension request, communicate, and reconcile manual payments before restarting the engine.

#### Observability for Financial Flows

**Why it matters.** Technical monitoring tells you that CPU is at 40% and that every service responds to health checks. It does not tell you that a payment has been sitting in "awaiting sanctions result" for 25 minutes, or that this morning's statement from the USD nostro bank never arrived. Treasury needs observability at the level of the business flow: where each payment, trade or file is, how long it has been there, and whether anything expected is missing.

**Three layers of observability.**

| Layer | Question it answers | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Infrastructure | Are the machines and networks healthy? | CPU, memory, disk, network latency |
| Application | Are the services working? | Request rates, error rates, latency (RED metrics), logs, distributed traces |
| Business flow | Is the money moving as expected? | Payments per state, time in state, value pending, missing files, unmatched acknowledgements, cut-off headroom |

**Tracking a payment end to end.** Each payment carries identifiers that survive across systems: the end-to-end ID from the client, the UETR for SWIFT gpi (Chapter 2.2), and internal IDs. Log and trace with those identifiers, so that one search shows the whole journey:

```text
  Funnel for EUR high-value payments, 16:10 CET          count     value (EUR m)
  ---------------------------------------------------   ------    -------------
  received                                               4,812         9,410
  validated                                              4,806         9,402
  sanctions screened (passed)                            4,771         9,355
     pending screening > 15 min                  <-- !       29            41
  liquidity check passed                                 4,760         9,301
  released to SWIFT gateway                              4,760         9,301
  ACK from network                                       4,744         9,270
     released but no ACK > 5 min                 <-- !       16            31
  settled (pacs.002 / camt.054 confirmed)                4,600         8,990
```

The two flagged lines are what matter. Both totals might be within normal technical error rates, yet both represent money that is stuck.

**Business flow signals worth alerting on.**

- **Time in state:** any payment in a non-final state longer than its threshold, with thresholds tighter as the cut-off approaches.
- **Value pending:** total value of payments not yet released, compared with the time left to cut-off.
- **Absence of expected events:** statement file (camt.053, MT940) not received by its expected time; no market data update for a curve for 10 minutes; end-of-day batch not started.
- **Completeness and balance:** count and sum of payments sent equal count and sum acknowledged; positions per nostro match the projected balance (Chapter 5.3).
- **Unusual patterns:** volume or value far outside the normal range for this time of day, which can indicate both technical problems and fraud (Section 15.3).

**Example: an "absence" check.** Missing data does not produce errors, so it has to be checked explicitly:

```python
from datetime import datetime, time

EXPECTED_STATEMENTS = {               # account -> latest expected arrival (CET)
    "USD-NOSTRO-JPM": time(7, 0),
    "GBP-NOSTRO-BARC": time(7, 30),
    "EUR-T2-MCA": time(6, 30),
}

def missing_statements(received: set[str], now: datetime) -> list[str]:
    return [acct for acct, due in EXPECTED_STATEMENTS.items()
            if now.time() > due and acct not in received]
```

**Logging in a regulated environment.**

- Use structured logs with consistent business keys (payment ID, UETR, trade ID, account) so that logs, metrics and traces can be joined.
- Do not log sensitive data in clear: mask account numbers and names, never log credentials, keys or full card numbers. Logs are often copied to systems with wider access.
- Keep logs needed as evidence (who released which payment) in the audit trail (Chapter 13.4), not only in the operational log platform, which may have shorter retention.

**Engineering view.**

- Define service level objectives in business terms: "99.9% of critical payments acknowledged by the network within 2 minutes of release", "statements processed by 07:30".
- Give operations dashboards that show the flow funnel and cut-off headroom, not only technical graphs.
- Emit business events from every stage of the flow; derive metrics from them rather than from log parsing.
- Make alerts actionable: each alert should name the affected payments or files and link to the runbook.

**Analogy.** Infrastructure monitoring is like checking that the conveyor belts in a parcel depot are running. Business flow observability is tracking each parcel: you know where it is, how long it has been there, and which parcels that should have arrived never did.

**Key takeaways**

- Technical health does not guarantee that money is moving; treasury needs business flow observability.
- Track each payment with stable identifiers across systems and measure time in state and value pending.
- Alert on the absence of expected events, such as missing statements or stale market data.
- Define SLOs in business terms tied to cut-offs, and keep sensitive data out of logs.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Name four business-level metrics for an intraday liquidity monitoring system and say what each would detect.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Design an alert for payments stuck in "released, no ACK" whose threshold tightens from 10 minutes to 2 minutes in the last hour before the cut-off. What data does the alert need, and what should it contain?
> 3. **Interview:** "All dashboards were green, but 300 payments missed the cut-off yesterday. How is that possible and what would you change?" *Hint:* technical metrics measured service health, not flow progress; a stuck state, a dependency returning success without doing anything, or a missing acknowledgement; add time-in-state, value-pending and absence alerts tied to cut-offs.

<a id="153-security"></a>
### 15.3 Security

This subchapter covers how treasury systems protect money and data: who may do what, how payment fraud is prevented, how payment files are signed and keys protected, and how secure development works when every change is subject to regulatory scrutiny.

#### Access Control and Entitlements

**Why it matters.** In treasury software, permissions are financial controls. The ability to release a payment, change a beneficiary's account, raise a limit or amend a booked trade is the ability to move or misstate money. Chapter 4.1 explains segregation of duties (SoD) and Chapter 13.4 explains maker-checker. This topic covers how those rules are implemented as an entitlement model in software, and how it is kept accurate as people join, move and leave.

**Authentication, authorization and entitlements.**

- **Authentication:** proving who someone is. For treasury systems: single sign-on with multi-factor authentication, and hardware tokens or smart cards for high-risk actions such as payment release.
- **Authorization:** deciding whether an authenticated identity may perform an action.
- **Entitlement:** a specific permission granted to an identity, usually combining a **function** (what action) with a **scope** (on which data, up to which amount).

**Models.**

| Model | How decisions are made | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| RBAC (role-based) | Users get roles; roles carry permissions | Simple to understand and review | Role explosion when scopes multiply ("EUR payments approver for entity DE up to 10m") |
| ABAC (attribute-based) | Rules evaluate attributes of user, action, resource and context | Expresses scopes and limits naturally | Harder to review: "who can release this payment?" requires evaluating rules |
| Hybrid (common in banks) | Roles for functions, attributes for scope and limits | Reviewable roles plus precise scopes | Two layers to keep consistent |

**Example: an entitlement for payment release.**

```text
  Entitlement
    user:          a.rossi
    function:      PAYMENT_RELEASE
    scope:
      legal_entity: [BANK-DE]
      currency:     [EUR, USD]
      max_amount:   EUR 25,000,000 (per payment)
    constraints:
      not_maker_of_same_payment: true
      requires_mfa_step_up:      true
    granted_by:    head of payments ops  (approved 2026-03-02)
    review_due:    2026-09-30
```

```python
def can_release(user, payment, entitlements) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    for e in entitlements.get(user.id, []):
        if e.function != "PAYMENT_RELEASE":
            continue
        if payment.legal_entity not in e.legal_entities:
            continue
        if payment.currency not in e.currencies:
            continue
        if payment.amount_eur > e.max_amount_eur:
            return False, "amount above release limit"
        if payment.created_by == user.id:
            return False, "maker cannot release own payment"      # four-eyes
        if not user.session.mfa_step_up_recent:
            return False, "step-up authentication required"
        return True, "ok"
    return False, "no matching entitlement"
```

The check returns a reason, which goes into the audit trail for both granted and denied attempts. Denials are useful security signals.

**Toxic combinations.** Some entitlements are acceptable alone but dangerous together. The entitlement system should block or flag them at grant time, not only in periodic reviews.

| Entitlement A | Entitlement B | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| Create payment | Release payment (same scope) | One person can pay anyone |
| Maintain beneficiary / SSI data | Release payment | Redirect a payment to an attacker's account, then release it |
| Book trades | Confirm trades or maintain counterparty data | Fictitious trades hidden from the counterparty |
| Change limits | Trade against those limits | Bypass of risk limits |
| Deploy to production | Approve own change | Unreviewed code in production |

**The access lifecycle (joiner, mover, leaver).**

- **Joiner:** access granted from role templates for the job, approved by the manager and the system owner.
- **Mover:** when someone changes job, old entitlements are removed, not just new ones added. "Entitlement creep" (keeping old access after moves) is one of the most common audit findings.
- **Leaver:** access revoked on the last day, automatically from the HR system.
- **Recertification:** managers and system owners review all access periodically (often quarterly for critical systems) and confirm or remove it.

**Privileged and technical access.**

- Administrators and support engineers get **just-in-time** access through a privileged access management (PAM) tool: requested for a ticket, approved, time-limited and session-recorded.
- **Break-glass** accounts exist for emergencies, are sealed, and every use triggers an alert and a review.
- **Service accounts** used by applications have only the permissions they need, credentials stored in a vault and rotated, and an owner who recertifies them.
- Developers do not have standing write access to production data.

**Engineering view.**

- Centralize authorization decisions in one service or library, so that rules are consistent across user interfaces, APIs and batch jobs.
- Enforce entitlements on the server side for every API, including internal ones. A hidden button is not access control.
- Make entitlements data with history (who granted what, when, why), so that auditors can ask "who could release payments over EUR 10m on 14 March?" and get an answer.

**Analogy.** Entitlements are like keys in a hotel. A guest's key opens one room for a few days; a cleaner's key opens one floor during working hours; the master key is locked in a safe and every use is logged. Nobody gets a key to everything just because it is convenient.

**Key takeaways**

- In treasury, permissions are financial controls; entitlements combine a function with a scope and amount limits.
- Hybrid RBAC/ABAC models are common: roles for functions, attributes for scope.
- Block toxic combinations (such as beneficiary maintenance plus payment release) at grant time.
- Manage the joiner-mover-leaver lifecycle and recertify access regularly.
- Privileged access is just-in-time, approved, time-limited and recorded.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Give three examples of toxic entitlement combinations in a treasury system and explain the risk of each.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Extend `can_release` to support a rule that payments to beneficiaries created in the last 24 hours require a second releaser, regardless of amount.
> 3. **Interview:** "An auditor asks which people could approve FX trades above USD 100m on a given date six months ago. How do you design the system so this can be answered?" *Hint:* entitlements stored with effective dates and history (bitemporal, Chapter 13.2), role-to-permission mappings versioned, limits as data, and a query that evaluates the model as of a past date.

#### Payment Fraud Prevention

**Why it matters.** Treasury payments are large, fast and often final: an RTGS payment cannot be recalled once settled, and recovering funds from a beneficiary bank abroad depends on its goodwill and speed. Fraudsters know this. The largest losses come less from breaking cryptography than from tricking people, abusing legitimate access or compromising the systems that create payment instructions. The 2016 Bangladesh Bank attack (Chapter 12.1) used the bank's own SWIFT connection.

**Common threats.**

| Threat | How it works | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Business email compromise (BEC) | An attacker impersonates a supplier or executive and asks for a payment or a change of bank details | "Our bank details have changed, please use this new IBAN for the invoice" |
| CEO / executive fraud | Urgent, confidential request apparently from senior management | "Wire USD 4m today for a confidential acquisition, do not discuss it" |
| Beneficiary data tampering | Bank details changed in master data before a legitimate payment run | Supplier IBAN changed in the ERP two days before the monthly payment run |
| Account takeover | Stolen credentials or session used to create and release payments | Phished credentials of a payment approver |
| Insider fraud | An employee abuses legitimate access | Payment created and released by colluding employees |
| Infrastructure compromise | Malware injects or alters messages between systems | Messages modified between the payment engine and the SWIFT interface; confirmations suppressed |

**Layers of defence.** No single control is enough. Effective fraud prevention combines preventive, detective and recovery controls along the payment lifecycle:

```text
  Beneficiary set-up       Payment creation        Approval / release        Transmission            After sending
  -------------------      -----------------       ------------------        ------------            -------------
  call-back on an          beneficiary must be     four-eyes; limits per     signed files /          reconcile sent vs
  independent channel;     on approved list;       approver; MFA step-up;    messages (next          approved; SWIFT
  four-eyes on changes;    duplicate checks;       rules engine and          topic); integrity       confirmations and
  cooling-off period;      velocity limits         anomaly score             check at gateway        statements; fast
  payee verification                                                                                 recall procedures
```

**Key controls in detail.**

- **Beneficiary verification:** new or changed bank details are confirmed by calling the counterparty on a number already on file, never one given in the request. Payee verification services check that the name matches the account: Confirmation of Payee in the UK, and Verification of Payee in the euro area, mandatory for euro credit transfers under the Instant Payments Regulation from 9 October 2025.
- **Cooling-off period:** payments to newly created or changed beneficiaries are held, or need extra approval, for a period.
- **Limits and velocity:** maximum amount per payment, per beneficiary per day and per approver; alerts on unusual numbers of payments in a short time.
- **Anomaly detection:** compare each payment with the history of the account and beneficiary: new country, unusual amount, unusual time, round amounts, a beneficiary bank never used before.
- **Independent reconciliation:** compare what left the bank (SWIFT messages, RTGS settlements) with what was approved in the payment system. Attackers who manipulate the payment system often also try to hide the payment from the bank's own view; an independent feed catches this. SWIFT's Payment Controls service offers this kind of monitoring at the network level.

**Example: a simple rules-based risk score.**

```python
from decimal import Decimal

def risk_score(p, history) -> tuple[int, list[str]]:
    score, reasons = 0, []
    if p.beneficiary_age_days < 7:
        score += 40; reasons.append("beneficiary created or changed in last 7 days")
    if p.beneficiary_country not in history.countries_paid(p.debtor):
        score += 25; reasons.append("first payment to this country")
    if p.amount > 3 * history.max_amount(p.debtor, p.beneficiary):
        score += 20; reasons.append("amount over 3x previous maximum")
    if p.amount % Decimal("100000") == 0:
        score += 5;  reasons.append("round amount")
    if not history.business_hours(p.created_at):
        score += 10; reasons.append("created outside business hours")
    return score, reasons

# score >= 50 -> hold for fraud review; 30-49 -> require additional approver
```

Rules are transparent and easy to explain to auditors. Machine learning models can add detection power, but they must be explainable enough for an operator to act on the alert and are subject to model risk management (Section 15.4).

**Fraud vs sanctions screening.** These are different controls. Sanctions screening (Chapter 9.4) checks whether the parties are on sanctions lists and is a legal obligation; fraud controls check whether the payment is genuine. A payment can pass one and fail the other.

**Engineering view.**

- Treat beneficiary and SSI master data as high-risk data: four-eyes on every change, full history, alerts on changes shortly before large payments.
- Ensure the content approved is the content sent: hash or sign the payment at approval and verify at transmission (next topic).
- Design hold queues and review workflows so that holding a payment for fraud review does not make it miss its cut-off unnoticed (Section 15.2).
- Log every rule decision with its reasons, to tune rules and to evidence controls.

**Analogy.** Payment fraud prevention is like airport security. Identity checks at check-in, bag scanning, a boarding pass check at the gate and a passenger count before departure each catch different problems. No single layer is perfect, but together they make it very hard to get something through unnoticed.

**Key takeaways**

- Most treasury payment fraud exploits people, master data and legitimate access, not cryptography.
- Use layered controls: beneficiary verification, cooling-off, four-eyes, limits, anomaly scoring and independent reconciliation.
- Verify bank details through an independent channel; payee verification is now mandatory for euro credit transfers.
- Fraud controls and sanctions screening are separate controls with separate purposes.
- Make sure the payment sent is exactly the payment approved.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** A supplier emails a new IBAN two days before a EUR 900k payment. List the controls that should stop a fraudulent change.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Extend the `risk_score` function with two more rules suited to interbank treasury payments (as opposed to supplier payments), and justify the weights.
> 3. **Interview:** "Attackers have compromised a server between the payment engine and the SWIFT interface and can alter messages. Which controls would detect or prevent fraudulent payments?" *Hint:* end-to-end signing from approval to gateway, integrity checks, independent reconciliation of sent messages against approved payments using network data, alerts on confirmations and statements, SWIFT CSP controls, segmentation.

#### Cryptographic Signing of Payment Files

**Why it matters.** A payment file often travels through several systems between approval and the bank: from an ERP to a treasury management system, through a file transfer server, to a bank connectivity gateway. At each step someone with access could change an IBAN or an amount. Transport encryption (TLS, SFTP) protects the file on the wire but not while it sits in a folder or passes through middleware. A digital signature lets the receiver check that the file is exactly what the authorized person approved, and proves who approved it.

**What a digital signature provides.**

| Property | Meaning | Payment example |
|---|---|---|
| Integrity | Any change to the signed content is detected | An altered IBAN or amount makes verification fail |
| Authenticity | The signature was created with a specific private key | The file was signed by treasurer A's key, not by someone else |
| Non-repudiation | The signer cannot plausibly deny having signed | Evidence in a dispute about who authorized a payment |

A signature does not provide confidentiality. Encryption is a separate step, with separate keys.

**How it works.**

```text
  Signer (approver or signing service)              Verifier (bank gateway or bank)
  ------------------------------------              -------------------------------
  payment file  --hash (SHA-256)--> digest          payment file --hash--> digest'
                                       |                                       |
            private key --sign-------> signature  ------------------>  verify(signature,
                                                                              digest', public key)
                                                                              |
                                                                     valid -> process
                                                                     invalid -> reject + alert
```

The signer hashes the content and signs the hash with a private key. The verifier recomputes the hash and checks the signature with the signer's public key, which it trusts through a certificate or a key registered in advance.

**Signing formats used in payments.**

| Format | Where used | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| XML Signature (XMLDSig, XAdES) | ISO 20022 XML files such as pain.001; SWIFT and bank channels | Requires canonicalization: XML that is logically identical can be byte-different, so both sides must transform it the same way before hashing |
| OpenPGP | Host-to-host file transfer between corporates and banks | Common, simple; key distribution and expiry need managing |
| CMS / PKCS#7 | Detached or enveloped signatures on any file | Widely supported in Java and .NET libraries |
| EBICS electronic signatures | File transfer with German, French, Austrian and Swiss banks | Signature versions such as A005 and A006 (RSA-based); supports distributed signatures (several signers, possibly at different times and places) |
| SWIFT PKI | Every message on SWIFTNet | Keys held in HSMs (Chapter 12.1) |

**Example: sign at approval, verify before transmission.**

```python
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import padding

PSS = padding.PSS(mgf=padding.MGF1(hashes.SHA256()), salt_length=padding.PSS.MAX_LENGTH)

def sign_file(content: bytes, private_key) -> bytes:
    return private_key.sign(content, PSS, hashes.SHA256())

def verify_file(content: bytes, signature: bytes, public_key) -> None:
    public_key.verify(signature, content, PSS, hashes.SHA256())   # raises InvalidSignature

# In production the private key is in an HSM and sign_file calls the HSM's API (next topic).
```

**Signing where it matters.** The value of a signature depends on what was signed and when:

- **Sign what the approver saw.** If the approver approves a payment in a user interface and a different component later builds the file, the signature covers the file, not the approval. Better: compute a hash of the canonical payment content at approval, store it with the approval, and verify at file generation that the content still matches.
- **Sign as early as possible, verify as late as possible.** Verify at the last trusted point before transmission (the bank gateway), so that every intermediate step is covered.
- **Protect against replay.** A valid signed file sent twice is still a duplicate payment. Include a unique message ID and creation timestamp in the signed content, and reject IDs already seen.
- **Manage certificates.** Expired or revoked certificates must fail verification. Certificate expiry is a common cause of outages, so monitor expiry dates and rotate in advance.

**Engineering view.**

- Never implement cryptographic algorithms yourself; use maintained libraries and the formats your banks require.
- Store the signature, the signer's certificate and the verification result with the payment, as evidence.
- For XML, test canonicalization carefully: whitespace, namespace prefixes and attribute order break signatures between different libraries.
- Prefer modern algorithms (RSA-PSS with at least 2048-bit keys, or ECDSA/Ed25519 where supported) and plan for algorithm migration, including post-quantum algorithms in the longer term.

**Analogy.** A digital signature is like a tamper-evident seal on a cash bag combined with the official's personal stamp. The seal shows whether the bag was opened on the way; the stamp shows who sealed it. A locked van (encryption in transit) protects the bag only while it is in the van.

**Key takeaways**

- Signatures provide integrity, authenticity and non-repudiation; encryption provides confidentiality. They are separate.
- Payment files are signed with XMLDSig, OpenPGP, CMS or EBICS signatures, depending on channel.
- Sign the content that was approved, as early as possible, and verify it at the last trusted point before transmission.
- Include unique IDs in signed content to prevent replay, and monitor certificate expiry.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain why SFTP alone does not protect a payment file from being modified by someone with access to the file transfer server.
> 2. **Intermediate:** An approver approves a batch of 120 payments in the TMS. The file is generated 10 minutes later by a separate service and sent through middleware to the bank. Design where hashing, signing and verification take place, and what is stored as evidence.
> 3. **Interview:** "Our bank rejected this morning's payment file because the XML signature is invalid, but nobody changed the content. What could cause this?" *Hint:* canonicalization differences, encoding changes (UTF-8 BOM, line endings) by middleware, pretty-printing, namespace changes, expired or rotated certificates, wrong key used.

#### HSMs and Key Management

**Why it matters.** Cryptography moves the problem of protecting data to the problem of protecting keys. If an attacker copies the private key that signs payment files or SWIFT messages, they can create payments that every system will accept as genuine. Hardware security modules (HSMs) and disciplined key management make it practically impossible to extract keys, and ensure that every use of a key is controlled and logged.

**What an HSM is.** An HSM is a tamper-resistant hardware device that generates, stores and uses cryptographic keys inside its boundary. Applications send data to the HSM and get back signatures or encrypted data; the private keys never leave the device in clear text. Physical tampering triggers erasure of the keys. HSMs are certified against standards such as FIPS 140-2 or FIPS 140-3 (Level 3 is typical for banking) and, for card payments, PCI HSM.

| Option | Where keys live | Typical use | Trade-offs |
|---|---|---|---|
| On-premises network HSM | Dedicated appliance in the bank's data centre | SWIFT PKI, payment signing, card and PIN processing | Highest control; requires specialist operations and redundant devices |
| Cloud HSM (dedicated) | Single-tenant HSM in a cloud provider's data centre | Cloud-hosted payment and signing services | Bank controls the keys; provider runs the hardware |
| Cloud KMS (managed) | Provider's multi-tenant HSM-backed service | Encrypting databases, storage and backups | Simple; keys controlled through the provider's access model |
| Software keystore | Files or OS key stores protected by passwords | Development and low-risk use only | Keys can be copied; not acceptable for payment signing |

**The key lifecycle.**

```text
  generate -> register / certify -> distribute -> use -> rotate -> revoke -> archive -> destroy
     |              |                  |            |        |         |          |          |
  inside HSM,   certificate       public key     logged,  scheduled  on compromise  for       verified,
  good entropy  issued by CA      to verifiers   access-  or on      or staff      verifying  recorded
                                                 controlled event    departure     old sigs
```

**Key hierarchy and envelope encryption.** Banks rarely encrypt data directly with a master key. Instead:

```text
  Master key (never leaves the HSM)
      |
      +-- Key-encrypting keys (KEKs), one per application or domain
              |
              +-- Data-encrypting keys (DEKs), one per file, table or record set
                      |
                      +-- data (database columns, files, backups)
```

With **envelope encryption**, data is encrypted with a DEK, and the DEK is encrypted ("wrapped") by a KEK held in the HSM or KMS. The wrapped DEK is stored next to the data. To read the data, the application asks the HSM to unwrap the DEK. Rotating the KEK means rewrapping small DEKs, not re-encrypting terabytes of data. Revoking access to the KEK makes all data under it unreadable, which is also how crypto-shredding works.

**Human controls on keys.**

- **Dual control:** sensitive operations (generating master keys, loading keys, changing HSM configuration) require two or more authorized people acting together.
- **Split knowledge:** no single person knows or holds a complete key. Key components are held by different custodians, often on smart cards with an M-of-N scheme (for example any 3 of 5 cards).
- **Key ceremonies:** master key generation and similar operations follow a scripted, witnessed and recorded procedure, with signed minutes kept as audit evidence.

**Engineering view.**

- Applications should authenticate to the HSM or KMS with their own identities and get only the operations they need (for example sign with key X, never export or delete).
- Log every key use with the calling identity; alert on unusual volumes, such as a signing service suddenly signing far more payments than usual.
- Do not put keys or secrets in source code, container images, configuration files or CI variables in clear. Use a secrets manager, and scan repositories for leaked secrets.
- Plan HSM capacity and redundancy like any tier 0 dependency (Section 15.2). If the only HSM cluster fails, no payment can be signed.
- Maintain an inventory of keys and certificates with owners and expiry dates. Expired certificates are a common cause of payment outages.

**Analogy.** An HSM is like a bank vault with a teller window. You can pass documents through the window and get them back stamped, but you can never take the stamp out. Opening the vault itself needs two managers with separate keys, and every visit is logged.

**Key takeaways**

- Protecting keys is the core of cryptographic security; HSMs keep private keys inside tamper-resistant hardware.
- Keys have a lifecycle from generation to destruction, and each stage needs controls.
- Key hierarchies and envelope encryption make rotation and revocation practical.
- Dual control, split knowledge and key ceremonies protect against a single malicious or mistaken insider.
- HSMs and certificates are critical dependencies: plan redundancy and monitor expiry.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain why a payment signing key stored in a password-protected file on the application server is not acceptable, even if the password is strong.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Describe how envelope encryption lets a bank rotate the key protecting 40 TB of encrypted transaction history without re-encrypting the data.
> 3. **Interview:** "The signing certificate used for host-to-host payment files with our main bank expires in 10 days. Walk me through the rotation." *Hint:* generate the new key pair in the HSM, request the certificate, exchange the new public key or certificate with the bank and agree an overlap period, test in the bank's test environment, switch over, verify, revoke the old one, update the inventory; ask why this was found only 10 days in advance.

#### Secure SDLC in Regulated Environments

**Why it matters.** Many attacks on banks exploit software weaknesses: injection flaws, vulnerable libraries, leaked credentials, poisoned build pipelines. In a regulated bank, security must be built into how software is designed, written, built and deployed, and there must be evidence that it was. DORA requires ICT security policies, testing and change management; supervisors and auditors check that they work in practice. A secure software development lifecycle (SDLC) provides both the protection and the evidence.

**Security activities across the lifecycle.**

| Phase | Activity | Treasury example |
|---|---|---|
| Requirements | Security and control requirements written with the functional ones | "Payment release requires MFA step-up and four-eyes; all release decisions are logged" |
| Design | Threat modelling (for example STRIDE: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege) | Threat model of the path from ERP to bank gateway identifies tampering in middleware |
| Implementation | Secure coding standards; peer review; secrets in a vault | Parameterized SQL; no keys in code; review by a second developer |
| Build | SAST (static analysis), SCA (software composition analysis of dependencies), secret scanning, SBOM generation, signed artefacts | Build fails on a critical vulnerability in a JSON library |
| Test | DAST (dynamic scanning), penetration testing, security regression tests | Annual penetration test of the payment portal; TLPT under DORA |
| Release | Approved change, verified artefact, segregation between developers and deployers | Only signed images from the pipeline can run in production |
| Operate | Vulnerability management, patching, monitoring, incident response | Critical vulnerabilities patched within an agreed number of days |

**A secured pipeline.**

```text
  developer --> pull request --> review by second engineer (four-eyes on code)
                    |
                    v
           CI build: unit + golden tests, SAST, SCA, secret scan, SBOM
                    |  fails on policy violations
                    v
           artefact signed, provenance recorded (which commit, which pipeline)
                    |
                    v
           deploy to test --> DAST, integration and regression tests
                    |
                    v
           change approval (Section 15.4) linked to the evidence above
                    |
                    v
           deploy to production by the pipeline (no manual copy);
           admission control only runs signed artefacts
```

**Supply chain security.** Modern applications contain far more third-party code than their own. Controls include pinning dependency versions, using an internal artefact repository that proxies and scans public packages, generating a software bill of materials (SBOM) for every release so that a newly published vulnerability can be traced to affected systems quickly, and recording build provenance (frameworks such as SLSA describe levels of build integrity). The 2021 Log4Shell vulnerability showed the value of an SBOM: banks with one knew within hours which systems were affected.

**Vulnerability management.** Findings from scans and tests are tracked with remediation deadlines by severity, for example:

| Severity | Internet-facing or payment systems | Internal systems |
|---|---|---|
| Critical | 7 days or less | 30 days |
| High | 30 days | 60 days |
| Medium | 90 days | 180 days |
| Low | Risk-based | Risk-based |

Exceptions (accepting a vulnerability temporarily) need a documented risk acceptance by the system owner, compensating controls and an expiry date.

**Segregation in the SDLC.** The same SoD principle that applies to payments applies to code:

- Developers cannot approve their own changes or merge without review.
- Developers do not have standing access to production; deployments go through the pipeline.
- Production data is not copied into development or test environments without masking or anonymization.
- Pipeline configuration is itself code, reviewed and protected, because whoever controls the pipeline controls production.

**Engineering view.**

- Automate controls in the pipeline; manual security gates become bottlenecks and are bypassed under deadline pressure.
- Keep evidence automatically: review approvals, scan results, SBOMs and deployment records linked to each release (Section 15.4).
- Threat-model changes to critical flows (payment creation, beneficiary maintenance, signing, entitlements), not only new systems.
- Write security tests for business rules: "a maker cannot release their own payment" is a test case, not only a design statement.

**Analogy.** A secure SDLC is like food safety in a restaurant kitchen. Ingredients are checked on arrival (dependencies), preparation follows hygiene rules (secure coding), dishes are checked before they leave (testing), and records are kept so an inspector can see that the rules were followed every day, not just on inspection day.

**Key takeaways**

- Security is built into every phase: requirements, design, implementation, build, test, release and operation.
- Automated pipeline controls (SAST, SCA, secret scanning, SBOM, signed artefacts) provide protection and evidence.
- Supply chain security matters because most code is third-party; an SBOM allows fast impact analysis.
- Vulnerabilities have remediation deadlines by severity; exceptions need documented, time-limited risk acceptance.
- SoD applies to code: reviewed changes, no developer access to production, protected pipelines.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain the difference between SAST, DAST and SCA, with one example of a vulnerability each would find.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Perform a short STRIDE threat model for a service that receives approved payments from the TMS and sends them to the bank over host-to-host. List one threat per STRIDE category and one control for each.
> 3. **Interview:** "A critical vulnerability is published in a library used by 30 of our services, including the payment engine, two days before quarter-end freeze. What do you do?" *Hint:* SBOM to find affected services and versions; assess exploitability; prioritize internet-facing and payment systems; emergency change process; compensating controls (WAF rules, network restrictions) if patching must wait; document risk acceptance.

<a id="154-change-management-in-regulated-banks"></a>
### 15.4 Change Management in Regulated Banks

This subchapter covers how changes to treasury systems and models are governed: model risk management, change approval, release freezes, management of vendors and other third parties, and the documentation that auditors and regulators expect.

#### Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)

**Why it matters.** Many treasury numbers are not facts but estimates produced by models: how long non-maturity deposits will stay, how fast mortgages will prepay, how much of a credit line will be drawn in stress, what the yield curve looks like between quoted points. If a model is wrong, or is used for something it was not designed for, the bank can hold too little liquidity, hedge the wrong exposure or report wrong capital ratios. Model risk management (MRM) is the discipline that controls this risk. For engineers, it means that changing a model's code, parameters or data is a governed event, not an ordinary release.

**SR 11-7.** The US Federal Reserve and the OCC issued *Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management* (SR 11-7) in April 2011. It became the global reference. Other regimes follow similar principles, such as the UK PRA's SS1/23 (effective May 2024) and the ECB's guide to internal models.

**What is a model?** SR 11-7 defines a model as a quantitative method, system or approach that applies statistical, economic, financial or mathematical theories, techniques and assumptions to process input data into quantitative estimates. A model has three components:

```text
  Inputs                       Processing                       Reporting
  (data, assumptions,  --->    (the theory and its      --->    (outputs turned into
   parameters)                  implementation in code)          information for decisions)
```

Model risk comes from two sources: the model has **fundamental errors** (wrong theory, wrong implementation, bad data), or it is **used incorrectly** (outside its intended scope, or its limitations are ignored).

**Treasury models.**

| Model | Purpose | Example risk |
|---|---|---|
| Non-maturity deposit behavioural model | Expected life and rate sensitivity of current and savings accounts (Chapter 5.1, 6.2) | Calibrated on a decade of low rates; overstates stickiness when rates rise quickly |
| Prepayment model | Expected repayment of mortgages | Ignores refinancing incentive; hedge too long |
| Yield curve construction | Discount and forward curves (Chapter 11.2) | Interpolation produces unrealistic forwards; mispriced FTP |
| FTP curve and liquidity premium | Internal pricing of funds (Chapter 6.4) | Wrong incentives for business lines |
| Stress outflow assumptions | Internal liquidity stress testing | Underestimates outflows in a fast digital run |
| Cash flow forecasting (statistical or ML) | Daily liquidity forecasts (Chapter 5.2) | Drift after a change in client behaviour |

**The three pillars of SR 11-7.**

| Pillar | Content | Who |
|---|---|---|
| Development, implementation and use | Sound theory, data quality checks, testing, documentation; implementation verified to match the design; used within its intended scope | Model owners and developers (first line) |
| Validation | Independent review: conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring (including process verification and benchmarking), and outcomes analysis (backtesting) | Independent validation team (second line) |
| Governance, policies and controls | Model inventory, tiering by risk, policies, approval before use, annual review, reporting to management and the board, internal audit review | Model risk function, senior management, internal audit (third line) |

The central idea is **effective challenge**: critical analysis by objective, informed parties who have the competence and the authority to make the model owner change things.

**The model lifecycle in practice.**

```text
  identify & register  ->  develop  ->  validate  ->  approve  ->  implement  ->  use & monitor
  (inventory ID, tier)     (docs,       (independent  (model        (code matches   (KPIs, backtests,
                            tests)       review)       committee)    validated      thresholds)
                                                                     version)            |
         ^                                                                               |
         +-------- change (material?) -> revalidation  <---------------------------------+
```

**Engineering view.**

- **Inventory linkage:** each model implementation carries its inventory ID and version in code and in its outputs, so that every reported number can be traced to the approved model version.
- **Implementation verification:** validators check that the code does what the documentation says. Make this easy: clear separation between model logic and plumbing, readable code, golden tests derived from the model documentation (Section 15.1).
- **Parameters as governed data:** calibrated parameters (decay rates, betas, prepayment speeds) are stored as versioned configuration with approvals, not hard-coded and not editable by users without an approval trail.
- **Change classification:** agree with the model risk function which changes are material (new methodology, recalibration, new data source) and need revalidation, and which are not (refactoring with identical results, which you prove with regression tests).
- **Monitoring built in:** produce the performance metrics the validation team defined (forecast error, backtesting exceptions, drift statistics) automatically on every run.
- **Reproducibility:** be able to rerun the model as of a past date with the same code, parameters and data (Chapter 13.2, bitemporal data).

**Example.** Treasury wants to update the deposit run-off model after a rapid rise in rates. The developers recalibrate the decay parameters and change the model to include a rate-sensitivity term. This is a material change: it needs documentation, independent validation (including backtesting against the recent outflows), approval by the model committee, and possibly a parallel run where IRRBB and liquidity metrics are produced with both versions before the new one becomes official. Deploying the new parameters "because the numbers look more realistic" would be a model risk policy breach, even if the new numbers are better.

**Analogy.** Model risk management is like the approval process for a new medicine. The developer must explain how it works and test it, an independent body reviews the evidence, it is approved for specific uses only, and its effects are monitored after release. Changing the formula requires a new review.

**Key takeaways**

- A model turns inputs into quantitative estimates using theory and assumptions; treasury relies heavily on behavioural and curve models.
- SR 11-7 (2011) sets three pillars: sound development and use, independent validation, and governance with an inventory.
- Model risk comes from fundamental errors and from incorrect use.
- Effective challenge by competent, independent people is the core principle.
- Engineers support MRM with inventory IDs in code, governed parameters, reproducibility, built-in monitoring and clear change classification.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Which of these are models under SR 11-7: (a) a deposit decay model; (b) a report summing balances by product; (c) a yield curve bootstrapper; (d) a spreadsheet that applies regulatory LCR run-off rates to balances? Explain your reasoning.
> 2. **Intermediate:** A developer refactors the prepayment model code for performance without changing the methodology. What evidence would you provide to show that no revalidation is needed?
> 3. **Interview:** "How would you design a platform that runs several versions of the same behavioural model in parallel for validation?" *Hint:* model registry with versions and approval status, parameters as versioned data, the same input snapshot for all versions, outputs tagged with model version, comparison reports, only the approved version allowed to feed official reports.

#### Change Approval Boards

**Why it matters.** Most production incidents are caused by changes: a release, a configuration update, a certificate renewal, a network rule. In a bank, a bad change to a payment or reporting system can cause financial loss and regulatory breaches, so changes are formally assessed and approved before they are made. The traditional mechanism is the Change Approval Board (CAB, also called Change Advisory Board). Done badly, it is a weekly meeting that slows everything down without reducing risk. Done well, it focuses human attention on the risky changes and lets routine ones flow through automated controls.

**Change types (ITIL).**

| Type | Definition | Approval | Treasury example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Standard | Low-risk, repeatable change with a pre-approved procedure | Pre-approved; logged | Adding a new currency holiday to the calendar through the governed reference data process; routine dependency patch through the pipeline |
