| Normal | Any change that is not standard or emergency | Assessed by risk; minor ones by a delegated approver, major ones by the CAB | New version of the liquidity engine; new payment routing rule |
| Emergency | Must be implemented urgently to restore service or fix a critical vulnerability | Emergency CAB (a small group available at short notice); full review after the fact | Hotfix for a defect blocking payments at 15:30 |

**What a CAB checks.** A change request should answer the questions the board would ask:

```text
  Change request CHG-2026-04817
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  Summary          Liquidity engine v4.12: new outflow rates for operational
                   deposits (regulatory interpretation update)
  Systems          liquidity-engine, lcr-reporting, data-mart
  Business owner   Head of Liquidity Reporting (approved)
  Risk rating      High: changes a regulatory metric
  Impact           LCR outflows +EUR 310m; LCR -1.8 pp (estimated, attached)
  Testing          Unit, golden (402/402 passed), regression vs v4.11 on
                   2026-09-30 data (differences only in affected lines, explained)
  Model risk       Not a model change (regulatory parameter), confirmed by MRM
  Timing           2026-10-22 19:00 CET, outside freeze windows; no reporting
                   deadline within 3 business days
  Implementation   Pipeline deployment; feature flag for new rates
  Back-out         Disable flag; previous version kept for 30 days
  Verification     Rerun of 2026-10-21 LCR; compare with expectation
  Communications   Regulatory reporting and ALCO secretary informed
```

**Making CABs effective.**

- **Risk-based routing:** classify changes by risk using objective criteria (system tier, type of change, size, test coverage, past failure rate). Low-risk changes are approved automatically when the pipeline evidence is complete; only high-risk changes reach the board.
- **Evidence from the pipeline:** test results, review approvals, scan results and deployment plans are attached automatically, so the CAB discusses risk instead of chasing documents.
- **Calendar awareness:** the CAB checks timing against freezes, period ends, regulatory deadlines and other changes to the same systems (Release Freezes below).
- **Learning:** failed changes are reviewed, and the risk criteria are adjusted.

DORA requires financial entities to have documented ICT change management, with changes recorded, tested, assessed, approved and implemented in a controlled way. It does not require a weekly meeting. Many banks combine continuous delivery with automated approvals for low-risk changes and human review for high-risk ones, and supervisors accept this when the controls are clear and evidenced.

**Engineering view.**

- Keep changes small. A small change is easier to assess, test and back out, and can be classified as lower risk.
- Separate deployment from release with feature flags, so that the risky part (switching on new behaviour) can be approved and reversed independently.
- Every production change, including configuration, reference data and infrastructure, must be traceable to an approved change record. Unauthorized changes are serious audit findings.
- Treat emergency changes as exceptions to be minimized; frequent emergencies indicate a process or quality problem.

**Analogy.** A CAB is like air traffic control. Most flights follow standard routes and are cleared quickly. Controllers focus on unusual situations, conflicts and bad weather. A control tower that inspected every aircraft in detail before every take-off would close the airport without making it safer.

**Key takeaways**

- Changes cause most incidents; banks assess and approve them before implementation.
- ITIL distinguishes standard (pre-approved), normal (risk-assessed) and emergency changes.
- A good change request covers impact, testing, timing, back-out and verification.
- Effective CABs are risk-based and use automated pipeline evidence, focusing people on high-risk changes.
- DORA requires controlled, documented change management, not a specific meeting format.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Classify each change as standard, normal or emergency: (a) renewing a TLS certificate through an automated, documented process; (b) adding a new product type to the TMS; (c) fixing a defect that stops all SWIFT payments at 14:00.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Design five objective criteria for automatically classifying the risk of a change to treasury systems, and explain how you would route each risk level.
> 3. **Interview:** "Our weekly CAB is a bottleneck: teams wait up to 10 days for approval and bundle changes into large releases. How would you fix it?" *Hint:* risk-based classification, pre-approved standard changes for pipeline deployments with complete evidence, smaller changes, feature flags, CAB time reserved for high-risk changes, metrics (lead time, change failure rate) to show the controls still work.

#### Release Freezes Around Period Ends

**Why it matters.** At month-end, quarter-end and especially year-end, treasury and finance systems are under the most pressure: closing the books, producing regulatory returns (LCR monthly, capital and leverage quarterly), running ALCO packs, and handling peak payment and settlement volumes. These are also the times when the bank can least afford an incident, because the numbers are published, audited and sent to supervisors. Release freezes stop non-essential changes during these windows.

**A typical freeze calendar.**

| Window | Typical period | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| Month-end | Last 2 business days of the month to business day 3 or 5 of the next month | Finance, accounting, regulatory reporting, liquidity and ALM systems |
| Quarter-end | Last week of the quarter to business day 5-10 of the next quarter | As above plus risk and capital systems; often wider |
| Year-end | Mid-December to mid-January | Usually bank-wide; also covers holiday staffing and annual audit |
| Event-driven | Around known peaks | Regulatory go-live dates, large migrations, TARGET or Fed holiday-adjacent days, market events |

```text
  December 2026 / January 2027   (year-end freeze, example)

  Mon Tue Wed Thu Fri
   14  15  16  17  18     <- freeze starts 16 Dec: only emergency changes
   21  22  23  24  25
   28  29  30  31   1     <- year-end close, statutory and regulatory runs
    4   5   6   7   8
   11  12  13  14  15     <- freeze ends 15 Jan after business day 10 reporting
```

**Exceptions.** Freezes allow exceptions for emergencies (restoring service, fixing critical vulnerabilities, mandatory regulatory changes with a fixed date). Exceptions need higher approval than normal changes, often from the head of the affected business and the CIO or their delegate, plus a clear reason why the change cannot wait.

**Enforcing a freeze in the pipeline.** Freeze calendars are more reliable when the deployment pipeline enforces them:

```python
from datetime import date

FREEZES = [  # (start, end inclusive, scope)
    (date(2026, 10, 29), date(2026, 11, 5), {"finance", "regulatory", "liquidity"}),
    (date(2026, 12, 16), date(2027, 1, 15), {"*"}),
]

def deploy_allowed(system_scope: str, change_type: str, today: date,
                   exception_approved: bool = False) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    for start, end, scope in FREEZES:
        if start <= today <= end and ("*" in scope or system_scope in scope):
            if change_type == "emergency" or exception_approved:
                return True, f"freeze {start}..{end}: allowed as {change_type} / exception"
            return False, f"freeze {start}..{end} applies to {system_scope}"
    return True, "no freeze"
```

The freeze calendar itself should be governed reference data, derived from the business day calendar and the regulatory reporting calendar, not a list typed into a wiki.

**Trade-offs.** Freezes reduce risk during critical windows but create side effects:

- **Batching after the freeze:** changes pile up and are released together in early January, creating a high-risk period of its own. Mitigate by releasing earlier and in small pieces, and by spreading releases after the freeze.
- **Pressure before the freeze:** teams rush to get changes in before it starts. A "soft freeze" a week earlier, with higher scrutiny, helps.
- **Stale systems:** long freezes delay security patches. Critical vulnerabilities must still be patchable through the emergency route.

**Engineering view.**

- Plan releases around the reporting calendar from the start of each quarter, not two days before a freeze.
- Use feature flags and dark launches so that code can be deployed before the freeze and switched on after it with a smaller, controlled change.
- Freezes do not stop operational work: reference data updates (for example new holiday calendars), market data configuration and user access changes continue through their governed processes.

**Analogy.** A release freeze is like a hospital postponing elective building work in the wards during the winter flu peak. The work is not cancelled, and anything urgent for patient safety still happens, but nobody starts rewiring a ward when every bed is full.

**Key takeaways**

- Period ends are when treasury and finance systems are most loaded and most visible, so non-essential changes are frozen.
- Freeze calendars cover month-end, quarter-end, year-end and event-driven windows.
- Exceptions need higher approval and a clear reason; critical fixes remain possible.
- Enforce freezes in the pipeline, using governed calendars.
- Mitigate side effects: avoid batching after the freeze, release small changes early, use feature flags.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain why a change to the liquidity reporting engine on the last business day of the quarter is riskier than the same change mid-month.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Extend `deploy_allowed` to compute month-end freeze windows automatically from a business day calendar (last two business days of the month to the third business day of the next).
> 3. **Interview:** "A regulatory change must go live on 1 January, inside the year-end freeze. How do you plan it?" *Hint:* deploy the code early behind a feature flag, parallel run in December, pre-approved exception with a clear activation plan and back-out, staffing over the holidays, verification of the first run, communication with regulatory reporting.

#### Vendor and Third-Party Risk

**Why it matters.** Treasury depends heavily on third parties: TMS vendors (Murex, Calypso, FIS, Kyriba; Chapter 13.1), market data providers, SWIFT service bureaus, cloud providers, SaaS reporting tools and consultants who build and run systems. The bank can outsource the work but not the responsibility. If a vendor fails, is breached or stops supporting a product, the bank is still accountable to clients and supervisors. Regulation requires banks to manage this risk throughout the relationship, from selection to exit.

**Regulatory framework.** In the EU, the EBA Guidelines on outsourcing arrangements (2019) and DORA's third-party pillar set the main requirements. DORA adds a **register of information** covering all contractual arrangements for ICT services, with more detail for those supporting critical or important functions, mandatory contract provisions, and direct EU oversight of critical ICT third-party providers (such as major cloud providers). Similar regimes exist in other jurisdictions, for example the US interagency guidance on third-party relationships (2023) and the UK PRA's SS2/21.

**The third-party lifecycle.**

```text
  planning & risk  ->  due diligence  ->  contract  ->  onboarding  ->  ongoing monitoring  ->  exit
  assessment          (security,         (mandatory     (integration,   (SLAs, incidents,      (planned or
  (critical function? financial          clauses)        access,         audits, SOC reports,   forced; data
   concentration?)    health, location,                  data flows)     risk reviews)          returned or
                      subcontractors)                                                           deleted)
```

**Tiering vendors.** Effort should match risk.

| Tier | Criteria | Treasury examples | Oversight |
|---|---|---|---|
| Critical | Supports a critical or important function; hard to replace | Core TMS vendor, cloud hosting the payment engine, SWIFT service bureau | Full due diligence, on-site or pooled audits, annual review, tested exit plan |
| Important | Material but substitutable within weeks | Market data provider, reconciliation SaaS | Due diligence, annual review, documented exit plan |
| Standard | Low impact | Office software, training providers | Standard procurement checks |

**Contract provisions that matter to engineers.**

| Provision | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Service levels with measurable targets | Availability and support response must match your own RTOs (Section 15.2) |
| Incident notification | The vendor must tell you quickly, so you can meet DORA reporting deadlines |
| Audit and access rights | You, your auditors and your supervisor can inspect the service |
| Data location and protection | Where data is stored and processed; encryption; key ownership |
| Subcontracting | Which subcontractors are used for critical parts, and approval of changes |
| Business continuity and testing | The vendor's DR is tested, and you can take part in tests |
| Exit and transition | Data returned in a usable format; assistance during migration; adequate notice period |
| Source code escrow (on-premises software) | Access to the source if the vendor fails |

**Assurance reports.** Vendors often provide independent assurance reports instead of hosting every client's audit: SOC 1 (ISAE 3402) on controls relevant to financial reporting, SOC 2 on security, availability, confidentiality and other trust criteria. Engineers should read the scope and exceptions, and especially the **complementary user entity controls**: controls the vendor assumes *you* operate (such as reviewing user access to the SaaS tool). If you do not operate them, the vendor's report does not cover your risk.

**Concentration and exit.** If many critical functions depend on one cloud provider or one vendor, a single failure affects them all. Banks assess concentration at the bank level, not system by system. Exit plans must be realistic: replacing a TMS takes years, so the exit plan for a critical TMS vendor focuses on keeping data accessible and the service running while a replacement is built, not on a quick switch.

**Engineering view.**

- Isolate vendor products behind your own interfaces and anti-corruption layers (Section 15.1), so that replacement is possible.
- Keep your data in formats and stores you control; make sure regular extracts give you a complete, usable copy.
- Monitor vendor SLAs with your own measurements, not only the vendor's reports.
- Track vendor product lifecycles (end of support dates, version roadmaps) and plan upgrades before support ends; running unsupported versions is a common audit finding.
- Feed the register of information from your system inventory, so that it stays accurate.

**Analogy.** Using a vendor is like hiring a contractor to build part of your house. You still have to make sure the work meets the building code, you need access to inspect it, you want the plans in case the contractor goes out of business, and you should not have every part of the house depend on one contractor without a backup.

**Key takeaways**

- Banks can outsource services but remain responsible for them.
- DORA and the EBA outsourcing guidelines require due diligence, specific contract clauses, a register of information, monitoring and exit plans.
- Tier vendors by the criticality of the functions they support.
- Read SOC reports carefully, including the controls the vendor expects you to operate.
- Design for exit: isolation layers, data you control, and realistic exit plans.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Name five contract provisions you would require from a SaaS provider hosting the bank's intraday liquidity dashboard, and why.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Your TMS vendor announces end of support for your version in 18 months, and the upgrade requires a database change. Outline the risk assessment and the plan, including how you would use the regression testing approach from Section 15.1.
> 3. **Interview:** "The payment engine, the TMS and the data platform all run in the same cloud region of the same provider. What is the risk and what would you propose?" *Hint:* concentration risk; regional outage scenarios; multi-region or alternate-site recovery for tier 0 systems; dependencies on the provider's identity and control plane; exit and portability; register of information and DORA expectations.

#### Documentation for Auditors and Regulators

**Why it matters.** In a regulated bank, a control that cannot be evidenced is treated as a control that does not exist. Internal audit, external auditors and supervisors regularly ask treasury and IT to show how systems work, what changed, who had access and whether controls operated. Good documentation answers these questions quickly and consistently. Poor documentation leads to findings, remediation programmes and sometimes capital add-ons, even when the underlying system is sound.

**Who asks, and why.**

| Party | Line of defence | Typical focus |
|---|---|---|
| Business and IT management | First line | Owns and operates controls; produces evidence |
| Risk management, compliance, model validation, information security | Second line | Challenges the first line; sets policies; monitors |
| Internal audit | Third line | Independent assurance that controls are designed and operating effectively |
| External auditors | Outside the bank | Controls relevant to the financial statements (IT general controls, key reports, accounting systems) |
| Supervisors (ECB/JST, national authorities, PRA, Fed) | Outside the bank | Risk management, regulatory reporting quality (BCBS 239, Chapter 14.3), operational resilience, model use |

**What is usually requested.**

| Area | Typical evidence |
|---|---|
| System inventory | List of systems with owners, criticality tier, dependencies, vendors, data classification |
| Data lineage | From each regulatory or financial report line back to source systems and transformations |
| Change management | Change records with approvals, test evidence and deployment records for a period |
| Access management | Access lists, joiner-mover-leaver evidence, recertification results, privileged access logs |
| Controls | Description of each control, its owner, frequency and evidence of operation (for example daily reconciliation results and break resolution) |
| Models | Model inventory, documentation, validation reports, monitoring results |
| Resilience | DR test results with achieved RTO/RPO, incident records and post-incident reviews, resilience test reports |
| Third parties | Register of information, due diligence, SOC reports, exit plans |

**Example: an audit request and a good answer.** "Show all changes to the LCR calculation between 1 July and 30 September, with their approvals and testing."

```text
  Change ID      Date        Description                        Approver(s)            Tests                      Deployed by
  ------------   ----------  ---------------------------------  ---------------------  -------------------------  -----------
  CHG-2026-3311  2026-07-09  Fix: HQLA haircut on covered bonds  Reg. reporting head;   Golden 398/398; regression  pipeline run
                                                                 CAB (normal, medium)   vs prod, 3 lines changed    #8812
  CHG-2026-3478  2026-08-21  New outflow category for brokered   Reg. reporting head;   Golden 402/402; parallel    pipeline run
                             deposits                            CAB (normal, high)     run over July month-end     #9104
  CHG-2026-3602  2026-09-12  Library upgrade (no logic change)   Delegated approver     Golden 402/402; regression  pipeline run
                                                                 (standard)             identical results           #9377
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Completeness check: all 3 production deployments of lcr-engine in the period match an approved change record.
```

The last line matters most: auditors test not only that recorded changes were approved, but that **every** change in production was recorded. They compare deployment logs from the platform with the change records.

**Principles for audit-ready systems.**

- **Evidence by design:** controls produce their own evidence as data (reconciliation results, approval records, test reports, access reviews), with timestamps and identities. Screenshots collected the night before an audit are weak evidence.
- **Traceability:** requirement or regulation, design decision, code, tests, change record and release are linked by identifiers. A traceability matrix for regulatory rules (for example each LCR article mapped to the code and golden tests that implement it) answers many supervisory questions directly.
- **Living documentation:** architecture diagrams, data flows and runbooks are kept in version control with the code and reviewed when the code changes. Architecture decision records (ADRs) explain why choices were made, which auditors and future engineers both need.
- **One version of the truth:** the system inventory, dependency map and register of information are generated from the same source, so that answers to different parties are consistent.
- **Retention:** evidence is kept for the required period (often 5 to 10 years for financial records and related controls), and can be retrieved.

**Example: a regulatory traceability matrix (extract).**

| Requirement | Implementation | Tests | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| LCR Delegated Regulation, Arts. 24-25: retail deposit outflow rates | `lcr/outflows/retail.py`, parameters `lcr_rates.yaml` v12 | Golden cases R-001 to R-018; property tests on bucket totals | Liquidity reporting |
| Art. 33: inflow cap at 75% of outflows | `lcr/inflows/cap.py` | Golden cases C-001 to C-006 (below, at and above cap) | Liquidity reporting |
| BCBS 239 completeness | Feed completeness controls DQ-011 to DQ-019 | Control test results stored per run | Data office |

**Engineering view.**

- Treat audit requests as use cases: if the same question comes every year, build a report that answers it.
- Keep the deployment platform as the single route to production, so that its logs are complete and match change records.
- When findings are raised, agree concrete, testable remediation and evidence of closure, not just a promise to "improve documentation".
- Write documentation for a knowledgeable outsider: an auditor who understands controls but not your code.

**Analogy.** Documentation for auditors is like a car's service book. A well-maintained car with no service history sells for less than an average car with a complete, stamped record, because the buyer cannot verify the maintenance. Evidence is part of the value.

**Key takeaways**

- In a regulated bank, a control that cannot be evidenced is treated as missing.
- The three lines of defence, external auditors and supervisors all request evidence on inventory, lineage, changes, access, controls, models, resilience and third parties.
- Build evidence into systems: controls produce timestamped, attributable records automatically.
- Maintain traceability from regulation to code, tests and releases, and ensure every production change matches an approved record.
- Keep documentation versioned with the code and written for knowledgeable outsiders.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** List the evidence you would provide to show that the daily nostro reconciliation control operated throughout a quarter.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Internal audit finds that 4 of 220 production deployments of treasury systems in the last year have no matching change record. Describe how you would investigate, remediate and prevent recurrence.
> 3. **Interview:** "A supervisor asks you to demonstrate that the LCR you reported for 30 June can be reproduced exactly today. How do you prepare?" *Hint:* bitemporal input data as of the reporting date, versioned code and parameters tagged to that run, recorded market and reference data snapshots, rerun in a controlled environment, comparison with the submitted figures, documentation of any manual adjustments and their approvals.

<a id="16-advanced-topics-and-emerging-trends"></a>
## 16. Advanced Topics and Emerging Trends

The previous chapters described how treasury works today and how its systems are built. This chapter looks at the areas where requirements are getting harder or changing fastest: supervisory and internal stress testing, the move from overnight batches to real-time treasury, tokenized money and distributed ledgers, and the failures of Northern Rock, Lehman Brothers, Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse. Engineers working on these topics build systems that supervisors examine closely, that run in the minutes that decide whether a bank survives a run, or that connect the bank to new forms of money whose rules are still being written.

<a id="161-stress-testing-and-scenario-analysis"></a>
### 16.1 Stress Testing and Scenario Analysis

This subchapter covers how banks and supervisors test whether a bank survives severe but plausible conditions: the supervisory exercises in the EU and the US, reverse stress tests that start from failure, the interaction between liquidity and solvency under stress, and how scenarios are designed and calibrated. Chapter 13.3 describes the scenario engine that runs these calculations.

#### Regulatory Stress Tests (EBA, CCAR)

**Why it matters.** Capital and liquidity ratios describe a bank on one reporting date. They say little about what happens if a recession, a rate shock and a property crash arrive together. After 2008, supervisors decided to ask that question themselves, in a common format, for all large banks at once. The results feed directly into capital requirements and dividend decisions, so a stress test is not an academic exercise: a weak result can force a bank to hold more capital or cancel a planned distribution to shareholders.

**How it works in general.** A supervisory stress test has four ingredients:

- **Scenarios:** a baseline (the expected path of the economy) and an adverse scenario (a severe recession with market shocks), defined as paths for GDP, unemployment, house prices, interest rates, FX rates, equity prices and credit spreads over a multi-year horizon.
- **Methodology:** rules for how banks translate the scenarios into credit losses, market losses, net interest income, fees and costs, including what they may and may not assume.
- **Projection:** the bank (or the supervisor, or both) projects the income statement and capital quarter by quarter or year by year.
- **Use of results:** the projected fall in capital ratios sets or informs a capital buffer, and results are usually published bank by bank.

**EU: the EBA EU-wide stress test.** The European Banking Authority coordinates a stress test every two years (2018, 2021, 2023, 2025, ...) for the largest EU banks, run in the euro area together with the ECB.

| Feature | EBA EU-wide stress test |
|---|---|
| Who runs the numbers | Banks, using their own models within strict EBA rules ("constrained bottom-up") |
| Horizon | 3 years |
| Scenarios | Baseline and adverse; the adverse scenario is designed by the ESRB and ECB |
| Balance sheet | Static: maturing assets and liabilities are replaced with similar ones; no management actions |
| Quality assurance | Supervisors challenge bank projections against benchmarks over several submission rounds |
| Outcome | No pass or fail; the capital depletion informs Pillar 2 Guidance (P2G) in the SREP |
| Publication | Bank-by-bank results in standard templates |

The static balance sheet assumption matters for engineers. It means projections cannot be improved by assuming that the bank shrinks, raises capital or reprices its loans. It also means that maturing positions must be rolled into identical replacements in the projection engine, which is a different logic from the dynamic balance sheet used in internal planning.

**US: CCAR and DFAST.** The US Federal Reserve runs an annual supervisory stress test for banks with USD 100bn or more in assets (Category IV firms every other year).

| Feature | Fed supervisory stress test |
|---|---|
| Who runs the numbers | The Fed, with its own supervisory models applied to bank-submitted data; banks also run company-run tests |
| Horizon | 9 quarters |
| Scenarios | Baseline and severely adverse; a global market shock and counterparty default component for the largest trading banks |
| Balance sheet | Projected to remain broadly constant in size, with planned dividends included |
| Outcome | The stress capital buffer (SCB) |
| Publication | Firm-level results each June |

CCAR (Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review) is the capital planning exercise around the test; DFAST (Dodd-Frank Act Stress Tests) is the statutory stress test itself. Since 2020 the result sets each firm's stress capital buffer:

```text
  SCB = max( 2.5%,  (starting CET1 ratio - minimum projected CET1 ratio)
                    + 4 quarters of planned common dividends / RWA )

  Example:
    Starting CET1 ratio                12.0%
    Lowest CET1 ratio in the 9 quarters 8.9%
    Peak-to-trough decline              3.1%
    Planned dividends / RWA             0.4%
    SCB                                 3.5%   (above the 2.5% floor)

    Requirement = 4.5% minimum + 3.5% SCB + G-SIB surcharge (if any)
```

Because the SCB changes every year with the scenario, it can make capital planning volatile. In 2025 the Fed proposed averaging results over two consecutive years and publishing its models and scenarios for public comment.

**Comparison.**

| Aspect | EBA (EU) | Fed (US) |
|---|---|---|
| Models | Bank models, constrained | Supervisory models |
| Frequency | Every 2 years | Annual |
| Horizon | 3 years | 9 quarters |
| Direct link to capital | Through P2G (supervisory judgment) | Mechanical, through the SCB |
| Main burden for the bank | Running projections, templates, QA rounds | Data submissions (FR Y-14), capital plan, own tests |

Other supervisors run similar exercises (the Bank of England's bank capital stress test, the ECB's thematic tests such as the 2022 climate and 2024 cyber resilience exercises). Liquidity stress tests are mainly internal (the ILAAP, Chapter 9.2), although supervisors run occasional liquidity exercises, such as the ECB's 2019 sensitivity analysis of liquidity risk.

**Engineering view.** A regulatory stress test is a large, deadline-driven data and calculation project.

```text
  Scenario release        Bank projection engine                   Submission
  (macro paths)                                                     and QA
       |            +---------------------------------------+
       v            |  satellite models: macro -> PD, LGD,  |
  +-----------+     |  NII margins, fee income, market      |     +-------------+
  | Scenario  +---->+  losses                               +---->+ EBA / Fed   |
  | loader,   |     |  balance sheet roll-forward (static)  |     | templates   |
  | versioned |     |  P&L and capital per year / quarter   |     +------+------+
  +-----------+     +-------------------+-------------------+            |
                                        ^                                v
                    starting point data | (reconciled to          supervisor challenge
                    from regulatory     |  FINREP / COREP)         -> resubmission
                    reporting           |                          (several rounds)
```

- The starting point must reconcile with published regulatory reports (Chapter 9.3). Differences are among the first things supervisors query.
- Each submission round must be reproducible: same inputs, same code version, same results. Use the versioning and lineage practices from Chapters 13.2 and 15.4.
- Templates change with each exercise. Generate them from a model of the data, not by hand in spreadsheets.
- Expect overrides and management adjustments. Record each one with its owner, reason and effect, because the supervisor will ask.

**Analogy.** A supervisory stress test is like a building inspector checking every skyscraper in the city against the same simulated earthquake. Each owner can describe their building's strength, but the inspector fixes the size of the earthquake, the rules of the calculation and how the results are compared.

**Key takeaways**

- Supervisory stress tests project capital under common baseline and adverse scenarios over several years and translate the result into capital requirements.
- The EBA test uses bank models within strict rules, a 3-year horizon and a static balance sheet; results inform Pillar 2 Guidance.
- The Fed test uses supervisory models over 9 quarters; the peak-to-trough CET1 decline plus planned dividends sets the stress capital buffer (minimum 2.5%).
- For engineers, the hard parts are a reconciled starting point, reproducible projection runs, template generation and audit trails for adjustments.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** A bank starts with a CET1 ratio of 13.2%, reaches a minimum of 10.4% in the severely adverse scenario and plans dividends equal to 0.3% of RWA over four quarters. Compute its stress capital buffer.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Explain how a static balance sheet assumption changes the projection of net interest income for a bank whose fixed-rate mortgages mature during the horizon. What data does the engine need to roll them forward?
> 3. **Interview:** "The supervisor's QA team says your projected credit losses for SME loans are below their benchmark. How would your systems support the response?" *Hint:* traceability from macro path to PD and LGD per segment, versioned satellite models, a breakdown of the gap by driver, rerunning with alternative parameters quickly, and an audit trail of the final decision.

#### Reverse Stress Testing

**Why it matters.** A normal stress test asks: "Given this scenario, how bad is the outcome?" The danger is that the scenarios chosen are the ones the bank already expects to survive. A reverse stress test turns the question around: "What would have to happen for us to fail?" It forces management to look at the combinations of events that would break the business model, including ones nobody had considered plausible. Supervisors require it (for example in the EBA Guidelines on institutions' stress tests and in the PRA rules) as part of the ICAAP, ILAAP and recovery planning.

**Defining "failure".** The starting point is a precise definition of the outcome to reverse-engineer:

| Failure point | Typical definition |
|---|---|
| Capital | CET1 ratio falls below the total requirement (minimum + Pillar 2), or below the point of non-viability |
| Liquidity | Counterbalancing capacity is exhausted within the survival horizon (Chapter 5.2) |
| Business model | The bank is no longer profitable enough to remain viable, or loses access to a key market |
| Recovery | A recovery indicator breaches its threshold (Chapter 7.3) |

**Approaches.**

| Approach | How it works | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Narrative | Management workshops build stories that lead to failure, then quantify them | Captures non-financial causes (fraud, IT failure, reputation) | Subjective, limited to what people imagine |
| Single-factor search | Increase one shock (rates, deposit outflow) until the failure point is reached | Simple, gives "distance to failure" per risk | Ignores combinations |
| Multi-factor search | Search over combinations of factors, often on a grid | Finds combinations | Many combinations, hard to rank |
| Most plausible scenario | Find the combination of shocks that reaches failure with the smallest statistical distance from today | Ranks scenarios by plausibility | Depends on a correlation model that may break in a crisis |

**The most plausible failure scenario.** If risk factor changes `x` are roughly normal with covariance matrix `Sigma` and the loss is approximately linear, `loss = s' x` (with `s` the vector of sensitivities), the most plausible scenario that produces a target loss `L` minimizes the Mahalanobis distance `x' Sigma^-1 x` subject to `s' x = L`. The solution has a closed form:

```text
  x* = L * Sigma s / (s' Sigma s)

  Plausibility: distance d = L / sqrt(s' Sigma s)  (in standard deviations)
  A larger d means the failure scenario is less plausible.
```

**Example.** A bank with CET1 capital of EUR 5.0bn fails when losses reach EUR 1.8bn (the headroom above its requirement). It is exposed to three factors: rates (bp), credit spreads (bp) and house prices (%).

```python
import numpy as np

# sensitivities: EUR m loss per unit move (rates +1bp, spreads +1bp, house prices -1%)
s = np.array([4.0, 6.5, 90.0])

# annual standard deviations and correlation of the factor moves
vol = np.array([80.0, 60.0, 8.0])
corr = np.array([[1.0, 0.3, 0.2],
                 [0.3, 1.0, 0.6],
                 [0.2, 0.6, 1.0]])
sigma = np.outer(vol, vol) * corr

L = 1800.0                                  # EUR m loss that breaches the requirement
x_star = L * sigma @ s / (s @ sigma @ s)
distance = L / np.sqrt(s @ sigma @ s)

print(np.round(x_star, 1))   # [65.5 77.6 11.5] -> +66bp rates, +78bp spreads, -11.5% house prices
print(round(distance, 2))    # 1.6 standard deviations
```

The result says that the most plausible way to lose EUR 1.8bn is a combined rise in rates and spreads with an 11.5% fall in house prices, about 1.6 standard deviations away. That is uncomfortably close, and it would lead to a discussion of hedges, concentration limits or more capital. Real reverse stress tests use non-linear full revaluation (search algorithms rather than the closed form) and stressed correlations, but the idea is the same.

**Liquidity example.** For liquidity, the question becomes: which run-off rate on corporate deposits exhausts the buffer within 30 days, given the other outflows? If the answer is 18% and SVB-style outflows reached 25% of deposits in a single day, the result is a strong signal that the funding profile needs work.

**From result to action.** A reverse stress test is useful only if it changes something:

- Identify the factors and concentrations that drive the failure scenario.
- Define early warning indicators that show when the world is moving toward it (Chapter 5.4, Contingency Funding Plans).
- Link to recovery options and their capacity (Chapter 7.3).
- Document the analysis for the board, which must review it.

**Analogy.** A normal stress test is like checking whether a bridge holds a 40-tonne truck. A reverse stress test asks what load, wind and temperature combination brings the bridge down, and then asks how close tomorrow's weather forecast comes to it.

**Key takeaways**

- Reverse stress testing starts from a defined failure point and searches for the scenarios that cause it.
- Failure can be defined for capital, liquidity, business model viability or recovery indicators.
- The most plausible failure scenario minimizes statistical distance from today; for linear losses there is a closed-form solution.
- The output should drive early warning indicators, limits and recovery planning, not sit in a report.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** A bank has a liquidity buffer of EUR 12bn and contractual net outflows of EUR 3bn over 30 days. Retail deposits are EUR 60bn. Ignoring other flows, which retail run-off rate exhausts the buffer?
> 2. **Intermediate:** Using the example above, change the correlation between spreads and house prices from 0.6 to 0.9. Does the failure scenario become more or less plausible? Explain why.
> 3. **Interview:** "Our reverse stress test says failure requires a 6-sigma event, so we are safe. What is wrong with this conclusion?" *Hint:* correlations and volatilities measured in calm periods, non-linear losses, liquidity and solvency feedback, non-financial triggers, and the history of supposedly 6-sigma events in 2008 and 2023.

#### Combined Liquidity and Solvency Stress

**Why it matters.** Banks traditionally ran capital stress tests (ICAAP) and liquidity stress tests (ILAAP) in separate teams with separate models. Real crises do not respect that split. A loss reduces capital, which triggers a rating downgrade, which raises funding costs and causes collateral calls and deposit outflows, which forces asset sales at a loss, which reduces capital further. Silicon Valley Bank and Credit Suisse both failed through this loop. A stress test that runs the two sides separately misses the second-round effects that do the most damage.

**The feedback loop.**

```text
              +------------------------------+
              |  Initial shock               |
              |  (credit losses, rate rise)  |
              +--------------+---------------+
                             |
                             v
   +-------------------> Capital falls ----------------------+
   |                         |                               |
   |                         v                               v
   |                Rating downgrade,                Higher funding cost
   |                market confidence lost           (spread on new funding)
   |                         |                               |
   |                         v                               v
   |            Deposit outflows, repo haircuts,        Lower NII
   |            collateral calls (CSA triggers)              |
   |                         |                               |
   |                         v                               |
   |            Buffer used; assets sold or pledged          |
   |            below book value                             |
   |                         |                               |
   +------ realized losses <-+-------------------------------+
```

**Transmission channels.**

| Channel | From solvency to liquidity | From liquidity to solvency |
|---|---|---|
| Rating | Losses lead to downgrades, which trigger collateral calls and outflows of rating-sensitive investors | |
| Confidence | Reported losses or capital shortfall trigger deposit runs | |
| Funding cost | | Higher spreads on new and rolled funding reduce NII |
| Fire sales | | Selling securities below book value realizes losses (especially amortized-cost portfolios) |
| Encumbrance | | Pledging the best assets leaves unsecured creditors with weaker assets, raising spreads further |
| Accounting | Selling from a held-to-maturity portfolio can taint the whole portfolio and force fair valuation | |

**How to model it.** A combined stress test projects capital and liquidity in the same time steps, with explicit links between them:

1. Apply the scenario for the period and compute losses and the new capital ratio.
2. Map the capital ratio (or rating) to behavioural parameters: outflow rates, haircuts, funding spreads.
3. Compute the liquidity position; if the buffer is insufficient, apply the counterbalancing actions in order (Chapter 5.4), including asset sales with their realized losses.
4. Feed the realized losses and higher funding costs back into the capital projection.
5. Repeat within the period until the numbers converge, then move to the next period.

**Example.** A simplified quarterly loop.

```python
def combined_stress(cet1, rwa, deposits, buffer, quarters, credit_loss, unrealized_loss_rate):
    """Very simplified joint projection; amounts in EUR bn."""
    for q in range(1, quarters + 1):
        cet1 -= credit_loss[q - 1]
        ratio = cet1 / rwa
        # behaviour depends on solvency: weaker capital -> larger run and higher spread
        outflow_rate = 0.03 if ratio > 0.12 else 0.08 if ratio > 0.10 else 0.20
        funding_spread = 0.002 if ratio > 0.12 else 0.006 if ratio > 0.10 else 0.015
        outflow = deposits * outflow_rate
        deposits -= outflow
        shortfall = max(0.0, outflow - buffer)
        buffer = max(0.0, buffer - outflow)
        # cover the shortfall by selling securities held at amortized cost
        realized = shortfall * unrealized_loss_rate
        cet1 -= realized + deposits * funding_spread / 4
        print(f"Q{q}: CET1 {cet1 / rwa:.1%}, outflow {outflow:.1f}, buffer {buffer:.1f}, "
              f"realized loss {realized:.2f}")

combined_stress(cet1=12.6, rwa=100.0, deposits=150.0, buffer=20.0, quarters=4,
                credit_loss=[0.4, 0.6, 0.6, 0.4], unrealized_loss_rate=0.15)
# Q1: CET1 12.1%, outflow 4.5,  buffer 15.5, realized loss 0.00
# Q2: CET1 11.3%, outflow 11.6, buffer 3.9,  realized loss 0.00
# Q3: CET1 9.5%,  outflow 10.7, buffer 0.0,  realized loss 1.03
# Q4: CET1 5.1%,  outflow 24.6, buffer 0.0,  realized loss 3.69
```

Run separately, the capital stress would show a loss of EUR 2.0bn of credit losses (CET1 from 12.6% to 10.6%) and the liquidity stress, with a fixed 3% outflow, would show a comfortable buffer. Together, the CET1 ratio falls below 10% in the third quarter and to about 5% in the fourth, as each loss makes the next run larger. The thresholds and rates here are illustrative; real models calibrate them from history and expert judgment and use many more segments.

**Engineering view.**

- Use one scenario definition, one balance sheet projection and one time grid for ICAAP and ILAAP. Separate engines with separate data snapshots cannot be combined reliably afterwards.
- Make behavioural parameters functions of the bank's own state (capital ratio, rating, news), not fixed inputs.
- Keep the order of counterbalancing actions configurable and record which actions were taken in each period.
- Iterative models can fail to converge or oscillate. Limit iterations, detect non-convergence and report it.
- Liquidity runs in days, capital projections in quarters. Combined models often use a daily grid for the first weeks and coarser buckets later.

**Analogy.** Solvency and liquidity are like a patient's heart and lungs. A doctor who tests each organ separately may find both acceptable, while the patient is in danger because a weak heart reduces oxygen, which weakens the heart further.

**Key takeaways**

- Liquidity and solvency stress interact through ratings, confidence, funding costs, fire sales and encumbrance.
- Separate ICAAP and ILAAP tests miss second-round effects that drove the failures of 2007-2008 and 2023.
- Combined models project both in the same time steps, with behaviour that depends on the bank's own solvency.
- Engineering requires one scenario, one balance sheet and one time grid, plus convergence controls for iterative loops.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** List three ways a two-notch rating downgrade affects a bank's liquidity position within 30 days.
> 2. **Intermediate:** In the example, change the unrealized loss rate on securities from 15% to 5%. What changes, and what does this tell you about the role of interest rate risk in the banking book in a liquidity crisis?
> 3. **Interview:** "Our ICAAP and ILAAP engines are owned by different teams and run on different data. How would you move toward a combined stress test without a big-bang rewrite?" *Hint:* a shared scenario library and starting-point data first, an interface that passes capital ratios to the liquidity engine and realized losses back, a reconciled time grid, and running both in a loop orchestrator before merging models.

#### Scenario Design and Calibration

**Why it matters.** A stress test is only as good as its scenarios. If the scenario is too mild, it gives false comfort; if it is implausibly extreme, management ignores it; if the variables in it are inconsistent (unemployment soars while house prices rise), the results cannot be interpreted. Scenario design is the work of turning a story ("a sharp recession with persistent inflation") into a complete, coherent and calibrated set of risk factor paths that every model in the bank can consume.

**Types of scenario.**

| Type | Definition | Example | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Historical | Replay the risk factor moves of a past period | Lehman weeks 2008, March 2020, 2022 UK gilt crisis | Plausible by construction, internally consistent | Tomorrow's crisis will differ |
| Hypothetical | A forward-looking story calibrated by experts | Taiwan Strait conflict, cyber attack on a major payment system | Addresses new risks | Calibration is subjective |
| Hybrid | A historical pattern rescaled or adapted to today's positions | 2008 credit spread moves, scaled to today's spread levels | Combines realism and relevance | Rescaling choices need justification |
| Sensitivity | One factor shocked, others unchanged | +200bp parallel rates (IRRBB, Chapter 6.2) | Simple, comparable | Ignores correlations |

**Design steps.**

```text
  1. Narrative        "Energy price shock, inflation persists, central banks hike,
                       recession in Europe, commercial property falls"
          |
  2. Core variables   GDP, unemployment, policy rate, 10y yield, house prices,
                      EUR/USD, equity index, credit spreads  (paths per quarter)
          |
  3. Expansion        Derive hundreds of secondary factors (full curves, sector
                      spreads, single-name equities, vols) consistently from the core
          |
  4. Calibration      Check severity (percentiles, history) and plausibility
          |
  5. Translation      Satellite models map factors to PD, LGD, run-off, margins
          |
  6. Governance       Approval, version, documentation, back-testing of severity
```

**Calibrating severity.** Common approaches:

- **Historical percentiles:** set the shock to, for example, the 1st percentile of historical 1-year moves, or "a 1-in-25-year event".
- **Worst historical episodes:** take the largest observed move, possibly with a margin, for each core variable.
- **Peer and supervisory benchmarks:** compare with the EBA adverse scenario or the Fed's severely adverse scenario.
- **Starting point dependence:** shocks should depend on where the economy is. A 300bp rise is severe when rates are at 1% and mild when they are at 10%. Supervisors increasingly make severity counter-cyclical: harsher when the economy is booming, to avoid procyclical capital demands in a downturn.

**Coherence through conditional expansion.** Experts set the core variables; the secondary variables should follow consistently. A standard technique uses the conditional mean of a multivariate normal distribution: given core moves `x_c`, the expected secondary moves are

```text
  E[x_s | x_c] = mu_s + Sigma_sc Sigma_cc^-1 (x_c - mu_c)
```

```python
import numpy as np

factors = ["10y_rate_bp", "equity_pct", "ig_spread_bp", "hy_spread_bp", "eurusd_pct"]
core, secondary = [0, 1], [2, 3, 4]       # experts fix rates and equities

# covariance of quarterly moves estimated from history (stressed period preferred)
vol = np.array([35.0, 9.0, 25.0, 110.0, 4.0])
corr = np.array([[ 1.0, -0.2,  0.1,  0.0,  0.2],
                 [-0.2,  1.0, -0.7, -0.8,  0.3],
                 [ 0.1, -0.7,  1.0,  0.8, -0.2],
                 [ 0.0, -0.8,  0.8,  1.0, -0.3],
                 [ 0.2,  0.3, -0.2, -0.3,  1.0]])
sigma = np.outer(vol, vol) * corr

x_core = np.array([120.0, -30.0])         # +120bp rates, equities -30%
s_cc = sigma[np.ix_(core, core)]
s_sc = sigma[np.ix_(secondary, core)]
x_sec = s_sc @ np.linalg.solve(s_cc, x_core)

for name, value in zip([factors[i] for i in secondary], x_sec):
    print(f"{name}: {value:+.1f}")
# ig_spread_bp: +55.5
# hy_spread_bp: +242.7
# eurusd_pct: -1.0
```

The equity crash implies much wider credit spreads, far more for high yield than for investment grade, as history suggests. The euro barely moves, because its positive correlation with rates offsets the effect of the equity fall. If the narrative calls for a flight into the US dollar, the modeller overrides that value and documents why. Expansion gives a consistent default; it does not replace judgment.

**Checking plausibility.** The Mahalanobis distance of the full scenario from the historical distribution (the same measure used in reverse stress testing) gives one number for how extreme it is. Comparing the distance of the designed scenario with that of historical crises helps answer "is this severe enough, and is it believable?"

**Common pitfalls.**

| Pitfall | Consequence | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| Correlations from calm periods | Spreads barely move in an equity crash | Estimate covariances on stressed windows, or blend |
| Missing factors | Positions without a shocked factor show zero loss | Coverage check: every risk factor used in pricing has a scenario value or a mapping rule |
| Inconsistent horizons | Shocks for a 10-day trading horizon applied to a 3-year banking book | Define the horizon and liquidity horizon per portfolio |
| Unchanged behaviour | Deposits behave as in normal times | Stress behavioural parameters along with market factors |
| Scenario never changes | The same scenario every year, positions adapt to it | Review annually against emerging risks |

**Engineering view.**

- Store scenarios as versioned data with their narrative, core variables, expansion method and approvals (the scenario library in Chapter 13.3).
- Run an automated coverage check before each run: list every risk factor in the portfolio without a scenario value.
- Keep the expansion code and its parameters with the scenario, so that the scenario can be regenerated exactly.
- Support fast ad-hoc scenarios. In March 2023 many banks were asked within days to rerun liquidity and rate scenarios inspired by SVB.

**Analogy.** Designing a scenario is like writing a disaster film script for an entire city. The writer sets the main events, but every street, hospital and power line must react consistently with them, or the audience stops believing the story.

**Key takeaways**

- Scenarios can be historical, hypothetical, hybrid or single-factor sensitivities; each has strengths and weaknesses.
- Good scenarios start with a narrative, fix a few core variables and expand consistently to all risk factors.
- Severity is calibrated against history, supervisory benchmarks and the current starting point.
- Conditional expansion and plausibility measures keep scenarios coherent; stressed correlations matter.
- Treat scenarios as versioned, approved data with automated coverage checks.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Classify each as historical, hypothetical, hybrid or sensitivity: (a) +200bp parallel shift; (b) March 2020 market moves applied to today's portfolio; (c) a 2008-style spread widening scaled to today's spread levels; (d) a cyber attack that stops a major RTGS for two days.
> 2. **Intermediate:** In the expansion example, change the equity shock from -30% to -10% while keeping rates at +120bp. Recompute the secondary factors (by reasoning or code) and explain whether the result is still consistent with a "stagflation" narrative.
> 3. **Interview:** "How would you design a scenario library so that a new ad-hoc scenario can be defined in the morning and results reported in the afternoon?" *Hint:* parameterized templates, automated expansion from core variables, coverage checks, cached base results with incremental revaluation, and a light but recorded approval step.

<a id="162-real-time-treasury"></a>
### 16.2 Real-Time Treasury

This subchapter covers the move from a treasury that sees the bank once a day, after the overnight batch, to one that sees and acts on positions continuously: real-time liquidity positions, streaming risk analytics, machine learning cash forecasts and automated funding decisions with human oversight.

#### Real-Time Liquidity Positions

**Why it matters.** Traditional treasury systems compute the liquidity position after the end-of-day batch: the cash ladder, the LCR and the funding gap are known the next morning. That rhythm no longer matches the world. Instant payments settle 24 hours a day, 7 days a week (SEPA Instant became mandatory for euro area payment service providers to send in October 2025), corporates move cash through APIs in seconds, and SVB lost USD 42bn in a single business day in 2023. Chapter 5.3 covered intraday liquidity for individual settlement accounts. A real-time liquidity position goes further: a continuously updated, bank-wide view of liquidity across accounts, currencies, legal entities and time buckets, including an estimate of the key ratios.

**From balances to a position.** A real-time position combines three layers:

| Layer | Content | Source | Certainty |
|---|---|---|---|
| Actual | Settled balances on central bank, nostro and internal accounts | RTGS and correspondent notifications (`camt.054`, `camt.052`), payment hub | High |
| Projected | Known future flows: scheduled payments, maturing trades, CLS pay-ins, coupon payments | Trade systems, payment queues, cash ladder | Medium (amendments, fails) |
| Expected | Statistical flows not yet known individually: client payments, deposit movements | Forecast models (next topic) | Low, given as ranges |

The end-of-day expected position for an account is:

```text
  expected_EOD = actual balance now
               + projected inflows  - projected outflows   (still to settle today)
               + expected net flows (forecast for the rest of the day, with a range)
```

**Architecture.**

```text
  Sources (events)                     Position service                     Consumers
  +---------------------+
  | RTGS / nostro msgs  |--+     +---------------------------------+     +-----------------+
  | Payment hub         |  |     | per account, currency, entity:  |     | Treasury        |
  | Trade booking       |--+---->|  actual, projected, expected    |---->| dashboard       |
  | CLS schedule        |  |     | per time bucket (today, D+1..)  |     +-----------------+
  | Deposit system      |--+     | estimated LCR, buffer, gaps     |     | Alerts, limits  |
  +---------------------+        | source freshness per feed       |     +-----------------+
           ^                     +----------------+----------------+     | Funding engine  |
           |                                      |                      +-----------------+
           |      reconciliation with             v
           +----- EOD official figures      event store + snapshots
```

**Estimating ratios intraday.** The official LCR is computed from the end-of-day balance sheet (Chapter 9.2). A real-time estimate starts from the last official LCR and applies the change in each component since then:

```text
  LCR_estimate = (HQLA_official + delta_HQLA) / (net_outflows_official + delta_net_outflows)

  delta_HQLA         = change in central bank cash + securities bought/sold or pledged
  delta_net_outflows = sum over deposit movements x (run-off rate of their category)
                       + new short-term wholesale funding maturing within 30 days, ...
```

**Example.** At 11:00 a large corporate client withdraws EUR 600m of non-operational deposits (40% run-off category) and moves it to another bank.

```text
                                      Official (yesterday EOD)   Real-time estimate 11:00
  HQLA (EUR m)                                  18,000                 17,400   (cash left)
  Net outflows over 30 days                     12,000                 11,760   (600 x 40% removed)
  LCR                                            150.0%                 148.0%
```

The LCR falls only two points, because the deposit had already been counted as a 40% outflow. If 20 such clients leave in a morning, as in a run, the estimate shows the trend hours before the official figure.

**Code sketch: an event-driven position.**

```python
from collections import defaultdict
from decimal import Decimal

class LiquidityPosition:
    def __init__(self):
        self.actual = defaultdict(Decimal)         # (entity, account, ccy) -> balance
        self.projected = defaultdict(Decimal)      # (entity, account, ccy, date) -> net flow
        self.seen = set()                          # processed event IDs (idempotency)
        self.last_event_at = {}                    # source -> timestamp, for staleness

    def apply(self, event):
        if event.id in self.seen:
            return                                 # duplicate delivery, ignore
        self.seen.add(event.id)
        key = (event.entity, event.account, event.currency)
        if event.kind == "SETTLED":                # money has actually moved
            self.actual[key] += event.signed_amount
            if event.was_scheduled:                # already in the projection: move it to actual
                self.projected[key + (event.value_date,)] -= event.signed_amount
        elif event.kind == "SCHEDULED":            # a known future flow
            self.projected[key + (event.value_date,)] += event.signed_amount
        elif event.kind == "CANCELLED":
            self.projected[key + (event.value_date,)] -= event.signed_amount
        self.last_event_at[event.source] = event.timestamp

    def expected_eod(self, key, today, forecast_net=Decimal("0")):
        return self.actual[key] + self.projected[key + (today,)] + forecast_net
```

When a scheduled flow settles, it moves from projected to actual, so the expected end-of-day figure does not change. Only surprises move it. In production, `seen` is a persistent store with expiry, and events carry sequence numbers per source so that gaps can be detected (Chapter 12.4).

**Design challenges.**

| Challenge | Why it is hard | Approach |
|---|---|---|
| Incomplete sources | Some correspondents send statements only at end of day | Show per source freshness; mark positions as partial |
| Double counting | The same payment is reported by the payment hub and by the RTGS | Match on end-to-end ID and UETR before applying; settle once |
| 24/7 operations | Instant payments flow at weekends while batch systems are down | Run the position service continuously; define what "end of day" means at weekends |
| Reconciliation | The real-time view drifts from the official ledger | Rebase daily on official EOD figures and report the difference |
| Legal entity and currency granularity | Liquidity in one entity may not be transferable to another | Keep positions per entity and currency; aggregate only where transfer is possible |

**Analogy.** An official end-of-day position is like a bank statement; a real-time position is like the balance in a banking app that also shows pending card payments and the salary you expect on Friday. Both are useful, but only the second helps you decide whether you can afford something right now.

**Key takeaways**

- Instant payments, APIs and digital runs make once-a-day liquidity positions too slow.
- A real-time position combines actual, projected and expected flows per account, currency, entity and time bucket.
- Ratios such as the LCR can be estimated intraday by applying deltas to the last official figure.
- Idempotent event processing, source freshness and daily rebasing on official figures are essential.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain the difference between actual, projected and expected flows, with one example of each for a EUR settlement account.
> 2. **Intermediate:** Using the LCR example, compute the real-time LCR estimate if 15 clients each withdraw EUR 600m of non-operational deposits during the morning (assume HQLA falls by the full amount).
> 3. **Interview:** "Design a real-time liquidity position for a bank with 12 legal entities, 35 currencies and instant payments 24/7." *Hint:* event sourcing per account with idempotent consumers, deduplication across sources, per-entity and per-currency positions with transferability rules, freshness indicators, weekend operating model, and daily reconciliation with the official ledger.

#### Streaming Risk Analytics

**Why it matters.** Risk numbers such as DV01 by tenor, FX net open positions and limit utilizations used to be computed overnight. Dealers and treasury managers now want them updated as trades are booked and markets move, so that they can hedge before a limit is breached rather than explain the breach the next morning. Stream processing makes this possible by computing aggregates incrementally on a continuous flow of events instead of recomputing everything from a database snapshot.

**Batch versus streaming.**

| Aspect | Batch | Streaming |
|---|---|---|
| Input | Complete snapshot of positions and market data | Unbounded sequence of trade, market and lifecycle events |
| Computation | Full recalculation | Incremental update of aggregates per event or per window |
| Latency | Hours | Milliseconds to seconds |
| Correctness | Easy to reason about: one consistent snapshot | Must handle late, duplicate and out-of-order events |
| Typical tools | Scheduled jobs on a compute grid | Kafka Streams, Apache Flink, Spark Structured Streaming |
| Typical treasury use | Official VaR, regulatory figures | Intraday sensitivities, NOP, limit utilization, P&L estimates |

**Key concepts.**

- **Event time and processing time:** event time is when the trade was executed; processing time is when the stream processor sees it. Aggregates for "trades up to 12:00" must use event time.
- **Windows:** tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping intervals, such as 1-minute buckets), sliding (overlapping) or session windows. Running totals such as a net position need no window at all; they are kept as state.
- **Watermarks:** a statement of the form "no more events older than T are expected". Results for a window are finalized when the watermark passes its end; later events are handled as corrections.
- **State:** the running aggregates, stored in a fault-tolerant store and checkpointed so that a restart neither loses nor double-counts events.
- **Exactly-once effect:** achieved by idempotent updates or transactional processing (Chapter 12.4); "exactly-once delivery" is not something networks provide.

**What can be computed incrementally.** Linear measures add up, so they are easy to stream. Non-linear measures need approximations.

| Measure | Incremental? | Streaming approach |
|---|---|---|
| FX net open position | Yes, sum of deltas per currency | Add each trade's amounts |
| DV01 by tenor bucket | Yes, for small moves | Add each trade's bucketed DV01 computed at booking |
| P&L estimate | Approximately | Sensitivities x market moves since start of day (Taylor expansion) |
| VaR | No | Add new trades' scenario P&L vectors to the morning vector, then recompute the quantile (Chapter 8.4) |
| CVA, exposure profiles | No | Periodic recomputation on a grid, triggered by material changes |

**Example: streaming DV01 with a limit check.**

```python
from collections import defaultdict

class StreamingDv01:
    def __init__(self, limits):
        self.dv01 = defaultdict(float)          # (book, tenor) -> EUR per bp
        self.limits = limits                    # (book, tenor) -> absolute limit
        self.applied = {}                       # trade_id -> (version, bucketed DV01)

    def on_trade_event(self, ev):
        prev = self.applied.get(ev.trade_id)    # (version, bucketed DV01) or None
        if prev and prev[0] >= ev.version:
            return []                           # duplicate or out-of-order old version
        old = prev[1] if prev else {}
        new = {} if ev.cancelled else ev.bucketed_dv01
        alerts = []
        # replace the previous version's contribution with the new one
        for tenor in old.keys() | new.keys():
            key = (ev.book, tenor)
            self.dv01[key] += new.get(tenor, 0.0) - old.get(tenor, 0.0)
            utilization = abs(self.dv01[key]) / self.limits[key]
            if utilization >= 0.8:
                alerts.append((key, round(utilization, 2)))
        self.applied[ev.trade_id] = (ev.version, new)
        return alerts
```

An amendment replaces the old contribution rather than adding to it, and a cancellation removes it. These lifecycle cases (Chapter 4.3) cause most of the bugs in streaming aggregates.

**Keeping streams honest.**

```text
  Start of day:  load official EOD positions and risk  -> state = official
  Intraday:      apply trade and market events          -> state = official + deltas
  End of day:    official batch recomputes everything
  Next morning:  compare streaming state at cut-off with the official result
                 -> difference per book and measure, investigated above tolerance
```

A systematic difference means missing events, a lifecycle bug or a model mismatch between the streaming and batch calculations. Monitoring this difference is the main correctness control of a streaming risk system.

**Analogy.** Batch risk is like counting all the people in a stadium by stopping everyone at the gate once an hour. Streaming risk is like a turnstile counter that updates with every person: much faster, but only correct if the turnstiles never double-count, never miss anyone and are reconciled with a full count from time to time.

**Key takeaways**

- Streaming analytics update risk measures incrementally as trades and market data arrive.
- Linear measures (positions, bucketed sensitivities) stream easily; non-linear ones (VaR, CVA) need approximations or periodic recomputation.
- Event time, watermarks, checkpointed state and idempotent updates are the core concepts.
- Amendments and cancellations must replace earlier contributions, not add to them.
- Reconcile the streaming state with the official batch every day.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** Explain the difference between event time and processing time, and give a treasury example where using processing time gives a wrong answer.
> 2. **Intermediate:** A trade is booked with a 5Y DV01 of EUR 12,000, amended to EUR 18,000 and then cancelled. Show the state of the 5Y bucket after each event in the example class, and what happens if the amendment arrives before the original booking.
> 3. **Interview:** "Our intraday DV01 dashboard and the official overnight figure differ by 3% every day. How would you investigate?" *Hint:* compare at trade level, look for missing event types (lifecycle events, fixings, maturities), market data timing differences, model differences between the incremental and full calculations, and trades booked directly in downstream systems.

#### Predictive Cash Forecasting with Machine Learning

**Why it matters.** Chapter 5.2 described cash flow forecasting with contractual flows and behavioural assumptions. A large part of daily cash movements is not contractual: corporate clients' payment habits, retail spending around payday, tax dates, seasonal patterns. Treasuries traditionally forecast these with averages and expert adjustments. Machine learning (ML) models can find patterns in years of transaction history and give more accurate forecasts with uncertainty ranges. Better forecasts mean smaller precautionary buffers, cheaper funding and earlier warning when actual flows deviate from normal.

**What is being forecast.** Typical targets are net flows per day (or per hour) for an account, client segment, currency or entity, over horizons from intraday to a few weeks. The forecast should be a distribution, not a single number: treasury cares most about the bad tail (an unexpectedly large outflow), so quantiles such as the 5th and 95th percentile matter more than the mean.

**Features.**

| Feature group | Examples |
|---|---|
| Calendar | Day of week, day of month, month end, quarter end, holidays in each relevant calendar, days since last business day |
| Known events | Payroll dates, tax payment dates, dividend dates, large scheduled payments |
| History | Lagged flows (1, 5, 20 days), rolling means and volatilities |
| Client and product | Segment, product type, number of active clients, balances |
| Market and macro | Policy rate, money market fund yields (they drive deposit migration), FX rates |

**Model choices.**

| Approach | Strengths | Weaknesses | Typical role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Moving averages, seasonal naive | Simple, transparent | Misses interactions | Baseline that every model must beat |
| Statistical time series (ARIMA, exponential smoothing) | Well understood, gives intervals | One series at a time, limited features | Stable, aggregate series |
| Gradient boosted trees (LightGBM, XGBoost) | Handles many features and interactions, strong on tabular data | Needs feature engineering, intervals via quantile loss | Main workhorse for segment-level forecasts |
| Neural networks (LSTM, temporal fusion transformers) | Learn complex patterns across many series | Data hungry, harder to explain and validate | Very large portfolios of similar series |

**Example: quantile forecasts with gradient boosting.**

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit

def make_features(df):
    out = pd.DataFrame(index=df.index)
    out["dow"] = df.index.dayofweek
    out["dom"] = df.index.day
    out["month_end"] = df.index.is_month_end.astype(int)
    out["payroll"] = df["payroll_day"].astype(int)
    out["tax_day"] = df["tax_day"].astype(int)
    for lag in (1, 5, 20):
        out[f"lag_{lag}"] = df["net_flow"].shift(lag)       # only past values: no leakage
    out["vol_20"] = df["net_flow"].shift(1).rolling(20).std()
    return out.dropna()

X = make_features(history)
y = history.loc[X.index, "net_flow"]

models = {q: GradientBoostingRegressor(loss="quantile", alpha=q, n_estimators=300, max_depth=3)
          for q in (0.05, 0.5, 0.95)}

# walk-forward validation: always train on the past and test on the following period
for train_idx, test_idx in TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5).split(X):
    for q, m in models.items():
        m.fit(X.iloc[train_idx], y.iloc[train_idx])
    # evaluate pinball loss per quantile and the coverage of the 5-95% interval ...
```

The 5% quantile is the "bad day" outflow that treasury plans against. Coverage tells you whether the interval is honest: about 90% of actual flows should fall between the 5% and 95% forecasts.

**Evaluation.**

| Metric | What it measures |
|---|---|
| MAE, RMSE | Error of the point forecast |
| MAPE | Relative error; unstable when flows are close to zero, which net flows often are |
| Pinball (quantile) loss | Quality of each quantile forecast |
| Interval coverage | Share of actual values inside the predicted interval |
| Improvement over baseline | Does the model beat the seasonal naive forecast, consistently and by segment |

**Pitfalls.**

- **Data leakage:** using information not available at forecast time (a same-day balance, a feature computed with future data). Walk-forward validation and point-in-time feature stores prevent it.
- **Regime shifts:** models trained in 2015-2021, when rates were near zero, failed to anticipate the deposit migration of 2022-2023. Monitor drift and include rate-sensitive features.
- **Stress is out of sample:** ML models learn normal behaviour. They are not stress models. Treasury must still use stress scenarios (Chapter 16.1) for buffers.
- **Hierarchy consistency:** forecasts for segments should add up to the forecast for the entity. Use hierarchical reconciliation methods.

**Governance.** A forecasting model used for liquidity decisions is a model under model risk management (for example SR 11-7 in the US and the PRA's SS1/23 in the UK): documented, independently validated, monitored, with explainability (such as feature importance or SHAP values) so that treasury understands why the forecast changed. Keep a human override with an audit trail.

**Analogy.** An ML cash forecast is like a weather forecast. It is very good at predicting tomorrow's normal weather, and it gives a probability of rain rather than a promise. It is not designed to predict a once-in-a-century storm; for that you still build sea walls (buffers and stress tests).

**Key takeaways**

- ML models forecast non-contractual cash flows from calendar, event, history and market features.
- Forecast distributions (quantiles), not only point values; treasury plans against the bad tail.
- Validate with walk-forward tests against a simple baseline, and check interval coverage.
- Guard against leakage, regime shifts and over-reliance on models in stress.
- Treat the model as a governed model: validation, monitoring, explainability and overrides.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **Beginner:** List five features you would use to forecast daily net flows on retail current accounts, and explain why each might help.
> 2. **Intermediate:** A model's 5-95% interval contains the actual flow on 72% of days in the test period. What does this tell you, and how would you fix it?
> 3. **Interview:** "Our ML forecast was very accurate for two years and then underestimated outflows for six months in a row. What happened and what would you change?" *Hint:* regime shift (rates, competition, a client event), drift monitoring, features that capture the driver, retraining policy, and the difference between forecasting and stress testing.

#### Automated Funding Decisions

**Why it matters.** Once a treasury has real-time positions and reliable forecasts, the next question is whether routine funding decisions can be automated: placing surplus cash overnight, borrowing to cover a forecast shortfall, choosing between repo, central bank facilities and intragroup loans, or rebalancing between currencies. Manual decisions are slow, especially at weekends with instant payments, and depend on the dealer on duty. Automation can be faster, cheaper and more consistent, but a wrong automated decision can move billions in seconds. The engineering challenge is to automate within strict guardrails.

**Levels of automation.**

| Level | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 0. Information | System shows positions and forecasts; humans decide | Liquidity dashboard |
| 1. Recommendation | System proposes actions; a dealer approves each one | "Borrow EUR 300m O/N in repo against Bund collateral" |
| 2. Automated with limits | System executes within pre-approved limits; humans monitor and can stop it | Automatic overnight placement of surplus up to EUR 500m with approved counterparties |
| 3. Fully automated | System decides and executes without routine human involvement | Intragroup sweeps between accounts of the same entity |

Most banks today operate at levels 1 and 2 for market funding and at level 3 only for internal sweeps and cash pooling (Chapter 10.2).

**Funding as an optimization problem.** Covering a shortfall at minimum cost, subject to constraints, is a linear program.

```text
  Minimize    sum over sources i of  cost_i x amount_i
  Subject to  sum of amount_i                    >= shortfall
              0 <= amount_i                      <= capacity_i     (limits, available collateral)
              amount from one counterparty group <= concentration limit
              LCR after funding                  >= internal target
```

**Example.** A forecast shortfall of EUR 900m for tomorrow, with four sources:

| Source | Cost (bp over €STR) | Capacity (EUR m) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Repo against government bonds | 2 | 500 | Uses unencumbered collateral |
| Unsecured interbank | 12 | 600 | Counterparty limits apply |
| Intragroup loan from parent | 8 | 300 | Subject to large exposure rules |
